The authors call it Cynarctus fortidens, a new species, in volume 14, number 10, pages 135 to 138.

The holotype, a right upper jaw with three teeth numbered 11353 in Kansas collections, came from a bluff on the west side of Turkey Creek, about seventy-five feet above the stream. Dalquest collected it on June 25, 1960, on the Raymond Farr Ranch in Donley County, near Clarendon, from Clarendon fauna of early Pliocene age. Two figures support the brief, technical description.
30635-the-talking-thrush-and-other-tales:
The Talking Thrush and Other Tales from India, collected by W. Crooke and retold by W. H. Drouse, illustrated by W. H. Robinson, was first published in October 1899 and reprinted in July 1902 and October 1922. An illustration warns that a crow is a crow forever, setting the tone for animal wisdom tales.

Contents open with the talking thrush, the rabbit and the monkey, the sparrow's revenge, and the judgment of the jackal. How the mouse got into his hole, King Solomon and the owl, the camel's neck, and the quail and the fowler follow. The king of the kites, the jackal and the camel, and the wise old shepherd close the named tales. Drouse retells Indian folk tales with clarity and humor.
30747-seaport-in-virginia-george-washing:
Gay Montague Moore wrote this history of Alexandria, Virginia, as George Washington knew it, published by the University Press of Virginia with a 1949 copyright and a second printing in 1972. Drawings by Worth Bailey and photographs by Walter Wilcox fill the volume. Moore dedicates it to her husband Charles Beatty Moore, with whom she delved into records that might throw some shadow of those who built and lived in Alexandria's old houses.

The book follows the seaport through its prologue and its growth, using houses, families, and town life to show how Washington's Alexandria worked. It is local history at its best: close, documented, and full of people rather than bare dates. Readers who love Virginia, Washington, or old American towns will find a rich guide to streets and homes that still carry their past.
30888-the-american-church-dictionary-and:
Rev. William James Miller, master of arts and bachelor of divinity, compiled this American Church Dictionary and Cyclopedia, published by Thomas Whittaker in New York in 1901. It is a reference book for churchgoers and clergy, giving short entries in alphabetical order on worship, doctrine, and church practice. Its entries cite rubrics, scripture, and the ordination office, so readers can see where a usage comes from.

Early entries show the method: Ablutions names the ceremonial washing of sacred vessels after Holy Communion, with holy wine and water reverently consumed by the priest. Absolution gives the forgiveness of sins through bishops and priests, with the ordination words on forgiving and retaining sins. It is a useful, old-fashioned guide to American church language and custom.
31096-the-lily-and-the-cross-a-tale-of-a:
Professor James De Mille, author of The Dodge Club, Cord and Creese, and the B. O. W. C. stories, wrote this tale of Acadia, published by Lee and Shepard in Boston in 1874, with pictures. Its frontispiece shows a meeting in mid ocean. Its twenty-six chapters run from A Voice Out of the Deep and A Meeting in Mid Ocean through New Friends, Mimi and Margot, and A Strange Revelation. They end with A French Frigate, Caught in a Trap, and Under Arrest.

Later chapters bring Grand Pré, Alone in the World, A Friend in Need, The Parson among the Philistines, A Stroke for Liberty, and The Manoeuvres of Zac. They continue with Flight, Reunion, Among Friends, and Louisbourg. The tale opens with a schooner belonging to Boston, registered under the name of the Reverend Amos Adams. It is a romance of Acadia, with captives, escapes, and a court martial.
31728-my-brave-and-gallant-gentleman-a-r:
Robert Watson's 1918 romance of British Columbia, published at Toronto, follows a second son. He grows up hearing that Lady Rosemary Granton will someday marry the man who would become Earl of Brammerton and Hazelmere. The narrator, merely the Honourable second son, faces that supposed calamity without much mental agony.

Twenty-six chapters carry him from second sons and a blacksmith named Jim to a viscount captain of the guards. They continue through a coaster voyage, a millionaire, a beach, a fight in the woods, and a knight proved true. Readers get a light adventure romance of the Canadian west, full of rivals, songs, and seaside scrapes.
31923-the-pearl-of-india:
Maturin M. Ballou's Pearl of India, in its second edition of 1895 with copyright in 1894, is a travel book on Ceylon, gem of the Orient. Ballou's preface says readers show growing satisfaction in contemplating foreign lands through the eyes of experienced travelers, and that both author and reader are gratified by such a work.

Asked which place of all he has seen he recommends, Ballou answers that no point presents more varied attractions to the observant traveler. No point more thoroughly exhibits equatorial life than Ceylon, accessible, safe, and healthy for the stranger. Readers get a Victorian travelogue of the fabled isle of Arabian story, for artist, botanist, antiquarian, scientist, and sportsman alike.
32129-area-handbook-for-albania:
Area Handbook for Albania, published in January 1971 as DA PAM 550-98, is a United States Army reference work on Albania, prepared by the Foreign Area Studies program at the American University. Its co-authors were Eugene K. Keefe, Sarah Jane Elpern, William Giloane, James M. Moore, Junior, Stephen Peters, and Eston T. White. Research and writing were completed on July 17, 1970, and the handbook sold for $2.50 through the Government Printing Office.

Its country summary states the essentials: the People's Republic of Albania. Albanians call it Shqiperia. It has been a national state since 1912, and under Communist control after 1944. Government follows the Party-state model of the Soviet Union, with the People's Assembly as highest state organ and the Albanian Workers' Party paralleling government at every level. Readers get a Cold War reference handbook, systematic and official in tone.
32178-los-gringos-or-an-inside-view-of-m:
Lieutenant Wise of the United States Navy published Los Gringos in New York in 1849, with Baker and Scribner. Its full title promises an inside view of Mexico and California, with wanderings in Peru, Chili, and Polynesia. The book belongs to the travel literature of the Mexican-American War era. Wise saw those coasts at first hand, rather than from a library.

Wise's preface begins with his title, Los Gringos, and the volume that follows offers an American sailor's view of Mexican and Californian life, then of South American and Pacific wanderings. Readers get a period eyewitness account: Mexico and California as a serving officer found them in the late 1840s, with Peru, Chile, and Polynesian stops completing a wide Pacific circuit.
32268-the-burning-of-chambersburg-pennsy:
Reverend B. S. Schneck's The Burning of Chambersburg, Pennsylvania, subtitled by an eye-witness and a sufferer, tells of July 30, 1864, when a town of six thousand people was burned. Schneck adds corroborative statements from seven others. They are the Reverend J. Clark, the Honourable A. K. McClure, J. Hoke, the Reverend T. G. Apple, the Reverend B. Bausman, the Reverend S. J. Niccolls, and J. K. Shryock. A notice tells how contributions for the sufferers arrived from friends and strangers abroad.

The citizens, Schneck writes, stated that a demanded sum could not be paid in gold or currency, and could not have been made in good faith. They remonstrated against burning a town as a monstrosity. The burning followed burnings in certain Virginia counties by General Hunter. The raiders, McCausland, Bradley Johnson, and Gilmore, commanded three thousand cavalry with artillery. Readers get a Civil War atrocity narrative, vivid and corroborated.
32507-the-planters-of-colonial-virginia:
Thomas J. Wertenbaker's Planters of Colonial Virginia, copyrighted in 1922 and reissued in 1959, studies the men who built Virginia's plantation society. Chapters move from England in the New World and the Indian weed, meaning tobacco, through the Virginia yeomanry, freemen and freedmen, and the Restoration period. Later chapters treat the yeoman in Virginia history, world trade, and life beneath the black tide, with notes, an appendix, and an index.

Wertenbaker writes from Princeton, where the book was revised in August 1957, and his account stresses land, labour, trade, and social rank. Tobacco, indenture, and the growth of a planter class shape the colony's politics and daily life. The book remains a standard, readable history for readers who want colonial Virginia explained through its planters and their world.
32573-history-of-the-colony-and-ancient-:
Charles Campbell's History of the Colony and Ancient Dominion of Virginia, published in Philadelphia in 1860, follows Virginia from early voyages of discovery through its colonial centuries. Campbell opens with Sir Walter Raleigh's colony, Captain John Smith's early life and adventures, and the landing at Jamestown.

Later chapters treat Smith's explorations and administration, the Indians of Virginia, the sufferings of the colonists, the wreck of the Sea-Venture, Pocahontas in England, and successive governors. Campbell takes Lord Bacon's maxim as his rule, to present events and counsels and leave observations to the reader's judgment.
32627-area-handbook-for-bulgaria:
Eugene K. Keefe and coauthors prepared this Area Handbook for Bulgaria for the Foreign Area Studies program of American University, with research completed in August 1973 and publication in 1974. A country summary opens with size, place, and people: 42,800 square miles, about 8.7 million people in 1973, and borders with Romania, Yugoslavia, Greece, and Turkey.

Four sections then cover social life, politics, economics, and national security in turn. Readers find chapters on land and climate, ethnic groups, faith, government, schooling, and the budget, making the book a compact reference for a country then ruled by its Communist Party.
32700-area-handbook-for-romania:
This handbook on Romania comes from the Foreign Area Studies program, with research completed in February 1972 and publication the same year. Eugene K. Keefe led its coauthors. A country summary gives the shape of the state: over 91,700 square miles, almost 20.6 million people in 1971, and land borders with Bulgaria, Yugoslavia, Hungary, and the Soviet Union.

Sections on social life, politics, national security, and economics follow. Chapters trace the 1965 constitution, Communist Party control, the Carpathians and plains, minorities, labor, and prisons, giving a full reference portrait of Romania in the early 1970s.
32708-the-golden-age-in-transylvania:
Maurus Jókai sets this historical romance in Transylvania near the close of the seventeenth century, translated by S. L. and A. V. Waite. The scene opens with a hunting party in 1666 and follows Prince Michel Apafi, placed on the throne by the Turks, to the murder of Denis Banfi, the last great Transylvanian baron.

Nineteen chapters move through courts, diets, battles, and banquet-hall justice, with figures such as Azraele and Corsar caught in love, fear, and war. Jókai paints wild Carpathian land, proud lords, and sudden turns of fate. The book was praised as his best, and it reads as a full, stirring chronicle.
32755-peasant-tales-of-russia:
V. I. Nemirovitch-Dantchenko offers four peasant tales of Russia, translated by Claud Field and published in London by Robert Scott in 1917. The contents run from the deserted mine through Mahmoud's family and a misunderstanding to the luck of Ivan the Forgetful.

The first tale opens at the Voskressensky mine at dawn, where silent miners in leather jerkins carry flickering lamps to descend into darkness. Old Ivan, thin and withered, insists on going down with them. Later tales follow Mahmoud Bey, a Turkish prisoner talking of families and flight from Adrianople, and Ivan the Forgetful, creeping through a warm spring night toward liberty.
33038-due-north-or-glimpses-of-scandinav:
Maturin M. Ballou's Due North, or Glimpses of Scandinavia and Russia, follows the author's earlier Due South on Cuba, and offers travel sketches from the far north. Ballou opens with the thought that only traveling which reveals the value of home and lets a traveler enjoy it better is truly good. His glimpses take readers through Norway, Sweden, Denmark, and Russia, with notes on castles, canals, and cities whose names he spells as he heard them.

The book is a traveler's notebook rather than a formal history, full of sights, people, and comparisons that a nineteenth-century American reader would enjoy. Its charm lies in Ballou's easy, observant voice and in the period detail of steamers, hotels, and northern light. For readers planning a mental journey north, or studying how Americans saw Scandinavia before modern tourism, it remains an engaging guide.
33272-green-spring-farm-fairfax-county-v:
Ross and Nan Netherton's history traces Green Spring Farm in Fairfax County, Virginia, from the Moss family of freeholders between 1770 and 1835. Orchard and dairy years under Fountain Beattie follow, to the end of the farming era under Michael Straight. Published in June 1970, it pairs historical notes with a full architectural study of the mansion house, the Tobey house, the barn, the log cabin, and the spring house.

The volume adds appendixes with a landmarks survey form, a summary of ownership, and old wills and inventories, making it useful for both visitors and researchers. Its tone is plain and local, rooted in deeds and buildings rather than legend. For readers of Virginia history, it is a thorough guide to one farm and to the county's changing land.
33306-the-king-of-arcadia:
Francis Lynde's novel, published in 1909, bears the title The King of Arcadia, a tale of a man who seeks a pastoral ideal in a modern world. Lynde, author of A Romance in Transit and The Quickening, writes of love, duty, and the pull of a simpler life. A heroine pleads for help in the book's opening scenes. The story is inscribed to his daughter Dorothea, whose loving heart and willing hands aided its writing.

The novel blends romance with a gentle satire of modern haste, as its king of Arcadia tries to hold to his dream against practical claims. Lynde's prose is clear and warm, suited to readers who like a story with both feeling and wit. For fans of early twentieth-century romance, it is a pleasant, well-told tale of an ideal tested by life.
33450-journal-of-a-trip-to-california:
C. W. Smith's Journal of a Trip to California, across the continent from Weston, Missouri, to Weber Creek, California, in the summer of 1850, records a gold-rush journey. Smith writes day by day of the trail, its hardships, and its hopes, in a journal made for readers who wanted the West as travelers lived it. The e-text draws on page images from the Internet Archive.

The journal's value lies in its plain, first-hand detail, from river crossings to camp life, told by a man on the road to gold. Its tone is honest and unadorned, suited to students of the overland trail. For readers of California history, it is a vivid, short record of a summer that changed many lives.
33480-under-fire-for-servia:
Colonel James Fiske, writing the fourth volume of his World's War series, sends American boy Dick Warner into the opening weeks of the First World War. Dick reaches Semlin, a border town in Hungary across the Save river from Belgrade, just as refugees pour through after Austria-Hungary's ultimatum to Servia. A visit to the busy American consul starts a chain of dangerous errands.

Across nineteen chapters Dick makes friends, survives a police raid, crosses rivers, rescues a wounded captain, and matches wits with enemy agents. The story moves between Semlin and Belgrade and builds toward flight, explosion, and a final confrontation. It is a boys' adventure tale grounded in the real geography and early wartime tension of the Balkans.
33484-valeria-the-martyr-of-the-catacomb:
W. H. Withrow draws on years of study of the Roman catacombs to tell a story of early Christian life in Rome. His heroine Valeria lives among believers who worship in secret, bury their dead in underground passages, and face arrest, torture, and death for their faith. The preface states his aim plainly: a popular account of primitive Christian character, kept as accurate as his research allowed.

The tale moves between the catacombs, where inscriptions and tombs mark the martyrs, and the pagan city above, where emperors and officials enforce the old gods. Valeria's courage becomes the thread that links scenes of worship, friendship, and persecution. Readers interested in early church history will find both a story and an introduction to what the catacombs reveal about that community.
33748-the-kitchen-encyclopedia:
Swift and Company issued this Kitchen Encyclopedia, twelfth edition, copyrighted in 1911, promising many helpful suggestions, all tried and practical, for ready reference in the kitchen. The volume opens as an advertisement for Swift's Premium Oleomargarine, described as a sweet, pure, clean spread made from rich cream and edible fats. It holds every nutrient found in the best creamery butter.

The book explains that butter fat in oleomargarine matches butter down to the microscope and the chemistry, differing only in how it is secured. These include part by churning, the rest pressed from choice fat of government-inspected animals, called oleo, with rich cream, fancy creamery butter, neutral, vegetable oil, and dairy salt as its only ingredients. Beyond its salesmanship, the encyclopedia preserves period recipes, household advice, and the food industry's early self-presentation.
33753-in-paths-of-peril-a-boy-s-adventur:
J. Macdonald Oxley, author of Donalblane of Darien, writes a boy's adventures in Nova Scotia in this 1903 Toronto book, with six illustrations. Twelve chapters run from the old world to the new, through a great bear hunt, setting a bad example, off to the woods, a moose hunt, in the nick of time.

The story opens with the Huguenot defence of La Rochelle. For more than a year the defenders defied the whole power of France under Cardinal Richelieu, enduring hunger, battle, and pestilence for their faith. From that heroic background, Oxley follows Raoul and his companions through wilderness peril. Young readers and lovers of historical adventure will enjoy its bears, moose, and loyal comradeship.
33812-the-aboriginal-population-of-the-n:
S. F. Cook wrote this University of California study of native peoples along the north coast, issued in 1956. It builds on A. L. Kroeber's 1925 handbook and offers estimates group by group: Yurok, Wiyot, Karok, Hupa, Tolowa, Pomo, Yuki, and many smaller peoples, with a summary of totals at the end.

Cook weighs old reports, mission records, and later counts to judge how many people lived in each area before contact. The work is careful and plain about its limits, and its tables still guide students of California native history. It remains a key source for the size and spread of coastal peoples.
33963-the-valiants-of-virginia:
Hallie Erminie Rives wrote this Virginia romance, copyrighted in 1912 by the Bobbs-Merrill Company, with color pictures by Andre Castaigne. John Valiant comes to Damory Court and finds a family past, a crash, and a secret thirty years old. Chapters follow a hunt, a trespass, a tournament day, and a Virginian Runnymede.

Love, pride, and old wrongs braid through the tale, as Katharine and John weigh what the past demands of them. Rives writes with color and feeling for old Virginia houses and customs. The novel remains a lush, old-fashioned romance of the South.
34015-the-coast-of-bohemia:
Thomas Nelson Page published this book of poems in New York in 1906, with copyrights in 1888 and 1906. The title poem opens a set that runs from The Voice of the Sea and Long Roll at Napoleon's Tomb to Youth, America, and poems on Matthew Arnold and his mother. A closing section gives dialect poems from Befo' de War.

Page moves between high lyric, memory, and Southern dialect voices, with Uncle Gabe and other figures from the old South. The book shows a Virginia writer in two modes: polished verse and folk speech. It remains a varied sample of Page's poetry.
34138-lady-maude-s-mania:
George Manville Fenn wrote this comic novel of a high family, opening with the Earl of Barmouth and his son, Viscount Diphoos, cursing street organs and their grinders. The viscount, heels on the library chimney-piece in a Portland Place mansion, smokes a cigar to steady himself for what he calls the operation. His father, plagued by gout, fears her ladyship may faint on return from church.

Tom, the viscount, grins at the scene his father pictures, recalling a wedding twenty-six years past, since when his mother grew stouter and his father thinner. Fenn writes with broad, cheerful humor. The novel offers a light comedy of an aristocratic household.
34196-porzia:
Cale Young Rice's 1913 verse play Porzia is set at Naples in about 1570, on the wedding day of Rizzio di Rossi, a young leader of men of letters suspected of heresy. His wife Porzia stands at the centre, between her husband, her kin, and officers of the Inquisition.

Giordano Bruno appears among the cast, and the play turns on faith, loyalty, and the risks of free thought under church watch. Rice writes in verse throughout, with terrace, garden, and bay views framing scenes of love, debate, and danger for a household under suspicion. The play is dedicated to Gilbert Murray.
34312-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
The Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition, called itself a dictionary of arts, sciences, literature, and general information. This file holds volume two, slice eight, running from Atherstone to Austria. The eleventh edition, issued in 1910 and 1911, is often ranked the finest general encyclopaedia in English.

The slice's article list maps its range. Town articles such as Atherstone, Athlone, and Atlantic City stand beside Athletic Sports and the Atlantic Ocean. Atlantis gets its entry, as do the Atlas Mountains, the atmosphere, and Augsburg. Lives include the naturalist Audubon, the novelist Auerbach, and the composer Audran. Long articles carry the edition's learning, while short ones fix names, dates, and places. Researchers still mine this edition for the state of knowledge on the eve of the Great War.
34455-give-me-liberty-the-struggle-for-s:
Give Me Liberty is a study of the fight for self rule in Virginia by Thomas Wertenbaker. Wertenbaker held a chair of the past of the United States at a famed school. The book came out in nineteen fifty-eight as part of a set of tracts of a lore guild. A paint of the great statesman of Virginia heads the book.

The front note holds that the far lands were the most free folk in the world in their day. They fought not to gain new rights but to keep the rights they had. Past long years they had ruled their own lives, and they would not bow when heads in London sought to rule them from far. To grasp the hearts of the great men of that fight, one must trace how self rule grew in the lands, the book says.
34485-the-circassian-chief-a-romance-of-:
The Circassian Chief is a romance of Russia by Kingston, told in two volumes of travel and war. The tale opens on the road between the old and new capitals of the empire. Two young horsemen ride south on a rough track of ruts and swamps. Their talk and bearing mark them as men of high station.

One rider has dark flashing eyes, black hair, and Grecian features. The other laughs with blue eyes and a fair face. Both wear half military dress, with pistols and heavy riding whips. They send their baggage cart ahead to Tver for the night. The pair will follow at leisure through brightening country. Kingston wrote many tales of adventure for boys. This one turns toward the Caucasus wars of the tsars.
3467-the-life-of-cesare-borgia:
Rafael Sabatini writes a life of Cesare Borgia, Duke of Valentinois and captain general of the Church, in Renaissance Italy. Sabatini warns that his book is no chronicle of saints and no history of devils. Instead it records very human, striving men in a lustful, flamboyant age, red with blood and pale with passion, an age of steel and velvet.

The narrative follows Borgia's rise with his father Pope Alexander the Sixth, his campaigns in Romagna, and his fall after his father's death. Sabatini judges Borgia by the standards of his own time rather than by modern morals. The book suits readers who want a vivid, readable life of one of history's most debated figures.
34813-caravans-by-night-a-romance-of-ind:
Harry Hervey wrote Caravans by Night, a romance of India held in 1922 and reprinted in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. A verse wish at the front asks for a tale woven on the loom of Asia, so readers at home may feel the glare and spice of its cities. Hervey gave the book to his mother.

The tale opens at the Great Bazaar of Indore, west of the Old Palace, with a rich silk and jewel dealer in a gold edged turban. Talk of a fair haired stranger and a blue eyed Punjabi dries him up at once, for a strange hand once touched his life. Fourteen parts move through Delhi, a house of the swaying cobra, fever, and a caravan to Gyangtse.
34848-mammals-of-the-san-gabriel-mountai:
Mammals of the San Gabriel Mountains surveys the beasts of one California range. Terry Vaughan wrote the study for the University of Kansas press. It came out in 1954 as a museum of natural history paper. Plates, tables, and a figure pack its seventy pages of text. The San Gabriels rise behind the Los Angeles basin in that state.

The study sorts the range into plant zones and beast groupings. Coastal sage scrub and oak woodland zones come first in its plan. Chaparral, yellow pine woods, and pinyon lands follow in the scheme. Sagebrush scrub and Joshua tree woodland close the zone list. Each mammal kind is then placed by the ground it haunts. Field notes and counts back the placing of each kind in turn.
35369-the-highlands-of-ethiopia:
Sir William Cornwallis Harris wrote The Highlands of Ethiopia, in a second form dated 1844 in London. Harris opens this form with two tasks that pull in two ways. He must thank the press for its warm and free praise of his work. He must also answer the jabs of one or two sheets of small rank.

Praise in such force, he says, drove him to comb his work with care for this form. He vows he has used the jabs of his foes as a spur to do better. Foes he has, and of a fierce and keen sort, he adds with heat. Their charges come in three kinds, he says. They fault his rich, high style as dark and hard to read. They fault the truth of some of his facts. They fault the lack of new facts the crowd felt was its due.
35447-comrades-a-story-of-social-adventu:
Comrades, a story of social adventure in California, is a novel by Thomas Dixon, published in 1909. Grosset and Dunlap issued this edition at New York, the copyright resting with Dixon. The book is dedicated to the author daughter Louise, the dearest little girl in the world.

Contents list thirty six chapters for the tale of a socialist venture in the West. The Woman in Red, A New Joan of Arc, and The Birth of a Man open the story in order. Among the Shadows, The Island of Ventura, and The Red Flag carry the colony into being in the list. Dixon novel argues against the socialist colonies then forming in California by showing one from inside. His Joan of Arc figure leads the faithful to an island heaven that turns, by his telling, into a school of human nature at its most selfish.
35454-o-thou-my-austria:
O Thou, My Austria is a novel by Ossip Schubin, turned from the German by Mrs. Wister and printed at Philadelphia in 1897. Copyright was held from 1890. The tale runs long, through forty-five chapters, and opens with a stolen piece of writing whose contents set the plot in motion.

Chapter heads move from a garrison town to a graveyard in Paris and back to Komaritz. Names recur across the heads: Baroness Paula, Olga, Lato Treurenberg, and Count Hans. Love, pride, and rank drive the turns, with quarrels, secrets, and a slanderer to be faced. The book gives English readers a full taste of Austrian society fiction.
35576-in-the-days-of-queen-victoria:
In the Days of Queen Victoria is a biography for the young by Eva March Tappan, printed at Boston in 1903. It belongs to the Makers of England series. The frontispiece shows the Queen in her state robes, from a painting of 1838. The chapters begin with Baby Drina and the schooldays of a princess.

Examination day follows, then a queen at eighteen and the coronation. The coming of the Prince, housekeeping in a palace, and a home of our own carry the story through Victoria's marriage. Later chapters treat the royal young people, the Queen in sorrow, and the little folk. Mother and empress, the jubilee season, and the closing years end the book. Pictures from famous paintings, engravings, and photographs illustrate it. Tappan wrote the lives of England's makers for school readers, and this volume brings the great Queen's long reign down to a child's scale.
35615-the-treasure-of-the-tigris-a-tale-:
Treasure of the Tigris is a tale of Mesopotamia by Mockler Ferryman. Black of London first published the adventure in nineteen o eight. Allan Stewart drew eight full page pictures in colour for the book. Ferryman also wrote Life Story of a Tiger and Hemmed In tales.

Chapters open with instructions, then cross Mesopotamia into the desert waste. Guests of the Aeniza, raiders, and the sheik story fill the early trek. The fire of the gods and Raspul the seer bring in old temple lore. A dash for freedom, rival doctors, and war alarm build the middle. The trail of the serpent, the devil well, and reunion close it.
35690-omens-and-superstitions-of-souther:
Edgar Thurston wrote Omens and Superstitions of Southern India for Fisher Unwin of London in 1912. He drew on his years running the Madras Government Museum and the Ethnographic Survey of the Madras Presidency. Photographs of offerings, yantrams, and exorcists illustrate the book.

Twelve chapters treat omens, animal superstitions, the evil eye, snake worship, vows and votive offerings, charms, and human sacrifice. Magic, divination, fortune-telling, farm ceremonies, and rain-making ceremonies close the survey. The opening chapter explains the so-called science of omens, kept in native calendars, and the signs read from a throbbing arm or eye, a topic the Hindu classics themselves discuss. Thurston records the beliefs as he found them, with cases and local detail.
35745-the-religion-of-the-indians-of-cal:
The Religion of the Indians of California, by Kroeber, was issued at Berkeley in September 1907 as volume 4, number 6 of the University of California Publications in American Archaeology and Ethnology. Kroeber opens with a broad claim: the faith of these Indians matched that of early peoples the world over. Its ground was animism, the belief that life, mind, and power dwell in living and lifeless things alike.

With animism came shamanism, the faith that certain men can do what daily life cannot. Belief in shaman power bore hardest on sickness and death, which most tribes blamed on shamans outright. Kroeber notes what set California apart: dancing and song filled its public rites, yet picture writing and rich ritual stayed weak. The study is an early landmark of California ethnology.
36006-diphtheria:
Diphtheria is a short pamphlet of the United States Public Health Service, issued at Washington in 1919. It is number four in the Keep Well series. Its cover promises three things: how to know the disease, how to keep from catching it, and how to treat those who do catch it. The first page speaks straight to parents.

After babyhood has passed, it warns, beware of diphtheria. More than a seventh of deaths among children of three and four came from it. The pamphlet calls the disease preventable and, with antitoxin, curable. Most child deaths, it says, trace to parents' ignorance and carelessness. It explains the germ, the false membrane in the throat, and the milder forms that look like a sore throat. Such leaflets were front line weapons of public health in 1919, teaching homes what doctors knew.
36039-the-giant-crab-and-other-tales-fro:
The Giant Crab and Other Tales from Old India retells stories for children, gathered and retold by Rouse. David Nutt published it at London in 1897, with pictures by Robinson. A warning to studious readers opens the book. Rouse hopes no one will take it for a scientific work: it is meant to amuse children, and if it does that, its aim is hit.

The tales rest on the great Buddhist collection called the Jataka, in the Cambridge translation. Rouse owns that he has altered them freely to suit young readers, so that Buddha himself might fail to know some of them. Titles in the contents include The Quail and the Falcon, Pride Must Have a Fall, and The Lion and the Boar. The Goblin City and The King's Lesson stand later. These are the birth stories of the Buddha, retold as animal fables with morals for the nursery.
3607-ismailia:
Samuel White Baker writes an account of his expedition up the Nile for the Khedive Ismail of Egypt, to the province later called Ismailia. Baker commanded a force meant to open Central Africa to trade, plant stations along the river, and suppress the slave trade that ravaged the region. His narrative follows steamers, soldiers, and porters south toward Gondokoro and beyond.

Baker describes the river, its peoples, its wildlife, and the hard labor of moving a modern expedition through swamp and desert. He writes as a Victorian explorer confident in his mission, yet frank about disease, desertion, and resistance. The book suits readers interested in African exploration and in the nineteenth century campaign against the slave trade.
36133-brenda-s-ward-a-sequel-to-amy-in-a:
Helen Leah Reed wrote Brenda’s Ward, a girls’ tale and a sequel to Amy in Acadia. Little, Brown, and Company issued the book in Boston in nineteen hundred six. Frank T Merrill drew the pictures from life like scenes. Martine, Brenda’s young ward, comes to Boston to open the tale.

Her new room, house, and city fill Martine with delight at once. She slips and calls her hostess Mrs Weston in thanks. Brenda laughs the stiff name off as a grandma’s tag. At twenty she will not feel old, she claims with spirit. A mirror test shows the pair near matched in looks. The year then runs from Boston rooms to old Plymouth. A lost trunk, class day, and the Isles of Shoals mark its turns.
36175-letters-of-major-jack-downing-of-t:
Letters of Major Jack Downing, of the Downingville militia, is a set of dialect letters on politics, here in a third edition from Van Evrie, Horton and Company in 1866. The Major writes to the president as an old friend and plain spoken adviser. His spelling is as rustic as his opinions are shrewd. A portrait signed yours till deth stands at the front.

The first letter announces that the Major still lives and is sent for by President Linkin, as he spells Lincoln. The president tells stories, takes advice, and thinks of an appointment on General McClellan's staff. Deacon Jenkins is sent for to cut and make the president's uniform. Ague and fever, delegations, temperance, and the negroes at Port Royal pass through the letters. The book is Civil War satire from the Democratic side, in the voice of a shrewd Yankee farmer.
36583-hania:
Henryk Sienkiewicz wrote Hania, translated from the Polish by Jeremiah Curtin. Little, Brown and Company published it at Boston in 1897. Sienkiewicz was the author of Quo Vadis and With Fire and Sword. A prologue, The Old Servant, opens the volume. The old servant was Mikolai Suhovolski, a noble from the village of Suha Vola. He had come to the author's father from his grandfather, with whom he served in the Napoleonic wars.

The title tale follows the prologue, and Tartar Captivity comes after it. Three shorter tales fill the middle. Charcoal Sketches and The Organist of Ponikla stand late in the book. Lux in Tenebris Lucet and On the Bright Shore close the set, with That Third Woman last. Hania, a tale of love and a Tartar raid, heads the collection.
36641-women-novelists-of-queen-victoria-:
Women Novelists of Queen Victoria's Reign, subtitled a book of appreciations, was published by Hurst and Blackett in London in 1897. The contributors, themselves women writers of standing, include Mrs Oliphant, Mrs Lynn Linton, Charlotte Yonge, and Edna Lyall. Each takes a novelist of the reign: Oliphant writes on the sisters Brontë, Linton on George Eliot, Lyall on Mrs Gaskell.

By design the volume covers only women who had died and who did all their fiction after the Queen's accession, excluding earlier figures such as Mary Shelley. Other chapters treat Mrs Henry Wood, Lady Georgiana Fullerton, and more. Written by peers rather than critics, the appreciations are a valuable record of how the Victorian literary world judged its own women novelists.
36749-the-stronghold-a-story-of-historic:
The Stronghold is a story of the historic Northern Neck of Virginia and its people, by Miriam Haynie. It came out at Richmond, Virginia, in 1959 from the Dietz Press. The book is given to the author's husband, William Harold Haynie, and to the memory of her mother and father of Pleasant Grove, Northumberland County. A second printing came in 1960 and a third in 1964.

The contents open with a first part on the seventeenth century. Tidewater, Ye Northerne Neck, and The People stand at its head. Indians and Early Explorers, Captain John Smith, and Powhatan's Empire stand in the list. The work is a local history told as a story: the land between the rivers, its first peoples, and the English who came to plant there, as its plan sets out.
36902-a-history-of-the-boundaries-of-arl:
A History of the Boundaries of Arlington County, Virginia, was issued by the office of the county manager in 1967. A map at the front shows the bounds of Arlington in nine dated forms. The years run from 1791 to 1966 on that map. Bert Johnson, the county manager, signs the volume.

The contents open with Arlington County today, in a short introduction. A first part treats the years from 1608 to 1789. Charters of James the First to the Virginia Company start the tale. The cession of 1789 took the county into the District of Columbia. Later chapters bring it out of the district and through its changes. Few counties in America have shifted their lines so often. This plain record traces every shift.
37002-tales-of-the-sun-or-folklore-of-so:
Mrs Howard Kingscote and Pandit Natesa Sastri gathered this set of tales from southern India, printed by W H Allen in London and Calcutta in 1890. Kingscote began by writing down tales her servants brought from the old women of the bazaars. She found those texts full of errors and foreign scraps, like the mixed stuff in a dish of curry and rice.

Sastri set her tales right and added many he had gathered himself, some first printed in The Indian Antiquary. Tales include The Three Deaf Men, The Soothsayer's Son, and The Brahmin Girl that Married a Tiger. The book keeps the oral stock of the south in a form scholars could trust and readers could enjoy.
37027-with-fire-and-sword-an-historical-:
With Fire and Sword, by Henryk Sienkiewicz, appears in a popular edition of 1904. Little, Brown printed it at Boston under copyrights of 1890 and 1898. Jeremiah Curtin made the authorized translation from the Polish. Curtin gives the volume to Professor John Fiske, his classmate and fellow traveller. The dedication is dated at Washington in April 1890. A map of the Polish Commonwealth stands among the pictures. King Vladislav and Bogdan Hmelnitski appear in old engravings. The subtitle calls it an historical novel of Poland and Russia.

An introduction traces the two Slav states, Poland and Russia, from their origins. Curtin's list of the author's works names The Deluge and Pan Michael as kin. Quo Vadis stands there too. The novel opens the great trilogy of Poland's wars in the seventeenth century.
37153-queen-victoria:
Queen Victoria, by Lytton Strachey, is a life of the queen in ten chapters and a bibliography. Chatto and Windus printed it in London in 1921. Strachey gives the book to Virginia Woolf.

A frontispiece shows Victoria, Albert, and the royal family, from Winterhalter's picture at Buckingham Palace. The chapters run in reign order: antecedents and childhood first. Lord Melbourne and marriage follow, then Lord Palmerston. The last years of the Prince Consort lead into widowhood. Gladstone and Beaconsfield share a chapter, and old age and the end close the life. Portraits mark the years: the princess in 1836, the queen in 1838, Albert in 1840. Later plates show her in 1860, in 1863, in 1876, and in 1897. A note promises a source in the footnotes for every fact.
37825-thirty-years-in-australia:
Thirty Years in Australia is a memoir by Ada Cambridge, published by Methuen in London in 1903. Cambridge is named as author of Path and Goal and The Devastators on the title page. She dedicates the book to her two living children and to the memory of one who died. Contents list twenty chapters for the thirty years of her Australian life.

Isle of Beauty, Fare Thee Well and Australia Felix open the memoir in order of the chapters. The Bush, The First Home, and Dik follow in the list of the book.  She knew nothing of Australia, she says, when she rashly consented to marry a young man bound to live there. Her thirty years, from parsonage to parsonage in Victoria, are the record of a novelist life lived at the other end of the world.
38076-our-philadelphia:
Our Philadelphia is a memoir of the city by Elizabeth Robins Pennell, with art by Joseph Pennell. One hundred and five lithographs by her husband picture the streets and squares. Lippincott published the book at Philadelphia and London in nineteen fourteen. Twenty chapters run from a childhood in the city to a return after years away.

The first chapters recall a child in Philadelphia and schooling at a convent there. The social adventure and the Assembly ball mark her coming out in society. A question of creed and a first awakening lead to the miracle of work. Philadelphia and literature, then Philadelphia and art, fill the middle chapters. Two chapters set the city at table, with its markets and manners of eating. The last chapters find the city changed after a quarter of a century.
3819-the-euahlayi-tribe-a-study-of-abori:
K Langloh Parker, who lived among the Euahlayi people of New South Wales, wrote this study of their life, law, and belief. Chapters cover Byamee the All Father, relationships and totems, medicine men and leechcraft, and a witch woman. They also follow a girl from infancy to womanhood and a boy to the Boorah initiation. Funerals, mourning, stars and legends, trapping, foraging, costumes, weapons, and amusements all receive their section.

Parker writes as a sympathetic witness of her time, and her notes on twin births, spirit beliefs, and bush bogies show both her care and her era's limits. The book remains a valuable early record of a single people's customs. Readers who study Australian Aboriginal culture should read it with that context in mind, as a pioneer work rather than a modern account.
38294-henrietta-maria:
Henrietta Maria is a life of that queen by Henrietta Haynes, out in nineteen twelve. Past ten plates fill it, the first a paint of the queen by a famed hand at a royal house. A list of press slips set right stands at the front. Parts run from her days as a girl of France to her days as a queen cast out, and to her found of a nuns house.

Heads name her the bride of the isle realm, the queen of the court folk, and the queen of the church of Rome in that land. Her turns of faith, the eve of the war in two parts, and the queen and the war in two parts take heads. The end closes the list. Back parts hold a tail piece and a word list.
38408-the-captive-in-patagonia:
Captive in Patagonia, by Benjamin Franklin Bourne, is a personal narrative of captivity. Gould and Lincoln of Boston issued the book in eighteen fifty three. Its second title is Life Among the Giants, with pictures bound in. Bourne says book making is not his trade in a brief preface.

Friends and strangers took deep interest in his fortunes, Bourne explains there. Their wishes, in speech and in letters, moved him to write the account. The front view shows hunting the guanaco in Patagonia wilds. Readers get a first hand tale of life held among tall Patagonian folk. The book stands as a record of his trials and his release.
38844-little-friend-lydia:
Ethel Phillips wrote Little Friend Lydia, for a Boston house in 1920. Butler illustrated the children's tale for Houghton Mifflin. Christmas Eve opens the contents of the story. The Real Christmas Present follows in the chapter list. The New Home and a Picture and a Party come next.

Little Gwen's story stands in the list. A doctor fills the middle contents. Cobbler, cobbler, mend my shoe sings one chapter's title aloud. Who stole the brown betty follows. Roger comes home to close the contents of the tale. Twenty little boys and girls watched for Santa in chapter one. Striped blouses and checked aprons dress them. Wheels on the driveway set faces pressing the window-pane. We'll ask her for a drink, Sammy responded in one plate. Phillips gives an orphanage Christmas its little friend.
38881-in-kali-s-country-tales-from-sunny:
In Kalis Country holds tales from sunny India by Emily Sheets. Drawings by Elma Childs dress the text of the small tale book. A plate shows a town girl in gems in her glad days of youth. Rights date the work to the year nineteen ten.

Ox carts and town lanes set the scene of the south land tales. The name of a dark goddess of that land gives the book its title. Girls, rites, and caste ways form the stuff of the brief tales inside. Church house presses in three lands put the work out for home shelves. Warm sight and plain talk tune the tales for young home readers.
39166-the-white-terror-and-the-red-a-nov:
The White Terror and the Red is a novel of Russia under the czars by Cahan, the author of Yekl. It was published in New York by Barnes in 1905. The book went through three printings in two months. Its chapters move between palace and cellar.

Pavel takes his first step toward revolt early in the tale. Clara gives up a safe life and becomes an outlaw in the cause. A day underground, a hunted monarch, and a plot against the czar fill the middle chapters. The white terror of the police answers the red terror of the rebels. A postponed wedding and a second courtship run beside the plot. The tale ends with a revelation and a hunted people.
39603-the-public-life-of-queen-victoria:
The Public Life of Queen Victoria, a biography by John McGilchrist, was published by Felt and Dillingham of New York. The contents map a life from ancestry to reign. McGilchrist begins far back, with Frederick the Wise, Elector of Saxony, the protector of Luther, and the staunch Protestantism of the queen's Saxon forefathers. The house of Saxe-Coburg fills the first chapter.

Prince Leopold of Saxe-Coburg, the queen's uncle and later king of the Belgians, gets a chapter as the greatest of the modern Coburgs. His marriage to the Princess Charlotte and his fatherly care of his orphaned niece are told in full. Then come the parentage and birth of Victoria, the death of her father the Duke of Kent, and her first years at Kensington Palace. Wilberforce and the infant princess, a narrow escape from death, and her youthful charities fill the childhood chapter.
39853-the-lance-of-kanana-a-story-of-ara:
The Lance of Kanana is a story of Arabia by Harry French, who also wrote as Abd El Ardavan. Lothrop, Lee and Shepard published the book at Boston, with rights from 1892 renewed in 1916. Pictures by Garrett illustrate the tale. Thirteen chapters carry the hero from his tribe to the court of a caliph.

Kanana is a Bedouin boy of the Beni Sad tribe, born on the desert. Strange to say, he has held a lance in his hand only once. Yet sheiks and chiefs of his day lie dead and forgotten while his name lives. The first chapter calls him the coward of the Beni Sads. An old sheik's promise and a white camel guide his path. French wrote desert adventure for boys, with Allah and Arabia as the watchwords.
40467-indian-and-scout-a-tale-of-the-gol:
Captain F S Brereton wrote Indian and Scout, a tale of the gold rush to California, issued by H M Caldwell Company in New York and Boston. Cyrus Cuneo drew the plates. Brereton had written The Great Aeroplane, A Hero of Sedan, and How Canada Was Won. Twenty four chapters fill the tale. Tusker Joe is the villain, and Jack Kingsley is the young hero.

Chapter one opens with Tusker Joe challenging a room in rough speech. If there was a man here who was a man, he growls, waiting might be of use. He asks if any man thinks he did not do it fair. Later chapters bring a hold up, a buffalo hunt, and a party surrounded by Indians. The gold rush, a find by Tom, and an ambuscade add pace. A great acquittal closes the tale. Boys got plains, gold, and peril in full measure.
40675-nurse-elisia:
George Manville Fenn opens a family tale at a bad-tempered breakfast in Lincolnshire. Cassell Publishing Company issued the novel at New York in an edition dated 1892.

Mr Ralph Elthorne of Hightoft attacks his egg with a savage chop. It is hard as lead, and the silver cup falls sideways. Rich yolk streams across the plate. His daughter pours tea and bears his scolding with sweet patience. She carries a cup round the table to the fierce old man. Then she bends and kisses his forehead before hurrying back to her place. Her brother Al offers kidneys from the hot water dish. Fenn wrote scores of tales for boys and families. This opening sets a nurse's quiet service against a father's rough tongue.
40900-a-literary-and-historical-atlas-of:
J G Bartholomew compiled a literary and historical atlas of Asia for Everyman's Library, published by Dent at London and Dutton at New York. The contents list colored maps in time order. The world according to Hecataeus, about 500 years before Christ, opens the series. Eratosthenes' world follows, then a map from Abu Rihan in the year 1030.

An Egyptian empire map of about 1450 before Christ comes next. A glossary and index support the maps. The transcriber lists small faults left as printed: missing longitudes and mismatched entries. Bartholomew's firm was Britain's leading map house. The atlas let general readers see Asian history as changing space.
41489-one-of-clive-s-heroes-a-story-of-t:
One of Clive's Heroes tells a boy's part in the fight for India, written by Herbert Strang. Oxford University Press issued the book at London, with rights dated 1906. A frontispiece shows a native officer falling into a trap. Long chapter heads in the old style sketch each turn of the tale.

The hero first meets Colonel Robert Clive at a court in Market Drayton. Talk of the golden East fires the boy's dreams. Blows, a night visit to an inn, and a sea fight fill the road out. In India a native prince and a storytelling clerk draw him deeper. Freedom is offered at the price of honour, and refused. Strang wrote brisk empire tales for schoolboys. This one rides on Clive's fame and the lure of the East.
41597-the-history-of-the-city-of-frederi:
Quinn wrote this history of Fredericksburg, Virginia, by order of its Common Council. The Hermitage Press printed the book in Richmond in 1908. Quinn gives the book to those who found the site in 1608. Three hundred years of town growth close at the present year.

Plates show churches, hotels, court house, and cemeteries of the city. Lists name a Baptist church, a Catholic church, and Chancellorsville Tavern. A Confederate cemetery and monument mark the war years in town. The book is an civic record made by the city for itself. A portrait of the author fronts the history.
41758-under-the-chinese-dragon-a-tale-of:
Under the Chinese Dragon is a boys' adventure tale of Mongolia by Captain Brereton. Blackie published the book at London in 1912, with pictures by Charles Sheldon. Brereton had written The Hero of Panama and other tales for boys. The contents run to twenty chapters.

The tale opens in an English village inn, where a boatman praises the mighty nose of Ebenezer Clayhill. From that comic start the hero David travels far. Chapters take him to London, to sea on a Chinese junk, and into a Chinese prison. A game of long bowls, a desert crossing, and a fight to a finish fill the later parts. The secret of certain ruins closes the story. A frontispiece shows a beast springing full at David. The book mixes schoolboy pluck with far travel.
41795-tales-of-northumbria:
Tales of Northumbria is a set of sketches of Northumbrian character by Howard Pease, published by Methuen in London in 1899. Pease dedicates them to Earl Grey, ever keenly interested in whatever concerns his native county. The tales had already appeared in the National Observer, the Queen, and Newcastle newspapers. The contents open with a sketch of Northumberland itself.

Stories follow: A Long Main, The Squire's Last Ride, T'Owd Squire, and An Amateur Detective. The Heckler upon Womenfolk, The Caleb Jay, Geordie Armstrong the Jesuit, and Geordie Ride-the-Stang keep the dialect titles coming. Yankee Bill and Quaker John, The Protégé, and The Spanish Doubloon close the list. A passage preserved in the copy marks the change reaching the county. New forces, it says, made havoc of the proud insularity of the Northumbrian squirearchy.
41917-the-confounding-of-camelia:
Anne Douglas Sedgwick wrote The Confounding of Camelia, published by Scribner in New York in 1899. Sedgwick also wrote The Dull Miss Archinard. Her heroine comes down into the country after her second London season. Camelia descends lightly on the home of her forefathers, unannounced, as much by caprice as her long absence had been. The neighbourhood's opinion of her, forming since her girlhood, hardens into judgement.

The Patons, her family, had always been good, quiet people. No black sheep disgraced their annals, and no skeleton filled their cupboards. Their wealth was real but not showy, and a sheep-like dulness kept their fleeces spotless. Against that tranquil excellence Sedgwick sets Camelia herself: brilliant, irregular, and determined to confound the family's placid order. The novel studies what a country house, and a county, do with a woman who will not fit the place prepared for her.
42033-assyria:
Assyria: Its Princes, Priests, and People, by Sayce, deputy professor of comparative philology at Oxford, was published in London in 1885 by the Religious Tract Society. The book is number 7 in the By-Paths of Bible Knowledge set. A front plate shows the monolith of Shalmaneser the Second, from the original in the British Museum. Five chapters run from the country and people through history, religion, and art, to manners, trade, and government.

Tables at the front list the kings of Assyria in order, and biblical dates checked against the Assyrian monuments. Other plates show Assur-bani-pal and his queen, and the god Nergal. Sayce wrote for Bible readers who wanted the new cuneiform finds made plain: what the stones of Nineveh could prove or correct in the Old Testament story. His tone is that of a lecturer with museum pieces in hand.
42357-the-adventure-of-princess-sylvia:
The Adventure of Princess Sylvia is a romantic novel by Mrs Williamson. Doubleday, Page published this authorised edition in New York in 1909. A list of the Williamsons' books opens the volume. The Lightning Conductor and The Princess Passes stand among them. The book is dedicated to the author's American princess, Mrs Postley. The contents list seventeen chapters of court adventure. The Adventure Begins opens with a Shakespeare song of Sylvia. The princess swears in her first speech of the tale.

Her grand duchess groans that someone might hear her language. The Inadvertence of Frau Johann and a young man with bare knees follow. Max versus Maximilian and honours of the day fill the middle. The Bear in His Den and A White Night raise the stakes. News by Telephone and The Chancellor's Luck come late. The Third Course closes the contents. The tale is a Ruritanian courtship romance.
43214-dr-arne-and-rule-britannia:
Dr Arne and Rule, Britannia is a music history by William Hayman Cummings, published in London in 1912. Cummings had already written the origin and history of God Save the King. A portrait of Dr Arne by Dunkarton forms the frontispiece.

In his preface Cummings states the puzzle. The glorious national song Rule, Britannia is familiar to the whole British race. Yet very few men and women know the history of its birth and parentage. In the pages that follow he sets out to chronicle all the facts that diligent research can discover. He promises to present them in an attractive and entertaining manner. The book thus treats one short song as a piece of national history, tracing its composer, its first setting, and its rise into an anthem.
43884-hallowed-heritage-the-life-of-virg:
Hallowed Heritage, the Life of Virginia, is a school survey by Dorothy Torpey. Torpey headed social studies at Hammond High School in Alexandria, Virginia. Whittet and Shepperton of Richmond printed the book in the year 1961. She gives the book to her mother and to Bill for their support. Seven chapters run from geographical life to the state's own government.

Historical life fills three chapters, from 1584 to her present day. Exploration, the golden age, and the Revolution fill the first of them. The War Between the States and Reconstruction fill the third history part. Economic life treats the work force, jobs, and transportation in the state. Cultural life covers letters, art, building, music, drama, and schooling. Political life closes with the Virginia Bill of Rights and state offices. Each chapter ends with a summary for the student reader's use.
44321-the-mentor-american-miniature-pain:
The Mentor for January 15, 1917, is an illustrated magazine issue on American miniature painters, written by Elizabeth Lounsbery. It is serial number 123, volume 4, number 23, in a series built on the motto of learning one thing every day. The number belongs to the magazine's department of fine arts. It sold for fifteen cents a copy.

The issue opens with a short piece on art and life. It argues that art is not separate from daily life but a vital part of it. It quotes William Morris on art shared by all, in sorrow and joy alike. The main study then turns to the miniature painters themselves. John Trumbull's work as a historical painter had been treated in an earlier number. Here the focus falls on the small-scale portrait art of America's early painters and the lives behind it.
45137-myths-legends-of-babylonia-assyria:
Myths and Legends of Babylonia and Assyria, by Lewis Spence, surveys the stories and beliefs of the two great kingdoms of ancient Mesopotamia. The book was published in London in 1916, with eight colour plates by Evelyn Paul and thirty-two other pictures.

Opening chapters place the lands in history and legend, then turn to the Babylonian account of creation and early religion. A full chapter retells the epic of Gilgamesh. Later chapters treat the later gods of Babylon, the great god Merodach, the gods of Assyria, and the worship of the stars. Further chapters cover priests and temples, magic and demons, and tales of the kings. The book ends with modern digging in the two lands and a closing chapter called The Twilight of the Gods.
46118-the-religion-of-ancient-scandinavi:
The Religion of Ancient Scandinavia is a short survey in a popular series. The series, Religions Ancient and Modern, lists many volumes. Clodd on animism and Harrison on Greece stand among them. Craigie, a joint editor of the Oxford dictionary, wrote the Scandinavian volume. Its opening claim sets the frame. The North's old faith was one form of a wider creed.

All Germanic peoples shared its main features, he holds. That creed grew from beliefs of the whole Aryan stock. Odin, Thor, and the old gods fill its pages. Myths, worship, and burial customs are surveyed in brief. The series put sound scholarship in cheap form. Craigie's volume served students of the Eddas and sagas.
4641-starr-king-in-california:
William Day Simonds wrote Starr King in California to set the record straight about a critical period in California history, and to deal justly with a man recent historians had slighted. He dedicates the book to Horace Davis of San Francisco, whose friendly interest and help he gratefully acknowledges. Up to Starr King's death, Simonds says, it was generally believed that King, more than any other man, had kept California and the whole Pacific Coast from falling into disunion.

Simonds adds that Abraham Lincoln held the same opinion, quoting Edwin Percy Whipple. Parts cover old New England, California in 1860, California's hour of decision, philanthropist and preacher, and a retrospect. Readers get a warm, partisan biography of a Unitarian minister whose preaching and patriotism shaped a state at war, and a useful guide to California's Civil War politics.
47051-descrittione-del-regno-di-scotia:
Descrittione del Regno di Scotia is an Italian description of the kingdom of Scotland by Petruccio Ubaldini. Written in 1588, it was reprinted at Edinburgh in 1829 for the Bannatyne Club. A transcriber's note explains that, apart from an introduction in English, the reprint makes no changes to the old text or its punctuation.

The volume was presented to the club by Andrew Coventry, and it opens with the club's roll of members for 1829. Sir Walter Scott heads the list as president. Peers, judges, and antiquaries follow, among them the Duke of Buccleuch, the Duke of Hamilton, Francis Jeffrey, Cosmo Innes, and Robert Jameson. The roll shows the circle of subscribers for whom such rare reprints were made, and it forms part of the book's record of Scottish antiquarian life in 1829.
47288-the-queen-s-daughters-in-india:
The Queen's Daughters in India is a reform book by Elizabeth Andrew and Katharine Bushnell, published by Morgan and Scott at London in 1899. Prefatory letters come from Josephine Butler and a member of Parliament. The book is dedicated to Butler as prophetess of truth, lover of holy justice, and friend of outcast women. Its text is a verse: remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them.

The preface owns a deep sense of duty to the womanhood of the world, and more, to God. The writers attack the state regulation of vice in British India, under which women were held for the use of soldiers. They note like laws being pushed in five American states. The book speaks for the new abolitionists on both sides of the Atlantic.
47424-the-shakespearean-myth-william-sha:
The Shakespearean Myth: William Shakespeare and Circumstantial Evidence is Appleton Morgan's brief against the Stratford man's authorship of the plays, published by Robert Clarke and Company at Cincinnati in 1881. Morgan, a lawyer who had written on the law of literature, frames the question as a case at law. His preface borrows Guizot's wondering summary of the problem: a butcher's apprentice, poacher, and actor who somehow wrote the supreme works of the language.

Morgan then weighs the surviving records of Shakespeare's life against the learning and range the plays display, treating each fact as evidence to be admitted or struck. The book is an early, lawyerly entry in the long authorship controversy, written before that debate hardened into camps. It preserves the Victorian doubt in its most orderly form, argued like a trial.
47493-fort-pulaski-national-monument-geo:
Ralston Lattimore wrote this guide as number eighteen in the National Park Service Historical Handbook series, printed at Washington in 1954 and sold for twenty-five cents. The foreword frames the fort's story as the age-old struggle between offense and defense. No nation, it says, has yet devised a refuge safe against new weapons and new tactics.

The handbook traces Cockspur Island from 1733, the building of the new brick fort, and its seizure under the Georgia flag in the Civil War. General Lee's return to the fort, its investment, and the bombardment of April 1862 follow, when a new weapon, the rifled cannon, broke the thick walls from a distance. Chapters on the surrender, the siege's meaning, and the Immortal Six Hundred prisoners close the history, and a guide to the area serves visitors.
48578-ludwig-the-second-king-of-bavaria:
Ludwig the Second, King of Bavaria is a life of the king by Clara Tschudi, turned from the Norwegian by Ethel Harriet Hearn. Tschudi also wrote lives of Marie Antoinette and the Empress Eugenie. The book came out at London and New York in 1908, with a portrait in colour at the front.

The chapters trace Ludwig from his youth and schooling to his sudden rise to the throne. They cover his bond with Richard Wagner, his broken pledge to wed, and the wars of 1866 and of France. Later pages follow his slow retreat from the world, his love of art and the stage, and the sad state of his brother Otto.
49058-ocmulgee-national-monument-georgia:
Ocmulgee National Monument, Georgia is a handbook in the National Park Service historical handbook series. The work was written by Pope the younger and printed in Washington in 1956. It guides visitors to the Indian mounds near Macon, Georgia. The front matter lists the contents, from the first peoples of Georgia to a guide to the grounds.

The text traces human life at the site across long ages. Chapters cover food from the waters and the rise of pot making as an art. Later chapters treat temple mounds, farming, and the early Creeks. The closing part describes the old fields and gives practical notes for a visit. Pictures show mound building and a temple mound village of about the year 1000 as an artist pictured it.
49139-the-life-of-carmen-sylva-queen-of-:
Baroness Deichmann translated The Life of Carmen Sylva from the German. Kegan Paul put out the London book in 1890. The German book was by Baroness Stackelberg, the note explains. Four portraits, a view, and a sample of handwriting fill the volume. Elizabeth, Queen of Roumania, fronts the book in a portrait plate. Carmen Sylva, song of the forest, was her pen name as a poet.

The translator knew Monrepos from her childhood, she writes. That beautiful seat of the Princess of Wied stands on a Westerwald slope. Edwin Arnold turned some of the poems into English for the book. Max Muller advised on the philosophical pages, she adds with thanks. The life traces the queen from her Wied home to the Roumanian throne. Her songs, tales, and good works fill the account of her reign.
49545-social-work-essays-on-the-meeting-:
Richard Cabot, a Boston doctor, wrote these essays on the meeting-ground of doctor and social worker. Houghton Mifflin published them in 1919, dedicated to Mary Richmond, whose book Social Diagnosis he calls an epoch in the field. An introduction traces the historical development of social assistance in medical work.

Cabot observes that the social worker's profession has grown in the United States within twenty-five years to some ten thousand persons, under titles from hospital social worker to probation officer. Part one treats medical-social diagnosis: the social assistant's standing and duties, history-taking, and economic and mental investigation, down to fatigue and industrial disease. Part two turns to social treatment, with samples of social therapeutics and a chapter on the motive of social work. His warning runs throughout: treating people in masses turns a person into a case, and the individual is lost sight of.
49588-one-year-in-scandinavia:
One Year in Scandinavia, by Erastus Snow, was published in Liverpool in 1851 for threepence. Snow, one of the Twelve Apostles of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, reports on mission work in Denmark and Sweden. The full title promises sketches of the land and people, late troubles, and the present state of affairs.

Letters and journal extracts make up much of the book, with notes to church leaders and family. Snow's own life story opens the volume, from his birth in Vermont in 1818 through prison in Missouri and the trek to Salt Lake Valley. Sections on Denmark and Sweden add notes on faith, law, and daily life.
49847-the-pilgrim-of-castile-or-el-peleg:
The Pilgrim of Castile, or El Pelegrino in Su Patria, is a prose romance by Lope de Vega, in the English version made by William Dutton and published in 1621. The first book opens on the shore near Barcelona, where fishermen pull a half drowned man from the planks of his wrecked ship.

The stranger hides his name and tells only of a voyage home from Italy for the Jubilee under Pope Clement the Eighth. Lope, the great Spanish playwright, poured travel, love, and adventure into this pilgrim's progress across Spain. Dutton's old English keeps the tang of the age that read it new.
50346-women-of-india:
Women of India, by Otto Rothfeld, was printed at Bombay by Taraporevala Sons and Company, with plates by M V Dhurandhar. Rothfeld served in the Indian Civil Service and had written Indian Dust. A Bombay lady stands at the front.

Chapters open with women as they are, then take up marriage in India and the Hindu woman in marriage. Later parts treat the ladies of the aristocracy, the middle classes, and the working and tribal classes. One chapter treats the dancing girl, and one treats woman dress. The last chapter is named The Moving Finger. Plates show women of many regions and castes, from a water carrier of Ahmedabad to a fisher woman of Sind. Readers get a British officer view of Indian womanhood in his day.
50496-mrs-albert-grundy-observations-in-:
Mrs Albert Grundy, Observations in Philistia, a satire by Harold Frederic, takes aim at the rule of Mrs Grundy. She is the famed figure of respectability, the neighbour whose opinion governs what may be done or said. The book calls the land she rules Philistia, a name borrowed from Heine for the home of the smug and narrow.

The narrator wonders at the start whether Philistia is even the right name for her realm. He jokes that there must have been a Mrs Grundy among the cave dwellers, beside the cave bear. Her reign, he says, is a comfortable and well regulated paradox. Frederic, an American novelist and journalist, mocks the fear of seeming improper that ruled polite society. The book mixes essay and story to show her sway over manners, art, and morals. It is a light weapon aimed at a heavy tyranny of opinion.
50570-custis-lee-mansion-the-robert-e-le:
Murray Nelligan wrote this guide as number six in the National Park Service Historical Handbook series, first printed at Washington in 1950 and revised in 1962, and sold for twenty-five cents. Its subject is the Custis-Lee Mansion at Arlington, Virginia, kept by the nation as the Robert Lee memorial.

The mansion, the handbook says, has dominated the scene across the river from the capital for more than a century, a Greek Revival house of dignity, strength, and steady grace. George Washington Parke Custis, adopted son of General Washington, built it, and for years it held many objects tied to Washington himself. Contents divide the history of Arlington at 1861 and 1865, then give a long guide to the house and grounds, visitor services, and suggested readings. A Brady photograph shows Lee in 1865.
50906-savrola-a-tale-of-the-revolution-i:
Winston Churchill wrote this tale of revolution in imagined Laurania. Longmans printed Savrola in New York in 1900, serial first. Churchill gives the book to officers of the Fourth Hussars. He lived four happy years in their company, the gift page says.

The story was written in 1897, his preface note records. Contents open with an event of political importance in Laurania. The head of state, the man of the multitude, and a deputation follow. A state ball, a council of war, and palace defence build the revolt. Life compensations close the contents of the Laurania revolution tale at its end.
51117-free-russia:
Free Russia, by William Hepworth Dixon, was printed in New York in 1870. Dixon had written Free America and a book on the Tower of London before this one. Two plates show a convent in the frozen sea and infantry on the eastern steppe.

Free Russia, Dixon says in his preface, is a word on every lip in that great country. It names the hope of a new empire born of the Crimean War. His fresh journeys ran from the Polar Sea to the Ural Mountains and from the Vistula to the straits. He visited the four holy shrines of Solovetsk, Pechersk, Saint George, and Troitsa. The book treats pilgrims, monks, village justice, and beggars at first hand. Kozaks, Kalmuks, workmen's guilds, and the division of land all get their turn.
51675-yosemite-national-park-california:
A government guide to Yosemite National Park came from the Department of the Interior in Washington in 1935. Harold Ickes was Secretary of the Interior, and Arno B Cammerer directed the National Park Service. The pamphlet tells visitors that the park stays open all year and explains how to use it.

Rules come first: where fires may be built and how camps must be kept. Campers space their sites, burn or bury trash, and leave trees and animals unharmed. Quiet hours hold at night, cars keep to a low speed limit, and an auto permit costs $2. Bears get a warning of their own. The guide then points readers to the valley's falls, cliffs, and trails. Such pamphlets taught a new motoring public how to visit wild country without spoiling it.
5211-the-famous-missions-of-california:
William Henry Hudson's Famous Missions of California, published in London in 1901, tells the story of the Franciscan missions of Alta California. It opens with Father Junipero Serra and the proposed settlement, follows his arrival at San Diego, and traces the founding of San Carlos at Monterey and San Antonio de Padua, among others.

Hudson, lately professor of English at Stanford, writes for general readers, joining history with affectionate recollection of California days. The book gives a clear, readable introduction to the mission chain, its founders, and the Spanish settlement of California, before later histories revised its romantic view.
52189-sketches-of-persia:
Sketches of Persia is a travel book by Sir John Malcolm, soldier, diplomat, and historian of Persia and India. A new edition was printed in London by John Murray in 1861. Malcolm had served as envoy to Persia, and his sketches come from his journeys on duty.

The contents follow the road from the sea. A voyage from Bombay to the Persian Gulf opens the book. Muscat and the Gulf follow, then the camp at Abusheher, with its horses and its Arab anecdotes. Hunting and hawking, an entertainment by a shaikh, and a mirage fill one chapter. The Elchee's lectures, a mehmandar's journal, and Persian ceremony fill another. Mountaineers, the valley of Kazeroon, and the beautiful valley of Desht-e-Arjun carry the party inland. Malcolm writes as a political officer who liked the country, and his sketches gave English readers their first familiar Persia.
52515-the-white-elephant-and-other-tales:
The White Elephant and Other Tales From Old India retells old tales for children. Georgene Faulkner, called the Story Lady, retold the tales, and Frederick Richardson drew the pictures. The Volland Company holds the copyright of 1929, and Faulkner gives the book to her radio family.

In a letter to children she says some tales come from the days of Buddha himself. They were taken from the Jataka Tales, which tell of the Buddha's earlier lives. The White Elephant, she notes, is much like Androcles and the lion in shape. The Timid Little Rabbit matches the English tale of Chicken Little. Other tales bring cunning jackals, a kingdom of mice, and men who ride tigers. A grain of corn tale comes from Flora Annie Steel's Punjab set.
52813-on-the-wallaby-through-victoria:
E M Clowes wrote a travel account of Victoria in Australia, published in London in 1911 with many photographs. A first chapter treats early days in Victoria. It tells of a wreck in 1797 on Furneaux Island in Bass Strait, from which three men reached shore. A convict settlement at Port Phillip six years later failed and moved away.

Later chapters give first impressions of Melbourne and the working man and working women of the city. Victorian youth, alien life, amusements, and the arts follow. Rural life, mountain, and forest get a chapter. Pictures show Cup Day at Flemington, fruit loading on the Murray, and ring barked trees.
5303-the-little-hunchback-zia:
Frances Hodgson Burnett's Little Hunchback Zia is set nearly nineteen hundred and sixteen years ago, in the world of the Nativity. Zia toils up a steep road in the deepest shadows, staggering with weariness, striking his foot on stones, and smothering cries of pain, terrified that any traveller might glance toward him.

Burnett, author of The Secret Garden, writes a Christmas story of a despised child drawn toward Bethlehem. Illustrated by Spencer Baird Nichols and W. T. Benda, the book offers young readers a tender tale of fear, pity, and the hope that reaches even the lowliest wanderer.
53041-numantia:
Numantia is a tragedy by Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra, translated from the Spanish by James Gibson. Kegan Paul printed it at London in 1885. Gibson also translated Cervantes' Journey to Parnassus. The book is dedicated to General Gordon of Khartoum, and its epigraph promises that a death with honour is supremest bliss.

Gibson's introduction calls this the first readable English verse rendering of Cervantes' one great drama. It played at Madrid about 1586, under Philip the Second, and won applause as a national work. Long thought lost, it was printed in 1784 by Sancha of Madrid. The tragedy tells the fall of a city that chose death over surrender.
53097-the-murder-of-delicia:
Murder of Delicia is a novel by Marie Corelli of a wife's slow death. Hutchinson published it in London in the year 1896. Corelli also wrote The Sorrows of Satan and The Mighty Atom. An introductory note calls it a slight sketch of an everyday tragedy. That tragedy is commonplace, she warns, yet drawn strictly from life.

The superior sex will disapprove, she predicts in that sharp note. They will call Lord Carlyon an impossible cad who never existed. Corelli answers that Carlyon and his wife both lived in fact. Both originals have departed this scene of earthly contest, she adds. Thousands of such murders happen daily, her note insists in anger.
53104-popular-sayings-from-old-iberia:
Popular Sayings from Old Iberia is a small book of Spanish maxims in English dress, printed at Quebec by Dawson and Company in 1877. Two editors who sign as Fieldat and Aitiaiche say they culled these buds of Spanish thought in hours of pastime. Each saying stands alone, split from the next by a row of stars.

The short lines deal with love, envy, faith, age, speech, and fate. Some are credited to named Spanish writers such as Ferrer de Couto and Ossorio Bernard. One line warns that a barking dog does not bite, and one holds that plain truth is a rare coin. The book gives a neat taste of Iberian folk wit.
53199-practical-points-in-anesthesia:
