Practical Points in Anesthesia, by Frederick-Emil Neef of New York City, was published in 1908 by the Surgery Publishing Company at 92 William Street. Neef spares the reader many words and begins in a concrete way, with the outline of a system of anesthesia largely followed at the German Hospital in New York.

The contents run through the whole course of a case. Induction comes first, then cardiac collapse and respiratory collapse, and the signs that the patient is ready for operation. Maintenance of the surgical plane, important reflexes, vomiting, and obstructed breathing follow. Later points treat the breathing tube, stimulation, the influence of morphine on narcosis, and awakening. Minor anesthesia with ethyl chloride, intubation anesthesia, and cases needing superficial, moderate, or profound anesthesia close the handbook.
53220-the-house-of-cariboo-and-other-tal:
Paul Gardiner wrote The House of Cariboo and Other Tales from Arcadia, published in New York in 1900 and illustrated by Robert Graef. Gardiner had earlier written Vacation Incidents and The Fifth Avenue Social Trust. The book joins two short pieces with a long tale set in the Cariboo country of British Columbia.

The House of Cariboo follows the Camerons from their farm to the gold fields and into the Cariboo Mountains. Chapters bring in a mining camp, a money lender named Nick Perkins, a mortgage coming due, and a trip on an ice raft. Leclare tells tales of an initialed tree and a Christmas tree along the way. The shorter pieces, The Archipelago, Along the Front, and The Growing Maskinonge, round out a volume of frontier and outdoor fiction.
53383-the-story-of-don-john-of-austria:
Padre Luis Coloma told The Story of Don John of Austria for Spanish readers. Lady Moreton turned the tale into English for this wide form. John Lane, the Bodley Head, issued it in London in nineteen hundred twelve. A Prado portrait of the prince in his prime fronts the book.

Steel breast plate, chain sleeves, and the Fleece mark that gay plate. Philip the Second, his grave half brother, takes the next plate. Born in fifteen hundred twenty seven, Philip wed four queens in turn. Mary Tudor of England stood second in that stately row. Luis Quijada, lord of Villagarcia, served the prince as guide. Charles the Fifth at Muhlberg, in Titian’s famed work, rides there too. Four books trace Don John from hid birth to high command. Lepanto’s great sea fight waits in the tale’s proud mid span.
5344-journals-of-expeditions-of-discover:
Edward John Eyre's Journals of Expeditions of Discovery into Central Australia, first volume. It records journeys sent by the colonists of South Australia in 1840 and 1841, from Adelaide toward King George's Sound. Its chapters follow the expeditions overland through country no European had mapped, with plates and maps listed in its contents, though not reproduced in this text.

This record holds only the first volume of Eyre's journals, while a companion record in this library carries the complete journals and another carries the second volume alone. Readers get a first-hand account of Australian exploration, with its hardships, discoveries, and encounters, told in the day-by-day form of a journal.
5345-journals-of-expeditions-of-discover:
Edward John Eyre's Journals of Expeditions of Discovery into Central Australia, second volume, continues the journeys sent by the colonists of South Australia in 1840 and 1841. While a companion record carries the first volume alone and another carries the complete journals, this record holds only the second volume. Its own chapters, plates, and maps trace Eyre's route.

The volume follows the expeditions further into the interior and toward King George's Sound, in the day-by-day form of a journal. Readers get the later, harder portion of Eyre's exploration, with its privations and discoveries, told without romance by the explorer himself.
5346-journals-of-expeditions-of-discover:
Edward John Eyre's Journals of Expeditions of Discovery into Central Australia, complete in this record, covers the expeditions sent by the colonists of South Australia in 1840 and 1841. They travelled overland from Adelaide to King George's Sound. Unlike companion records in this library that carry the first or second volume alone, this record holds the whole journals.

Its chapters follow Eyre's parties through the interior, with lists of plates. Maps mark the extent of his journeys, though the plates themselves are not reproduced here. Readers get the full first-hand record of Australian exploration, in journal form, from departure to the far coast.
53535-common-trees-of-pennsylvania:
Common Trees of Pennsylvania is a state identification guide prepared by Ibberson, Mickalitis, Aughanbaugh, and Morris, with illustrations by Francis, issued by the Commonwealth's Department of Environmental Resources at Harrisburg in 1971.

It opens with a diagram of the functions of a tree's parts: medullary rays conducting food and water, pith, annual rings marking one year each, and leaves taking carbon from the air. Heartwood gives support, sapwood carries food upward, cambium is the growing layer, and roots absorb through tiny hairs. A glossary explains words, terms, and signs that may be unfamiliar, from capsule and catkin to leaf scar and lenticel. Common and scientific names follow the standard list of 1942.
54059-northern-lands-or-young-america-in:
Northern Lands, or Young America in Russia and Prussia, is a travel tale. William Adams wrote it under his pen name Oliver Optic. Lee and Shepard published it at Boston in the year 1872. It forms the second series of the Young America Abroad books. Adams dedicates it to Davis Divine of San Jose, California, his friend.

Adams met Divine at St Petersburg and travelled with him widely. They crossed Russia, Austria, Turkey, Italy, Spain, and Portugal together in life. A front plate shows a scene called the Second Degree at page 129. Optic's other tales, Outward Bound and Down the Rhine, line the front. Boys got geography, sights, and adventure in one instructive package of fun.
54863-joseph-and-his-friend-a-story-of-p:
Joseph and His Friend is a novel of Pennsylvania by Bayard Taylor. Putnam of New York published it in the year 1870 for readers. A motto from Shakespeare's sonnets fronts the quiet domestic tale. The better angel is a man right fair, that motto says. Taylor addresses readers who prefer quiet pictures of life in it.

Such readers choose character's growth over the mysteries of elaborate plot. They like men and women in mixed strength and weakness shown truly. Wholly virtuous ideals and wholly evil examples do not please them. Joseph's friendship and marriage among Pennsylvania farmers fill the tale. Taylor, famed as a traveller, here writes of home ground instead.
55465-the-peoples-of-india:
The Peoples of India, by Anderson, belongs to the Cambridge Manuals of Science and Literature. Anderson taught Bengali when he wrote the little survey for that series. Cambridge University Press issued it from Fetter Lane in London. A plate of Brahmans of the Mirzapur district stands in the front matter.

Race, caste, language, and faith across the subcontinent fill the short volume. Such manuals packed a whole field into a pocket survey for general readers. India of many peoples, tongues, and customs is the puzzle the book sets out. A teacher of Bengali writes for English readers who knew India mostly as an empire. The manual stands as a fair sample of Cambridge short guides of its years.
56218-following-the-sun-flag-a-vain-purs:
John Fox wrote of following the sun flag in a vain pursuit through Manchuria, printed at New York in 1905. Fox gives the book to the men of many wars, with congratulations to those on whom fell a better fortune than his. The trail of the Saxon opens the tale, then hardships of the campaign and lingering in Tokio.

Making for Manchuria, on the war dragon's trail, and the white slaves of Haicheng follow. The backward trail of the Saxon closes the book. An amphitheatre of feathery clouds ran half round the horizon at Yokohama, he begins, and toward Russia rose a great dark shadow through which the sun shone faintly. Fox chased the Russo Japanese war as a correspondent and mostly missed the battles. His honest, bright pages show war reporting's grind.
56269-cupid-s-cyclopedia:
Oliver Herford and John Cecil Clay compiled this comic dictionary of love for Daniel Cupid. Scribner's Sons published it at New York in 1910, dedicated to you, and all whom you love and all who love you. Their note argues that love-making belongs in the school curriculum, since few know how to make love properly or how to keep it.

The entries run alphabetically with jokes and small morals. A stands first because it begins Amour, Ardor, Art, Affinity, Affection, and Adoration, and because it was doubtless the only letter when Adam learned to write. Absence is the sixth sense, arrived at by excluding the other five. Adamant is a very hard word; see father. Admiration is parsed as love-food. Alimony is the fine for speeding in the joy-ride of matrimony, and the altar is the forge where hearts are fused, from halter, to hitch.
57153-enchanted-india:
Enchanted India is a travel book by Prince Bojidar Karageorgevitch, written in French and translated by Clara Bell, published by Harper and Brothers in 1899 in advance of the French edition. The itinerary in the contents runs the whole subcontinent: Bombay, Ellora, Baroda, Ahmedabad, Palitana, Hyderabad, Madura, Calcutta, Darjeeling, Benares, Agra, Delhi, Lahore, Srinagar and Kashmir.

The book opens at sea, coasting the Indian shore by night. The water fills with medusae: white ones like ostrich eggs, and huge blue ones fringed with green. At daybreak the mist lifts on temple-shaped mountains and the rosy roadstead of Bombay. The style is the point: a Serbian prince's India, seen as colour, perfume and phosphorescence before it is seen as fact.
57364-adventures-in-bolivia:
Adventures in Bolivia is a travel book by Prodgers, printed in London in 1922. John Lane, the Bodley Head, put the book out that year in London. Cunninghame Graham wrote the introduction that stands before the tale. Pictures come from the author's own sketches and photographs on the road. A gold firm's headquarters on the Tipuani fronts the picture list.

The book is given to riders in high and lower altitudes alike. Graham says the tale breathes sincerity like a pine drops rosin. It shows a curious man who might step from Purchas or Hakluyt. It also clears mist from the lives of the Spanish conquerors of old. Those men were judged by foes in faith, race, and interest, he says. To-day their deeds get weighed on their merits by fairer eyes. Prodgers rides the high Bolivian ground and tells what he found.
57535-medical-sketches-of-the-expedition:
James McGregor wrote Medical Sketches of the Expedition to Egypt from India, printed at London for John Murray in 1804. McGregor served as surgeon to the Royal Regiment of Horse Guards. He had lately been superintending surgeon to the Indian Army in Egypt. He dedicated the sketches to the members of the Army Medical Board. The first part is a journal of the Indian expedition itself.

The second part treats the causes of the diseases that prevailed in the Indian Army. The third takes up the diseases in turn: the plague first, then the ophthalmia of Egypt. Fever, hepatitis, and dysentery follow, with pneumonia, small-pox, scurvy, and the guinea-worm. Tables state the diseases and deaths in the army. A closing section compares the yellow fever with the plague. The record served military medicine for years.
57580-on-sunset-highways-a-book-of-motor:
On Sunset Highways is a book of motor rambles in California by Thomas D Murphy. It belongs to a series called See America First, the hosted copy shows. Each volume of the series has a decorative cover and many pictures. Murphy also wrote a volume on Oregon for the same series. Prices of six dollars are listed for most of the set.

The list at the front ranges over the whole country. Titles treat New Mexico, Texas, Arizona, and Colorado. Canada, Alaska, and Utah earn volumes of their own. A wonderland of the East covers the mountain and lake country of New England. Virginia is seen from its historic river James in another volume. The California book thus sits in a shelf of scenic tours of its day.
57750-the-heart-of-asia:
The Heart of Asia, by Skrine and Ross, is a history of Russian Turkestan. Methuen issued it at London in 1899 with maps and plates. Skrine had served in the Indian civil service; Ross taught Persian in London. Nineteen plates from Verestchagin sketches join photos through the work in full.

Part one runs from earliest times to the Russian occupation of the khanates. Alexander, the Huns, Arab invasions, and Chingiz Khan fill its first sweep. Timur and his heirs, then the Shaybanides, carry the tale further on. Part two tracks Russia across the threshold into Central Asia in force. Railways, Bokhara, and Samarkand close the story to 1898.
57835-george-washington-birthplace-natio:
George Washington Birthplace National Monument, Virginia, is handbook number twenty six of the National Park Service. J Paul Hudson wrote it, and it was issued at Washington in nineteen fifty six. The book costs twenty five cents from the Superintendent of Documents. Its contents trace the Washington family at Popes Creek farm.

Early heads treat John Washington, then Lawrence Washington, then Augustine Washington. Augustine's early life, first marriage, and purchase of the Popes Creek farm follow. The building of the birthplace house takes a section of its own. A surveyor's picture stands near the front of the book. The series, a front note says, describes the historic and archaeological areas of the park system. It aims to conserve the nation's scenic, scientific, and historic heritage.
5789-personal-recollections-of-early-mel:
William Westgarth recalls early Melbourne and Victoria from personal experience, with portraits of pioneers like Edward Henty and John Pascoe Fawkner. Westgarth writes as a participant in the colony's founding decades, recalling streets, businesses, politics, and the men who shaped a new city. His recollections carry the tone of a memoirist who watched a settlement grow into a capital.

Readers get Australian colonial history from inside, without the polish of later official accounts. Westgarth's anecdotes preserve names, dates, and local color that formal histories often lose. The book suits readers of Australian history, Melbourne local history, and pioneer memoirs, offering a firsthand view of a city being built by its first generation.
58098-children-of-wild-australia:
Children of Wild Australia is a small book for the young by Herbert Pitts. Pitts had writ a past book on the black folk of that land and the church. Eight plates in full hue grace this book. It is given to a small girl, his own child, as a book on the black boys and girls of a far land.

In a note to his readers Pitts wishes he could take them all to the spots he saw in eight years there. He tells of a bright land where grass dies, streams dry, and young ones starve for food. Storms then flood the land, and flies and biters plague the young. Yet fair blooms rise past the rains, and love in the hearts of the young is the best bloom of all, he says.
58150-the-princess-sophia:
E F Benson wrote The Princess Sophia, issued by Thomas Nelson and Sons. Benson gave the book to a dear friend, critic, and sister. Twelve chapters plus an intro and an epilogue fill the novel. A plate shows the princess sweeping past a man with an air of utter scorn. Sophia is princess of Rhodopé, a small invented state on the wooded coast of Albania.

The intro places Rhodopé on the Adriatic, south of Greece border lands and north toward wider rule. Its base runs some twenty miles as the crow flies, but near a hundred by its bays and points. Chapters promise marriage bells, the last days of Prince Demetrius, and plots and counter plots. A fool comes to Rhodopé and a fool later leaves it. Benson mixes court farce, love, and statecraft in a light, sharp tale. Readers of Ruritanian romance will feel at home.
58226-the-ghost-in-the-tower-an-episode-:
A ghost tale by Earl H Reed, privately printed in 1921. The subtitle calls it an episode in Jacobia. Its narrator lays down a rule at once. A ghost never appears before more than one person at a time. Crowds would destroy the mystery ghosts need. His own encounter honours that rule.

The scene is a friend's country place in Michigan. A water tower stands high on the Jacobia hills. On Christmas Eve the narrator interviews its ghost alone. Winter presses on the Lake Michigan shore outside. Broken ice, bleak bluffs, and roving gulls fill the view. Nobody else can dispute the ghost's existence, he notes. He and the presence were the tower's only occupants. The tale keeps that playful, unverifiable charm.
585-running-a-thousand-miles-for-freedom:
William and Ellen Craft tell how they escaped slavery in Georgia in 1848, travelling a thousand miles to freedom in the North. Ellen, light-skinned, posed as a white gentleman, while William acted as her servant. The Crafts escaped in December 1848, travelling by train and steamer to Philadelphia.

Their narrative moves by train and steamer through dangers, questions, and close calls, told in plain, urgent prose. The Crafts later spoke in Britain against slavery, and their book remains a powerful firsthand account of escape. Their book, published in 1860, aided the abolition cause in Britain as well as America.
58794-the-englishwoman-in-russia:
The Englishwoman in Russia is a book of impressions by a lady who lived ten years in that country. John Murray printed it in London in 1855. Its subtitle promises the society and manners of the Russians at home. A frontispiece shows a review, with a charge of ten thousand cavalry.

The author, who dedicated the pages to her brother, skips the sea voyage from England to Archangel. Sea journeys, she says, all show the same features. She goes straight to the life she found in her long residence. The text takes care with Russian names, explaining the endings that mark a father's name. Written as the Crimean War ran its course, the book gave English readers a rare inside view of the enemy's drawing rooms and streets.
59270-armenia-and-her-people-or-the-stor:
Rev George H Filian, a native pastor banished by the Turkish Government from Marsovan in Armenia, wrote Armenia and Her People, or The Story of Armenia by an Armenian. The American Publishing Company at Hartford, Connecticut, issued the book in eighteen ninety six. Filian gave the book in remembrance of the martyrs of Armenia who sacrificed their lives for Christ. Ten chapters and many plates fill the volume.

Chapters treat the land of Armenia, its people, and its dynasties from oldest dates. Armenian histories and church records ground the tale. Rulers of the Ottoman Empire and the great powers and the Armenian question follow. Causes of the atrocities and a detailed account of the massacres fill the heart of the book. Plates show Mount Ararat, Kurdish bandits, an oriental threshing floor, and Armenian flags. Readers get a native, anguished history and plea.
59413-the-wooing-of-wistaria:
The Wooing of Wistaria is a love story of Japan by Onoto Watanna. It came out in 1902. The tale is told as the memories of the Lady Wistaria in her calm old age.

Her first memory goes back to babyhood and a long trip with her father. He carried her in his arms on foot for part of the way. At Yedo they stood in a hushed crowd and watched a great pageant pass. Shields, breastplates and prancing horses filled her eyes with colour. That early scene of pomp and dread frames her later tale of love. Her tale looks back on lost days with grace and calm.
59810-shenandoah-national-park-virginia:
Shenandoah National Park, Virginia is a park service guide for visitors. Its contents move from introduction to fun. At home in the park, Skyland, and Big Meadows follow. Lewis Mountain and the Drive take the middle. Geology, plants, wildlife, and the seasons stand in the list.

Shenandoah is one of seven national parks east of the Mississippi. It stands in the heart of Virginia's Blue Ridge Mountains, it says. Panoramas from the crest are its famous feature. The lush beauty of the slopes matches those views, the guide adds. Dickey Ridge center starts the northern visit. It stands just inside mile four and a fraction, it notes. Ranger-naturalists conduct field trips daily in summer to points of interest. Nightly campfire programs stand in the visitor's day as well. The guide gives a motor-age park in one small book.
6024-the-duke-of-gandia:
Algernon Charles Swinburne stages a Borgia drama set in Rome from 14 June to 22 July 1497. The persons include Pope Alexander VI, Francesco Borgia Duke of Gandia, and Caesar Borgia Cardinal of Valencia. Michelotto the agent, a Tiber waterman, two assassins, Vannozza Catanei, and Lucrezia Borgia complete the cast.

The play opens in the Vatican. There Caesar asks his mother whether he is less her son than his brother, and whether their holy father thrilled her womb with more Italian passion for the elder. Swinburne writes in high verse, turning family rivalry into a contest for Rome itself. Murder waits just offstage.
6037-the-one-woman-a-story-of-modern-uto:
Thomas Dixon Jr. dedicates The One Woman to his mother, whose Scotch love of romantic literature gave him a heritage of eternal youth. The chapters move from the man and the woman through visions in the night, a banker and his fad, a shorthorn deacon, and the cry of the city.

A stolen kiss, sweet danger, a spider, a black cat, and a broken heart-string lead toward the wedding of the annunciation, freedom and fellowship, and a new heaven. Dixon calls the tale a story of modern utopia, where love, faith, and social hope collide. Courtier and queen meet irony of fate.
6060-philistia:
Grant Allen opens Philistia with children of light, the coasts of the Gentiles, Magdalen Quad, and a little music, then Askelon Villa at Gath and a trip down the river. Ghostly counsel, the camp of the Philistines, the women of the land, and the daughters of Canaan follow, with culture set against culture.

Later chapters bring a quiet wedding, fire, literature, music, and drama, the Philistines triumphant, streets of Askelon, and clouds beginning to break. Ronald comes of age, a precontract of marriage is made, and the tide turns. Allen uses biblical names to stage a modern struggle between art and convention.
6081-biographia-literaria:
Samuel Taylor Coleridge opens Biographia Literaria with motives for the work, his first publication's reception, school discipline of taste, and Bowles's sonnets, comparing poets before and since Pope. Later chapters test the supposed irritability of genius against facts and weigh the charge's injustice.

Coleridge treats his debts to critics, modern criticism, Southey's works, the Lyrical Ballads, and the distinction between fancy and imagination. He traces association from Aristotle to Hartley, weighs dualism from Descartes through Spinoza, and defends his own poetic ground. The book is literary autobiography and theory in one.
6083-the-boy-allies-with-haig-in-flander:
Clair W. Hayes opens in Flanders rain, as Hal Paine and Chester Crawford creep from American trenches facing the enemy across No Man's Land. In the trenches all seems silent, as if men were dead or asleep, yet most sleep on their arms, ready for night raids, while vigilant sentinels watch.

Hal and Chester leave with full knowledge of those sentinels, lest they be shot by their own side. The Boy Allies serve with Haig and the fighting Canadians of Vimy Ridge, in a tale of trenches, raids, and alarms. Hayes writes wartime adventure for boys, where caution and courage share the night watch.
60955-the-polite-people-of-pudibundia:
R A Lafferty wrote The Polite People of Pudibundia, a short science fiction tale. It ran in Worlds of If Science Fiction in January nineteen hundred sixty one. The head note says good manners on that world mean more than work. They can mean death, it warns.

Pilots tell Marlow that the Puds never look straight at a guest. Each Pud wears tinted glasses fit for each bond. Amber serves for strangers, blue for new friends, red for kin. Worse, the Puds shift shape to match the guest they meet. Two young pilots who told such tales have died young. Speech there winds round and round to shun plain names. Marlow must learn why fine manners kill.
61428-with-lawrence-in-arabia:
Lowell Thomas told the tale of Lawrence in Arabia from his own road there. The book came out in New York and London in 1924. Chase took the first-hand photos that fill its pages. Thomas gave it to eighteen men of Chicago with thanks. He calls Lawrence a new knight of Arabia in his front words.

Lord Riddell and Louis Froelick of Asia spurred him to write. Elsie Weil and Alan Bott gave aid in the book's making. Dale Carnagey and his own wife share that warm thanks list. Thomas grants more fit men could tell the tale than he. Yet his own eyes saw the war of the sands at first hand. Wild deeds in a wild land fill it.
6145-tales-of-the-punjab-folklore-of-ind:
Flora Annie Steel gathers Tales of the Punjab, folklore of India. It opens with a preface to the little reader and stories like Sir Buzz, The Rat's Wedding, The Faithful Prince, and The Bear's Bad Bargain. Prince Lionheart and his three friends, the Lambkin, Princess Aubergine, and Valiant Vicky the brave weaver follow.

The Tiger, the Brahman, and the Jackal, the King of the Crocodiles, Little Anklebone, and the Jackal and the Partridge mix cunning with morals. Raja Rasalu's birth, journeys, forsaken friends, and giant-killing close the set. Steel preserves Punjab tales in English, told for children and kept for all.
61791-the-arab-conquests-in-central-asia:
The Arab Conquests in Central Asia is a history by Gibb, lecturer in Arabic at the School of Oriental Studies in London. It was printed in 1923 for the Royal Asiatic Society as the second volume of the James Forlong Fund. Five chapters and a list of chief works carry the story from the Oxus basin to the reconquest of Transoxania.

Gibb opens by calling the Oxus a boundary of tradition rather than of history. It never barred imperial armies, he notes, and Alexander fixed his frontier not there but on the Jaxartes. The chapters follow the early raids, the conquests of Qutayba, a Turkish counterstroke, and the winning back of the land beyond the river, all drawn from the Arabic sources.
62069-an-australian-ramble-or-a-summer-i:
J Ewing Ritchie, writing as Christopher Crayon, published an account of a summer in Australia at London in 1890. He dedicates it to Edmund Webb of Bathurst, New South Wales, under whose hospitable roof many pages were written. Chapter one, off to Australia, sails on the Orizaba. It mixes reasons for traveling, a bishop, soda and whisky, and the Spanish coast.

Gibraltar and the wickedness of Naples follow before Port Said. Chapter two runs from Egypt to Colombo, coaling at Port Said and passing the Suez Canal. Ritchie was a prolific journalist of popular travel. His ramble gives English readers a chatty tour of the colonies.
62403-sketches-in-holland-and-scandinavi:
Sketches in Holland and Scandinavia is a travel book by Augustus Hare. Hare also wrote Cities of Italy and Wanderings in Spain. George Allen published it in London in 1885. A preface dated November 1884 explains its modest aim. The sketches are only the result of ordinary tours, Hare says. Yet the days they recall were so delightful that he hopes others will follow. The tour in Norway left a specially sunny memory.

The contents divide the book into four country sections. Holland comes first, then Denmark, then Sweden, and last Norway. The Holland sketch opens at Roosendal, on the road from Antwerp. The travellers cross the boundary between Belgium and Holland there. They expect a marked change on reaching a new country. They hope to see Dutch paintings come to life at once. The book records a genteel tour in a plain, warm voice.
62622-savon-saloilta-kuvauksia-ja-muiste:
Lauri Soini wrote sketches and memories of the deep woods of Savo, a province of Finland. Otava of Helsinki published the book in 1896. The contents list holds sixteen short pieces. Their names range from a tale of two brothers to pieces on a pipe and a foal.

The first sketch tells of the old master of Lähdemäki. He was a cottage lad who built his farm with his own hands in cold forest, eating bark bread and toiling without rest. His two sons worked the farm in peace while their mother lived. Then the brothers courted at the same time and brought two mistresses into the house. The women quarreled over who should rule, and the men took sides. In the morning the brothers parted and split the land in two. The younger built a new farm in the forest and would not shake his brother's hand.
62637-the-princess-sonia:
Julia Magruder wrote The Princess Sonia, a novel put out in New York in 1895. Charles Dana Gibson drew the plates for the book. The first plate shows a fair young woman who steps back from her easel. The tale opens in Paris, in the Latin Quarter.

Martha Keene has worked for months in the art room of a master named Etienne. She looks frail, yet she has not missed a day of work. Her art is not bright, but she sticks to her task each day. That grit wins the notice of the old master in time. Plates show a tall old man, a bride, and the throng of her land folk in Paris. Love, art, and rank pull the cast through the tale.
63045-aunt-olive-in-bohemia:
Aunt Olive in Bohemia is a novel by Leslie Moore, published in 1913. Moore also wrote The Cloak of Convention. The book is dedicated to the author's mother. Its chapters open with The Beginning of the Fairy Tale and move into Bohemia, the artists' world of the title. A courtyard with six artists stands at the tale's heart.

Chapter titles promise a lady of the blue dress, a faun in the garden, and Princess Pippa waking. A fairy godmother interferes late in the story, and a ring of Eros appears. Barnabas schemes with Cupid in another chapter. The novel mixes London society with the art world in a light romantic vein.
63420-eight-lectures-on-india:
Mackinder wrote Eight Lectures on India for the Visual Instruction Committee of the Colonial Office, printed in London in 1910. Mackinder had led the London School of Economics and wrote on Britain and the seas. The talks were made to be shown with lantern slides in schools across the empire.

A full set of 480 slides, sixty for each talk, was sold with the book, many from views taken in India by Hugh Fisher. The board held that far flung lands of the empire could be held by shared knowledge of their maps, past, wealth, weather, and peoples. That knowledge, they held, had to reach the young in class. The talks thus serve as a school tour of India.
63451-california:
Ina Coolbrith wrote California, a long poem printed at San Francisco by the Book Club of California in 1918 in five hundred copies. John Henry Nash printed the book, with decorations by Lawrence Haste and a portrait by Dan Sweeney. The poem opens with questions: was it the sigh of leaves, the murmur of the meadow brook, or the voice of the far sea that sang within her shining shores?

Coolbrith hears the old song of the blind singer in the reeds, the rose musk, and the smell of laurel up the slopes of Tamalpais. California speaks in the poem and asks if she is less fair than the dead queens of far off shores. The Golden Gate shines as a gate of fire against the outer world in her telling.
64103-little-paulina-christmas-in-russia:
Little Paulina: Christmas in Russia was printed at Boston in 1906. Dana Estes issued the tale under copyright that year. Anna Robinson adapted it from Mary Cowden Clarke. The story opens on the day before Christmas. Snow falls thick and a keen north wind heaps the drifts. A man stands lost in the pine forest solitudes. His dress is a serf's: sheepskin tunic and cloak, bearhide gloves, wolfskin cap. Yet he is plainly a stranger in this country. He shouts for aid, and the frozen air deadens the sound.

An answering cry comes back, high-pitched and faint. A small dark figure, muffled in fur, moves toward him along a forest path. Only eyes, nose, and mouth show in the close sheepskin cap. The meeting sets the Christmas tale in motion, in a Russia of serfs and snow.
6424-a-modern-utopia:
H. G. Wells calls this book probably the last of a series beginning with Anticipations, written to clear a muddle in his mind about social and political questions. He meant Anticipations as his sole digression from imaginative writing, but questions he could not keep out of his work distressed him when touched in a stupid, haphazard way. A Modern Utopia answers them in fiction's form.

Old utopias were perfect, static states, Wells argues, a balance of happiness won forever against unrest. A modern utopia must be kinetic, a hopeful stage leading to a long ascent of stages. We build now not citadels but ships of state, floating on the great stream of things. Wells writes a dreamer's topography, where an agreeable, distracting Utopian talks and the author listens, learning his own hopes aloud.
64469-wages-in-1873-address-read-before-:
Thomas Brassey, a member of Parliament, read an address on wages in 1873 before the Social Science Association at Norwich, printed at London by Longmans the same year. In the following address I shall review, I hope in an impartial spirit, the most recent phases of the labour movement, he begins. The great advance of wages is a conspicuous feature of modern English industry.

The long depression after the panic of 1866 gave way to a time of great activity in every branch of export trade, he says. The demand for labour far exceeded the supply. Exports rose from 190,000,000 pounds in 1869 to 256,257,000 pounds in 1872. Workmen took their chance to win advances, and strikes pressed employers. Brassey, the great railway contractor, speaks as an employer who paid wages on three continents.
64684-hawkins-davison-houses-frederica-s:
Margaret Davis Cate wrote about two early houses at Frederica, on St. Simons Island in Georgia, in a piece reprinted in nineteen fifty-six. The piece first ran in The Georgia Historical Quarterly and was issued by the Fort Frederica Association. Fresh digging at the town site had stirred new interest.

Fort Frederica was founded in seventeen thirty-six under James Edward Oglethorpe as a guard post. It shielded Georgia and lands to the north from the Spanish in Florida. Forty settler families built the fort and the town beside it. The town held eighty-four lots in two wards, ringed by a moat and a stockade wall.
64697-children-of-india:
Children of India, by Janet Harvey Kelman, is a missionary children’s book with eight coloured illustrations. Fleming Revell published the volume at New York, Chicago, and Toronto. A village street shows among the first pictures of the book. The contents open with The Story of the World.

A story of India’s children follows that wide beginning, chapter by chapter. Kelman wrote for young readers at home about young lives abroad. Such books taught the children of the churches to picture India. Homes, schools, temples, and festivals fill her account in turn. The coloured pictures carry half the teaching for small readers. The book belongs to the great age of missionary publishing for children. Sympathy, in its pages, is meant to grow into giving.
64765-twenty-years-on-horseback-or-itine:
Twenty Years on Horseback, or Itinerating in West Virginia, is a preacher's memoir by Bishop Weekley of the United Brethren Church. The United Brethren Publishing House at Dayton, Ohio, issued it in 1907. Weekley had also written Getting and Giving and From Life to Life. His motto is the charge to take one's part in suffering hardship as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.

Portraits show Weekley at twenty and at thirty, and a view of traveling a district. The first chapter claims that the Virginias have turned out more United Brethren preachers than any other section of the same size between the oceans. These pulpiteers, he says, ranged in ability and efficiency from A to Z. A passage preserved in the copy honours the heroes who spent their lives building up their Zion among the Virginia hills. Many have gone to glory, he writes.
6506-old-mission-stories-of-california:
Charles Franklin Carter gathers seven short tales from the days of the old California missions, when Spanish priests and Native people shared a hard desert land. Most of the stories rest on a scrap of real past fact, while one, about Juana, is made up yet set against that same past. Desert lakes, dry hills, and mission walls give each tale its place.

A sibyl's warning, a priest on the run, hidden money, and a pious woman named Juana all pass through these pages in turn. Carter writes in a calm, plain style, keen to show daily life, faith, and fear as people then knew them. Readers get a gentle, old-style view of Nueva California before the missions faded.
65166-rambles-in-australia:
Rambles in Australia is a travel book by Edwin Grew and Marion Sharpe Grew, in Mills and Boon's Rambles series. The series note explains the plan: the books are not designed as guides, though up to a point they may be used as such. They are really very pleasant essays by writers who know their subjects, the Liverpool Courier is quoted as saying. They may be read with pleasure and instruction apart from any use to the traveller.

Companion volumes ramble around French châteaux, about the Riviera, and in the Black Forest, and with an American in Great Britain. The Australian volume carries one illustration in colour by Douglas Macpherson and thirty-two from photographs. Such rambles took their readers town by town and road by road, mixing scenery, history, and the daily life of the settlers.
65170-antonia:
Antonia is a novel by George Sand, held in a set of her works. This copy is the thirteenth volume of that house set of her tales. Prints show a tryst in a dark bower and a rite for a lily. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

The tale opens in Paris in April of the year seventeen eighty five. Lilacs crowd so thick at a young painters glass that blooms spill in. Julien paints flowers, as his sire did, in a small bright work room. Love for a great lady named in the plates then snares his calm life. Sand weaves art, rank, and heart ache in her lush French mode.
652-rasselas-prince-of-abyssinia:
Samuel Johnson writes a philosophical tale in this 1759 novella, printed here in Cassell's 1889 edition. Rasselas, prince of Abyssinia, lives in a happy valley yet longs to know the world, so he escapes with his sister Nekayah and the sage Imlac to test every way of life. Johnson wrote the tale in a week to pay his mother's debts and burial costs.

Johnson writes with grave, balanced prose, weighing courts, hermits, scholars, and lovers and finding each wanting. The tale asks whether happiness can be found in any single state. It endures as a classic moral fable, where a prince learns that choice itself, not contentment, is the human lot.
65440-an-introduction-to-the-birds-of-pe:
George Miksch Sutton wrote An Introduction to the Birds of Pennsylvania, a book put out in 1928. Sutton was the state bird man of Pennsylvania and head of its game board bureau for facts. A color plate shows Baltimore Orioles in an orchard in Adams County. His own pen and ink drawn views fill the text.

Sutton gives the book to his mother, with a jest in fond terms. She let him bring birds home, live, dead, or worse than dead, he says. The book is for those who start the study of birds in that state. It is not a full work of facts, and its notes on each bird are kept brief. Many birds on record in the state are left out on purpose.
65549-louise-queen-of-prussia:
Louise, Queen of Prussia is a short biography translated from the German of Heinrich Merz by George P Upton. A C McClurg of Chicago published it in 1909 in the Life Stories for Young People series, with three illustrations. Upton had translated other German lives for the same audience.

The translator's preface ranks Louise below no queen in purity and love. Greater queens, he grants, ruled in England, Russia, and Austria. None was purer, nobler, or lovelier than Louise, and none suffered more. She bore the calamities of her family, the insults of a victorious enemy, and her country's misfortunes. Napoleon's brutal attempt to destroy her reputation stains his own fame, Upton argues. The little life gave American young people a heroine of the Napoleonic wars, drawn from the German national memory of her.
65637-the-hawks-of-hawk-hollow-a-traditi:
The author of Calavar and The Infidel turns home to Pennsylvania for a tale of the Delaware valley. Carey, Lea, and Blanchard issued volume one at Philadelphia in 1835. The motto comes from Coriolanus, on the city of kites and crows.

The introduction plays with its reader. Hear me, but do not believe me, says Calderon, quoted at the start. The writer grants that facts run through the tale. He refuses to sort them from the fiction. That task, he says, would cost too much time and labour. He owns one fixed point of faith: the Delaware is the finest and noblest river in the world. That was a cardinal item of his childhood creed. The Hawks of the title give the book its wild, river-haunting family.
65976-archangel-the-american-war-with-ru:
A Chronicler wrote Archangel, the American War with Russia, in 1924. McClurg at Chicago put out the history that year. Cudahy is named as the chronicler inside the book. Nothing extenuate, nor set down aught in malice, stands as motto. The book is dedicated to a sergeant of the infantry.

Bowman died of wounds near Toulgas in 1919. Archangel and Gallipoli opens the contents of the history. Russia and the expedition's objects follow. The plan of campaign and the railway take the middle heads. Onega, Kodish, and Pinega stand as chapters. Retreat closes the contents of the northern campaign. Many people have asked about the Russian campaign, the author says. Why American soldiers went to Siberia, and what they did there. Blockhouses where men were crippled stand among its plates. The book gives intervention its American witness at last.
66275-wayside-sketches-in-tasmania:
Wayside Sketches in Tasmania is a travel book by Wintle, published at Melbourne in 1880. The author guides the reader through the island's districts in a series of sketches. The first, on north-eastern Tasmania, opens at a dreary junction called the Corners. There the traveller leaves the railway car for a four-wheeled conveyance toward George's Bay.

Wintle grants that Tasmania is noted for its healthy climate and fine scenery from end to end. Still, he claims the north-east coast near George's Bay beats all other parts. It joins majestic grandeur with gentle beauty, he says. The Corners itself he calls perhaps the dreariest, dullest spot on earth, a sheep run with a lone dreary hotel. That dull start only heightens the scenes ahead. Further on, at a hostelry kept by Herr Schmidt, the traveller meets the South Esk river for the first time since the city.
66643-byliny-book-hero-tales-of-russia:
Byliny Book tells hero tales of Russia for young English readers. Marion Chilton Harrison told the tales from the Russian for this book. Stewart drew the illustrations that stand through the Cambridge book of 1915. Heffer and Sons brought the work out while a great war ran on. Byliny means stories about what-has-been in Russia's old days, she explains.

Jason, Perseus, Theseus, and Heracles stand as the Greek names children know. Russia had splendid heroes too, who fought Huns and Tartars for freedom. Russia, France, Italy, and England stood side by side when she wrote. Four heroes fill this book: Volga, Mikula, Svyatogor, and Ilya the great. The Volga tale is quite short and easy, the preface promises. Russian letters in the pictures look strange but sound out kindly. Learning a people's heroes is a way to know the people.
66711-the-almond-in-california:
The Almond in California is an agricultural bulletin by Taylor, issued in August 1918. It is bulletin number 297 of the University of California's experiment station. The College of Agriculture at Berkeley published it. Its staff lists show the station's divisions, from horticulture to poultry husbandry. Taylor worked in the division of pomology. The almond, he writes, is supposed native around the Mediterranean.

The bulk of the world's supply still comes from that region. The tree resembles the peach in growth, blossom, and leaf. Its wood differs from the peach's, the bulletin begins to explain. California growers were then building an almond industry to rival the Mediterranean's. The bulletin gives them the station's tested knowledge. Varieties, soils, and culture are its practical field.
66954-memories-of-my-life-being-my-perso:
Memories of My Life is the autobiography of Sarah Bernhardt, the French actress. Appleton published it in New York in 1907. The subtitle promises personal, professional, and social recollections as woman and artist. Bernhardt begins with her mother and aunts, her nurse, and life in a concierge's lodge. She then moves to a boarding school at Auteuil run by Madame Fressard.

From there the contents trace her convent years at Grandchamps, the school plays, and her father's death. A family council argues over her fate, with the Duc de Morny advising that she be aimed at the stage. The memoir shows the making of the most famous actress of her age out of a sickly, willful convent girl. Bernhardt tells her own legend with the same flair she brought to her roles.
67536-letters-from-australia:
John Martineau wrote these letters from Australia, most of them in 1867, and Longmans published the book in London in 1869. The letters had appeared in the Spectator during 1867 and 1868. Some are reprinted unchanged, others enlarged, and others new. Martineau warns readers not to expect a complete account. He spent fifteen months divided among three colonies, far too little for countries so large.

He made no attempt to mould the letters into continuous history. The colonies old enough to have histories had them written already. He also confesses gaps: school education, for which some colonial legislatures deserved credit, never came under his notice. There are no exciting adventures and no bush rangers stopped him on the road. What the letters give instead is a thoughtful visitor's record of colonial politics and society in the eighteen sixties, written close to the scenes it describes.
67938-through-russian-central-asia:
Stephen Graham, the great walker of Russia, crossed her Central Asian lands in the last years of peace. Cassell printed Through Russian Central Asia in 1916, with plates from his own photographs. The tomb of Timour stands as its front piece.

Leaving Vladikavkaz opens the road south. Where the Desert Blossoms and Wonderful Bokhara follow. Mohammedan cities and their faith take a full part. The history of the tribes and the Russian conquest frame the present. To Tashkent, on the road, and the pioneers fill the middle. A midsummer night among the tent-dwellers and the Chinese frontier carry it east. Then war is declared, and the old road closes behind him.
6840-queen-lucia:
E. F. Benson opens Queen Lucia on a hot July morning, as Mrs. Lucas walks the half-mile from Riseholme station to her house, The Hurst, on her own brisk feet. Her maid and luggage go on in the fly her husband ordered, for after four hours in a train a short walk will be pleasant. Yet another motive, veiled even from herself, prompts the walk.

All Riseholme will know she arrives by the 12:26, and the village street will be full of friends at that hour. They will see the fly draw up with luggage, and no one but the maid get out, a little thrill for gossips. Benson writes with sly, social comedy. Queen Lucia is a sparkling tale of a village queen and her court.
68572-my-mother-india:
My Mother India is a book on India by Dalip Singh Saund, published at Stockton, California, in 1930 by a Sikh society. Saund held advanced degrees, and he dedicated the book to a beloved friend, a Sikh teacher. Its nine chapters form a survey of Indian life and politics for American readers.

The contents begin with the position of women in India, asking whether she is bond or free, and with the Hindu ideal of marriage. Chapters on the civilization and ethics of India and on the caste system follow. Then the book turns to politics: Gandhi and his message, India's experiment with passive resistance, and the massacre at Amritsar. It closes by asking why India is poor and by tracing the origin and growth of Indian nationalism. The first chapter opens with an ancient lawgiver's praise of honoured women.
69355-footing-it-in-franconia:
Footing It in Franconia is a book of walks and birds by Bradford Torrey. The author wrote a shelf of such walk books for keen home readers. Franconia here names the white hill realm in the state of New Hampshire. The book came out in Boston in the year nineteen hundred and one.

Parts track the year on foot: fall, spring, a June day, and berry time. Red leaf days, sky larks, and a still morn fill the back half in turn. A climb to a great peak and a vale day close the set of walks. A Lamb verse on each man and his bent sets the key up front. Soft sight of bird and leaf tunes the whole gay book.
69407-outposts-of-asia:
Outposts of Asia is a book of travel in the Far East. Morilla Norton wrote it and had it printed in Manila in 1909. She had writ verse on the isles and seas of that world. The trip was made by train, on lines of the crown road.

The road ran on the track of a late war in that part. Her route crossed the lands where the war had been fought. She went through the north lands, the mid land, and the isle realm. A pledge to a trade group in Manila shaped the end of the book. Its last part is on Manila and the isles she called home. The book opens with a grave song to her dead mother.
69529-the-aborigines-of-australia:
Richard Sadleir wrote The Aborigines of Australia, at Sydney in 1883. Thomas Richards, the government printer, put out the book. Contents open with origin, language, marriage forms, and relationships. Population, tribal divisions, intelligence, laws, and customs fill chapter one. Ceremony and funeral customs close that survey.

Chapter two treats religion, traditions, cave figures, and superstitions. Sorcery, diseases, songs, wit, and humour stand in its heads. Corroborees, weapons, manufactures, and dwellings fill the same chapter. The massacre of the crew of the Maria is told in it. Chapter three turns to the first settlement of the colony. Claims of the Aborigines and extracts from Collins stand there. Bennelong and Colebe, and massacres on the plains, take their pages. Efforts to civilize and missions to the lakes follow in the book. Sadleir gives a settler official's survey of the first peoples.
69996-the-dawn-in-russia:
Henry W Nevinson wrote scenes in the Russian revolution, published in 1906, with a frontispiece called Pacification showing the Kremlin of Moscow at Christmas 1905. Nevinson had reported the Ladysmith siege and the thirty days' war between Greece and Turkey. Contents begin with a summary of chief events since the Japanese war's outbreak in February 1904. Scandals of the war and Tolstoy's protest are listed.

The assassination of Bobrikoff and Plehve and the Zemstvo petition follow. Nevinson reported from Russia during the 1905 revolution. His dawn is the hope of constitutional change after Bloody Sunday. Harper published the book in London and New York.
70050-racehorses-in-australia:
Racehorses in Australia, with paintings by Martin Stainforth, was printed and published in Sydney in 1922, and in London by Constable. Stewart McKay and Ken Austin edited the large art book, with Harry Julius as producer. Color plates show famed horses such as Trafalgar, Musket, Carbine, Trenton, and Maltster. A whisky ad plate in the front is part of the book's period charm.

Essays treat the thoroughbred homes of Australia, the secret of staying power, and the great courses at Randwick and Flemington. Frank Wilkinson writes on famous racehorses, and a part covers racing in New South Wales. Fine printing, big plates, and expert text make a sumptuous record of the Australian turf.
70174-madam-constantia:
Jefferson Carter edited a romance of a prisoner of war in the Revolution, printed at New York and London in 1919. A fourth time I tried and, failing, gave over and laid my face against the saddle, a picture quotes from deep in the book. Sir Edward's preface opens the contents, then under King's Mountain and Madam Constantia herself.

At the smithy, the swamp fox, on parole, and Hickory Knob follow. The man with two faces, the court is closed, and the woman's part and the man's part fill the middle. The mill on the Wateree and Constantia at Saratoga close the tale. The Historical Manuscripts Commission has not printed the narrative of the fifth baronet's experiences in South Carolina among the Craven family papers, the editor says. Other sources show his regiment was the Thirty Third Foot. Love and captivity ride the Carolina war.
70331-educational-laws-of-virginia:
Educational Laws of Virginia is the personal narrative of Margaret Douglass, a Southern woman who was jailed for one month in the common jail of Norfolk under Virginia law. Her offence, as the title page states it, was teaching free coloured children to read. The Boston house of Jewett published her account in 1854.

Douglass opens by saying the public cannot be interested in her earlier life, and that her sudden notoriety was not of her own seeking. She stresses that she was not the agent or the voice of any association. Her case set her alone, as the narrative's closing pages put it, against the authorities of Norfolk and the whole strength of the state of Virginia. The book stands as a firsthand protest against laws that made literacy itself a crime for free Black children and for those who taught them.
70385-south-australia-and-western-austra:
Anthony Trollope wrote on South Australia and Western Australia from his travels. Chapman and Hall issued the part-work in London in 1874. It forms a slice of his larger book, Australia and New Zealand. Seven chapters treat South Australia, four treat the western colony.

South Australia alone of the colonies never held a single British exile, Trollope notes. Others began as convict depots or lived on forced labor for a time. Adelaide, land, wool, minerals, and the telegraph fill his survey. Readers gain a famed novelist's plain, sharp report on young colonies.
70575-marooned-on-australia:
Ernest Favenc wrote a tale of two men cast away on the coast of Australia. Diedrich Buys is said to tell the tale in his own voice. The year is set as about 1630 in the sub-title. Favenc wrote on the search past of Australia as well. He gave the book to a lost friend who loved that past.

In his front note, Favenc links two old threads of tale. One is a famed French trip to that south land. One is the wreck of the Batavia and its cruel deaths. Two of its mutineers were left on that wild shore. From their fate he weaves Paul and Diedrich's tale.
7071-in-times-of-peril-a-tale-of-india:
G A Henty sets In Times of Peril in India during the uprising of 1857, opening in bright, pretty cantonments at Sandynugghur in early spring. Contents promise life in cantonments, the outbreak, the flight, and broken down, then back under the flag and a dashing expedition. Delhi, a desperate defense, saved by a tiger, and treachery follow, with retribution, dangerous service, and Lucknow.

The besieged residency, spiking the guns, a sortie, and escape from Lucknow lead to the storming of Delhi, a riot at Cawnpore, and the relief and last capture of Lucknow. A sad parting and rest after labor close the tale. Henty writes the Mutiny as a boys adventure of siege, flight, and steadfast courage under fire.
70811-gloria:
Gloria is a tale by Mrs Southworth, first held in rights in eighteen seventy-seven. Southworth was known past the land for a long shelf of tales of love and strife. A list at the front names past fifteen of her books in cloth at a low price. A verse on blind rage heads the first part.

The tale opens on a small sand isle on the shore of a south state. A girl past her youth, fair, good, and rich yet in despair, asks a poor fish man of the estate to wed her. Her voice is low and firm, as one who stands on a burn ship and must pick her death. He takes off his old hat and waits her words in awe. The clash of her rank and his want sets the tale.
70854-the-countess-of-pembroke-s-arcadia:
Ernest A Baker edited this edition of The Countess of Pembroke's Arcadia by Sir Philip Sidney, printed by Routledge of London with Dutton of New York. Baker adds a life of Sidney and a long introduction, plus notes. The text takes in the additions of Sir William Alexander and Richard Beling, who wrote the sixth book.

Sidney began the romance for his sister, the Countess of Pembroke, while out of favor at court and living at Wilton House. It first appeared in 1590, four years after his death, unfinished. Its fame rivalled that of Euphues, and writers rushed to continue it. Baker traces its seed in Shakespeare's Lear, in Webster, and in Quarles's poem on Argalus and Parthenia.
70959-ikom-folk-stories-from-southern-ni:
Dayrell gathered Ikom Folk Stories from Southern Nigeria, printed at London in 1913. He was district commissioner in Southern Nigeria at the time. The Royal Anthropological Institute issued the set as occasional papers number three. His address line is 50 Great Russell Street in London. A preface tells how the tales came to him from native tellers.

Each story came through an interpreter, and often through two of them. Some tales are very old, handed down from generation to generation. Their true age is almost impossible to judge, he owns. Dowry is a word that comes often into the tales, he warns. It means the sum paid to a girl's parents by the husband. Andrew Lang had urged bride-price as the better term in an earlier book. A man's bush book of stick bundles counts his years of payment.
71028-friendless-felicia:
Friendless Felicia is a girls tale by Eleanora Stooke, or A Little City Sparrow. A Partridge house of London brought it out with four cuts. Felicia, age twelve, sews at a round stand by an attic pane. Her dam lies worn to a shade on a bed in that poor room. They dwell in a let house side street in the core of Bristol.

Blouse and apron piece work by the dam kept them these two years past. Sew hum racks her head and steals her sleep in the night hours. Part names run from attic home through white lilies to a waste place. A dog find, a grand sire meet, and church house kin fill mid parts. Uncle Guy fire, plain speech, and a storm close the scheme of parts.
71129-travels-in-nubia:
Travels in Nubia, by the late John Lewis Burckhardt, was published in London in 1819 by the Association for Promoting the Discovery of the Interior Parts of Africa. A portrait of Burckhardt at age twenty-four fronts the book. Front pages list the association's committee, headed by lords and by Joseph Banks, with Henry Salt and James Rennell among the members.

Burckhardt, a Swiss explorer who traveled in Arab dress, crossed Nubia toward the Red Sea and the Sudan. His journals record towns, tribes, trade, antiquities, and the hardships of desert roads, from wells and caravans to slave markets. Maps aid the text. The book, issued after his early death, stays a prime source on the Nile lands above Egypt in the 1810s.
71353-the-four-corners-in-california:
Amy Blanchard wrote this Corner tale, the Four Corners in California. Jacobs printed it at Philadelphia in September 1907. Contents open with Going Forth amid great home commotion in October. Nan flies up and down stairs like a hen on a griddle.

Mary Lee packs a leather satchel, Jean sops spilt ink off Jack. The old gentleman, among the missions, and hunting a home follow. The home of Ramona, a tournament of roses, and the tomale man appear. At the ranch, in Santa Barbara, and homeward bound close it. A little Scotch air brought bunny to his shoulder, one plate caption tells readers.
71379-mountain-life-in-algeria:
Edgar Barclay wrote Mountain Life in Algeria, issued at London in 1882 with pictures by the author. The book treats the land below the snow peaks east of Algiers. Folk there are Kabyles, of a race and tongue apart from the Arabs. Barclay says most English guests see too little of the district.

A day at Fort National is the most that most guests give the area. Barclay stayed longer and saw it with fresh eyes. He tells of old Kabyle rule, faith, and tribal law. Guest law was strict in old days, he notes. A village fund paid to feed guests, and each house took its turn. Safety of the guest and his goods was a shared charge.
71585-the-cave-dwellers-of-southern-tuni:
The Cave Dwellers of Southern Tunisia, by Daniel Bruun, was translated from the Danish and published by W Thacker and Company of London and Calcutta in 1898. Its subtitle is recollections of a sojourn with the Khalifa of Matmata. Bruun travelled from Tunis through Susa and Sfax to Gabés, then inland to the Matmata mountains. The book is at once a travel record and an account of a strange way of life.

At Matmata the people live in caves dug into the hills, and Bruun describes their dwellings, dress, and food. He attends bridal festivities at Hadeij and records songs and dances. Chapters treat the religion, language, and history of the cave folk, and the horsemen of the Tuareg. A supplement surveys the tribes of Tunisia and their costumes. Twenty four illustrations and a map support the text.
71756-the-humour-of-russia:
Voynich turned a set of Russian wit tales into English for this book. Stepniak wrote its first words. Paul Frenzeny drew its plates. The book came out in London in 1895. It sits in a Humour set with French, German, and more kin works.

Gogol's Marriage leads the list, and his Madman's Diary stands there. Gorbounov gives court and guest scenes of droll, dry talk. Ostrovsky adds a home scene and a pair ill matched in bent. Uspensky, both men of that name, fill the mid row of wits. Shchedrin's rogue tales and a famed crocodile tale by Dostoyevsky close it. A note from a past age ends the gay set. Stage wit and prose mix.
71863-nigeria:
E D Morel wrote Nigeria, Its Peoples and Its Problems. Smith, Elder and Company issued it at London in 1911. Morel edited The African Mail newspaper. He wrote Red Rubber and King Leopold's Rule in Africa before this. The book honors the memory of Mary Kingsley. Maps and photos aid the text.

Part One gives thoughts on trek through the country. Chapters treat the carrier, courtesy, and the meaning of religious. Part Two walks Southern Nigeria and the Niger Delta. Lagos earns the name future Bombay of West Africa. Part Three turns to the North and its old cities. Kano and its market get a full chapter. A reformer's survey of a new colony, the book presses British readers to look hard at rule abroad.
71971-an-ivory-trader-in-north-kenia:
An Ivory Trader in North Kenia is the record of an expedition by Arkell-Hardwick. Longmans, Green published it in London in 1903. Twenty-three illustrations from photographs, and a map, accompany the text. The journey ran through Kikuyu country to Galla-land in East Equatorial Africa.

The subtitle also promises an account of the Rendili and Burkeneji tribes. The first chapter is given wholly to preparations for the march. Engaging porters, choosing trade goods, and laying in arms fill its pages. Swahili, Nyamwezi, and Kamba porters are weighed against each other. The government refused to register the party's porters, the contents confess. Reports of native hostility and a past disaster darken the start. On the march the party meets flooded rivers, lions, and ticks.
72006-the-useful-trees-of-northern-niger:
H V Lely, assistant conservator of forests in Nigeria, wrote The Useful Trees of Northern Nigeria, published at London in 1925 by the Crown Agents for the Colonies at ten shillings. A plate of the kuka or baobab tree stands at the front. His preface says the text and plates were made for the naming of trees in the savannah forests of the north. The volume is in no sense a flora, and does not try to hold all the kinds found there.

Some one hundred twenty kinds, from thirty families, are set out in the order of their botanical names. Each account runs in order: form, height, girth, habitat, then bark, thorns, wood, leaves, flowers, fruits, and seeds, with notes on uses. Drawings from specimens show flower, leaf, thorn, fruit, and seed. Tables of flowering seasons close the book.
72360-a-year-in-russia:
A Year in Russia is a book of notes by Maurice Baring. Methuen brought it out in London, first printed in the year 1907. Baring had written With the Russians in Manchuria before this work. He gives the book to Lady Constance Lytton at its front. Lines from Dante and a saying of Doctor Johnson head the pages.

Nineteen chapters run from the capital to the opening of the Duma. The October strike and manifesto, then the Moscow December rising, come early. Chapters on the thinking class and the start of reaction follow on. Baring writes on parties, the land question, and Easter at Moscow. The foreign loan and the elections fill the later part of the book. Baring calls the whole a bundle of impressions from one year's stay. He claims no full or final word on Russia's great change.
72476-demonologia:
Demonologia, or Natural Knowledge Revealed, is an expose of old and new superstitions. Its title page names its theme in full: the credulity, zeal, and imposture of the ages. It ties them to the doctrine, caballa, and jargon of a long row of things. Amulets, apparitions, astrology, charms, demonology, devils, divination, and dreams stand in the row.

Deuteroscopia, effluvia, fatalism, fate, friars, ghosts, gipsies, and hell stand there too. Hypocrites, incantations, the Inquisition, jugglers, legends, magic, magicians, and miracles stand in the list as well. Monks, nymphs, oracles, physiognomy, purgatory, and predestination stand among them. The book was printed in London by W. Wilson of Skinner Street. It is a skeptic's survey of the world's false wonders, set out in alphabetic scope on its own title page.
72772-lavinia:
Rhoda Broughton wrote a novel whose heart is the young Lavinia Carew. The book came out in London and New York in 1902. Her past list names Goodbye Sweetheart and Cometh up as a Flower. Joan, Belinda, and Dr Cupid share that long shelf of tales. The first page finds Lavinia at the home of a woman called Prince.

I shall never get over it, that woman says as her wont. Lavinia hears it in calm, sure the grief will pass by next call. Yet this time her calm rests on a fresh ground of care. She holds her tongue for a cause quite flipped from the old. Heart plots and sharp talk mark Broughton's hand at work. Each call turns the screw.
7282-the-captivi-and-the-mostellaria:
Henry Thomas Riley translates two plays of Plautus literally, with notes: the Captivi and the Mostellaria. The Captivi opens in Aetolia with Hegio, father of Philopolemus, seeking a captive son, while Philocrates, an Elean captive, and his servant Tyndarus trade places in a plot of loyalty and disguise. An acrostic argument, supposed to be by Priscian the grammarian, lays out the tale: one son taken in battle, the other sold at four years old by a runaway slave.

Riley's plain version lets students follow Roman comedy without losing its jokes or its twists. The Mostellaria joins it as a second sample of Plautus at his most theatrical. Together the plays show captives, masters, parasites, and slaves in fast, humane farce.
72873-gloria:
Gloria is a novel by G. Frederic Turner, published in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1910. Colour illustrations by Relyea appear through the text, and the frontispiece shows a scene from late in the story. The chapter list runs to thirty-three chapters plus an epilogue.

Chapter titles sketch a European adventure. A patient meets his doctor, a bargain is struck, and the action moves through a ski-ing expedition, a chapel royal, and a war on a wine-shop. Figures named in the headings include Ulrich, Trafford, Meyer, and Bernhardt. A king stands at the centre of the plot, with councils, parleys, and recruits around him. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
72916-through-deserts-and-oases-of-centr:
Through Deserts and Oases of Central Asia is a travel book by Ella Sykes and her brother, Sir Percy Sykes. Macmillan published it in London in 1920. Ella Sykes also wrote Through Persia on a Side-Saddle. Her brother, a brigadier-general, wrote the history of Persia. A verse from Pushkin on losing the track in the wilds heads the book.

Part one crosses the Russian empire in war time. It goes beyond the Tian Shan to Kashgar and describes life at the consulate there. The Sykes pair travelled the old silk roads of Chinese Turkestan in 1915. Their book mixes desert travel, oasis towns, and the politics of the Great Game on China's frontier.
73127-early-german-music-in-philadelphia:
Early German Music in Philadelphia is a scholarly monograph in the Americana Germanica series. The University of Pennsylvania issued the series as its official publication. That programme studies the cultural relations of Germany and America. Marion Dexter Learned directed the institute behind the work.

The series list around this volume shows the field it works in. Translations of German poetry in American magazines stand as its first number. The Harmony Society earns a chapter of German American culture history. Schiller in America and Schwenkfelder hymn singing receive volumes of their own. The German settlement of Louisiana's coast closes the list before this number. Priced at one dollar, the music study takes its place in that survey. Philadelphia's German settlers and their musical life are its chosen ground.
73154-hypatia:
Hypatia, or Woman and Knowledge, is a short book by Dora Russell, put out at New York in nineteen twenty five. It stands in a set of small books on the days to come, named for two days in its own name. Its mates in that set treat the lore of the days to come, the fate of man, the dress of men, and the war of the fire craft.

The name of the book is that of a famed maid of the old world who taught deep lore in a great town of Egypt. She was slain by a mob of the new faith for her free mind and her sway past men. Russell takes that name as the flag of her theme: what the world of men has done to the lore of women, and what loss that bar has cost both.
73610-sketches-of-social-life-in-india:
Buckland, styled father of the Bengal Civil Service in 1881, sketched the social life of British India from long service. Allen printed Sketches of Social Life in India in London in 1884. Its first two chapters had run in the Army and Navy Magazine.

Buckland held, he says, nearly all the posts he describes. He knew the whole machine of Indian rule as seen from Calcutta and the Lower Provinces. Clubs, messes, hunts, and the round of calls fill such a book: how the rulers lived when off duty. He writes for home readers who knew India chiefly by its wars and its famines. A servant of the Raj shows its drawing rooms.
7385-old-calabria:
Norman Douglas travels through Calabria, the toe of Italy, and writes a book that is part travel tale, part history, and part folklore. His chapters wander from Saracen Lucera and Manfred's town to cave shrines, the land of the poet Horace at Venosa, and the Bandusian fountain. He stops in mountain villages, talks with locals, and digs into whatever past each place throws up.

Further south come brigandage, Albanian settlers and their college, the Greek-speaking Sila, and a chapter on Milton in Calabria. Douglas treats the region as a layered country: Greek, Roman, Byzantine, and Norman traces all lie close together. The result is a lively, opinionated guide to a corner of Italy that most travelers skipped, written by a man who plainly loved its rough edges.
74077-the-deseado-formation-of-patagonia:
Frederic Brewster Loomis wrote The Deseado Formation of Patagonia, printed in 1914. Loomis was professor of comparative anatomy at Amherst College. The book came out under the trustees of Amherst College. It reports the eighth Amherst expedition, of 1911, to Patagonia. A plate shows the skull of a great fossil beast at one-eighth size.

Contents open with the organization of the expedition and the history of the work. The Amherst locality and the age of its beds follow in the account. A table of the animals, their feeding habits, and their habitat comes next. The origin of the elements of the Deseado fauna gets its study there. Systematic chapters then describe the fossil mammals order by order. Strange names crowd those pages, from litopterns to toxodonts. Loomis gives a lost South American bestiary from the rocks.
74192-my-further-disillusionment-in-russ:
Emma Goldman published My Further Disillusionment in Russia with Doubleday, Page of Garden City in 1924. The book continues her earlier account, My Disillusionment in Russia. A publishers' note explains the odd history of the text. Twelve closing chapters reach print only here.

Goldman had been deported from the United States to Russia. She went expecting the nearest approach to a utopia yet produced. Experience cured that hope, and she wrote it down. The first book came out in 1923 missing its last twelve chapters. The newspaper syndicate that held the rights never handed them over. No one noticed until the book was already in circulation. The chapters printed here treat Odessa, Moscow, and Petrograd. Kropotkin's death and funeral, Kronstadt, and the persecution of anarchists follow.
74458-victoria:
Knut Hamsun wrote a short novel about young love in Norway. Arthur Chater turned it into English. This form came out in New York in 1923. The hero is Johannes, the son of a miller. As a boy he rows the rich man's young ones to an island. He knows each bird, tree, and stone near the mill.

The tale tracks Johannes as he grows and loves Victoria, the girl from the big house. Class stands between them at each turn. Small scenes at the mill dam and in the woods build the mood. Readers get a spare, sad love tale. Love, loss, and hope stay at the core of the short, tense tale.
74660-panama-to-patagonia:
Panama to Patagonia is a travel and survey book by Charles M Pepper, published at Chicago in nineteen hundred six. Its subtitle names the Isthmian Canal and the west coast countries of South America. Pepper, author of Tomorrow in Cuba, writes with maps and illustrations. He dedicates the book to his wife and his daughter, both named on the dedication page.

The Panama Canal was then being dug, and American eyes were fixed on the isthmus and the Pacific coast beyond. Pepper reports on lands, trade, politics, and peoples from Panama down to Patagonia. A mountain bridge fronts the book as a sign of the terrain. Commerce and curiosity drive the journey alike.
74776-the-early-court-of-queen-victoria:
The Early Court of Queen Victoria is Clare Jerrold's study of the young queen's world, published by Putnam in New York in 1912. Jerrold had written The Fair Ladies of Hampton Court. The contents begin before the crown, with Princess Victoria's relatives, her mother and uncle, and her tuition in politics. Her suitors get a chapter of their own.

Then come the accession, her advisers, her circle, and her prime minister. Later chapters treat her ladies and lovers, her disloyal subjects, and her tragic mistake. The book closes with her love, her early married life, her Tory ministry, and her home. Portraits of Melbourne, Peel, Wellington, Stockmar, and Prince Albert illustrate the text. Jerrold writes court history for general readers, with the personalities kept firmly in front.
74893-cousin-hunting-in-scandinavia:
Cousin-Hunting in Scandinavia is a travel book by Mary Wilhelmine Williams. Badger of Boston and Copp Clark of Toronto shared it in 1916. Williams held the rights and gives the book to Ella May Adams. Eleven chapters run from the entrance into Scandinavia to good-by at last. Riddarholm's Church in Stockholm fronts the illustrated travel tale here.

Copenhagen and its country gardens fill the first two chapters told. Bornholm and the Bornholmers get a chapter of island life next. Lund, Helsingborg, and Gothenburg introduce Sweden to the traveller's road. Stockholm, the two Uppsalas, Gefle, and Dalecarlia follow across the land. Trondhjem, Molde, the fiords, Bergen, and Christiania fill the Norway part. Roskilde and Odense close the cousin hunt in Denmark once more. Here I am at last in the land of the Viking, she opens. Danish soil was still home to her mother, she tells readers.
75292-travels-to-tana-and-persia:
Travels to Tana and Persia gathers old Italian travel tales in one volume. Josafa Barbaro and Ambrogio Contarini stand as the two named travellers. The Hakluyt Society issued the book in its first series in 1873. Burt Franklin of New York later reprinted the society's edition whole. Lord Stanley of Alderley edited the tales with an introduction added.

William Thomas turned Barbaro's tale from the Italian in Tudor days. Roy rendered Contarini's narrative into English for the society's readers. Six narratives by Italians of travel in Persia fill the full set. Their journeys fell about the time of Shah Ismail's reign there. Tana, the old trading post by the Don, names Barbaro's road east. Old spellings and small inconsistencies stand kept as first printed here. A list of printing faults found stands printed at the end.
75542-the-coins-of-india: The Coins of India belongs to the Heritage of India Series, a set of short books on Indian religion, art, and history, edited by Bishop Azariah of Dornakal and the scholar Farquhar. Other volumes treat Buddhism, the emperor Asoka, Indian painting, and Tamil hymns. This volume takes up coinage, the small struck record of India's rulers and trade. The opening pages here are the series list and proposed subjects, so the coin chapters lie beyond this head.
75968-the-minute-boys-of-philadelphia:
The Minute Boys of Philadelphia, a boys tale of the Revolution by James Otis, was copyrighted in 1911 by Dana Estes and Company of Boston. Pictures by L J Bridgman go with the text. Otis wrote a string of Minute Boys books, for Long Island, the Wyoming Valley, and other grounds of the war.

The narrator is one of the lads who served the patriot cause while General Howe held the city. He swears he does not mean to blow his own horn, and begs pardon if he seems of too much consequence. Sixteen chapters run from a spy and a suggestion through Swede's Ford, Valley Forge, and Barren Hill. A carnival, a jail wall scaled, and a narrow escape spice the duty. Men high in the army, the boys were told, praised their small work.
76058-aspasia:
Aspasia, a romance of art and love in ancient Hellas, is a historical novel by Robert Hamerling, translated from the German by Mary Safford. This first of two volumes appeared in New York in 1882. Its subject is Aspasia of Miletus, the celebrated companion of Pericles, set at the height of Athenian glory.
