Restoring work ran from 1872 to 1878. A castle, a new town hall, and a priests' school fill out the town. Cloth, tobacco, soap, machines, pots, and leather are made there. Its own counts ruled till 1414. Trier then bought the place, and Nassau took it in 1803. Austrians beat the French here in September 1796.
britannica-1911-lissa-dalmatia:
Lissa is an island in the Adriatic Sea, part of Dalmatia in the Austrian realm. It is the far most isle of its chain, set south of a great port town. Its shape is a long rough square, ringed by a wall of rock that guards a rich plain at its heart.

Rock breaks on three sides form fine natural ports, the 1911 Britannica entry says. Its high point is a mount in the south west. The isle splits between two communes named for its chief towns, one north and one west. The north town, the seat of rule, has a strong fort port, the palace of old Venetian counts, and a friary. Near it lie the ruins of the old city that stood there in Greek and Roman times.
britannica-1911-lobelia:
Lobelia, a plant genus, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It is the typical genus of its tribe in the bellflower order. The name honours Matthias de Lobel, a native of Lille who was botanist and physician to James the First. The genus numbers about two hundred species. They are native to nearly all the temperate and warmer regions of the world.

The plants are annual or perennial herbs or under-shrubs, rarely shrubby. Remarkable tree-lobelias grow at high levels on the mountains of tropical Africa. Two species are British, in lakes and on Dorset and Cornwall heaths. The genus stands apart from Campanula by its irregular crown and fully united anthers. The earliest described species appears to be the cardinal flower of eastern America. Several species are grown as ornamental garden plants, including a dwarf blue one from the Cape.
britannica-1911-louis-ii-of-bavaria:
Louis the Second, king of Bavaria from 1845 to 1886 in the years of his life, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a son of Maximilian the Second and Maria, a daughter of Prince William of Prussia. He was born at Nymphenburg on 25 August 1845. His brother Otto was three years younger.

Their learned father set a plain and grave course of schooling for both boys. It was shaped on the German Gymnasien, with the old tongues of Greece and Rome at its core. Of modern tongues the prince learned only French, which he loved all his life. The training had small use in real life. He got his first pocket money at age eighteen and knew little of what money was worth.
britannica-1911-lucania:
Lucania was a district of southern Italy in ancient geography. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica stretches it from the Tyrrhenian Sea to the Gulf of Tarentum. It took in most of modern Basilicata and parts of Salerno and Cosenza. Rivers Silarus and Bradanus marked its north bounds on two sides.

Apennine masses fill almost the whole of the district in height. Monte Pollino, its high peak, tops seven thousand feet in the south Apennines. Rivers to the Tarentum gulf outweigh short streams to the west sea. The Lucani people who gave it its name won it in the fifth century BC. Greek colonies held its coasts before that conquest came.
britannica-1911-lycaonia:
Lycaonia, a large region in the inner part of Asia Minor, is described in a geography entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Taurus mountains bound it to the south, Cappadocia to the east, and Galatia to the north. Its bounds shifted a great deal across the ages. Xenophon names it on the march of Cyrus, and the Acts place Lystra within it.

Strabo calls Lycaonia a cold land of high plains, good pasture for wild asses and sheep. It is part of the inner tableland and stands more than three thousand feet high. Lack of water is its chief flaw, made worse by salt in the soil. The north part is near barren save for small patches near towns. Where water is stored and shared with care, the soil yields well. In old times such care let the land hold many cities.
britannica-1911-lycia:
Lycia, in ancient geography, was a district in the south west of Asia Minor, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It held the coast between Caria and Pamphylia. Inland it reached as far as the ridge of Mount Taurus. The region is a peninsula that juts southward from the great mountain masses of the interior.

For the most part it is a rugged mountain land. Spurs of the Taurus range cross it and end on the coast in high headlands. The coast is cut by a run of bays, though less than the coast of Caria. The most marked bay is the Gulf of Macri in the far west. Several ranges bore their own names in ancient times. One central peak rose to ten thousand feet, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-lydia:
Lydia, a district of Asia Minor in ancient times, is the subject of a history entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its borders are hard to fix, the entry warns at the start. They varied a great deal at distinct epochs in the past. The name first appears in Assyrian inscriptions in a slightly distinct form.

In Homer the people appear under another name, the Maeonians. The place of Sardis, the later capital, is taken by a town called Hyde. The earliest Greek writer to use the name Lydia is named and dated. Herodotus is then brought in as a key source. The entry sorts a tangled early record with care.
britannica-1911-macedonia:
Macedonia, as treated in this 1911 Britannica article, was the name then given to a part of European Turkey. It was bounded north by the Kara-Dagh range and the frontier of Bulgaria, east by the river Mesta, and south by the Aegean Sea and Greece. The Macedonia of old times was smaller, lying inland west of the Axius river.

Most of the land was lived in by a Slavonic people, mainly Bulgarian in character, with Greeks along the coast and in the south. Turks, Vlachs, and Albanians lived in scattered groups. The coast is broken by the Chalcidice peninsula, with its three points of Athos, Longus, and Cassandra. The river Vardar splits the country in two, and its valley has always been the main route from central Europe to the Aegean.
britannica-1911-malaria:
Malaria is an Italian word, from mala and aria, bad air. Macculloch brought it into English medical writing in 1827. It took the place of older, narrow terms such as marsh miasm or paludal poison. The word names a clear ill state of the body known by many names. They include ague, marsh fever, jungle fever, hill fever, and fever and ague. A single fit of plain ague may strike a man in full health, or it may come after a spell of low spirits.

The fit of ague starts with chills that seem to rise from the low back. The cold spreads till it takes the whole body. Shakes of the muscles go with the cold, from the jaw to the limbs and trunk. The face turns pale or dark, with rings under the eyes. The skin shrinks, the features pinch, and the fingers look dead, the article says.
britannica-1911-manchuria:
Manchuria is the name by which Europe knows the land of the Manchus in the east of Asia. The Chinese call it the country of the Manchus. The name Manchu means pure and was chosen by the founder of the line that now rules Manchuria and China. The land runs from 39 to 53 degrees north and from 116 to 134 degrees east.

China and Mongolia bound Manchuria on the west and north-west. Korea and the Russian land on the Amur bound it on the east and north. The Amur river bounds it on the north and the Usuri on the east. The land so set out is about 800 miles long and 500 miles wide. It holds about 390,000 square miles. It splits into three provinces: a northern, a central, and a southern one.
britannica-1911-manfredonia:
Manfredonia, a town in Apulia in Italy, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It sits on the coast south of Monte Gargano and gives its name to the gulf east of it. Its people numbered 11,549 in 1901. Manfred founded it in 1263, and the Turks destroyed it in 1620. The castle of the Angevins and parts of the town walls still stand in good shape.

The article notes old paintings of the fourteenth century in one church chapel. Two miles south-west stands the fine church of Santa Maria Maggiore di Siponto, built in 1117 in the Romanesque style, with dome and crypt. That spot marks ancient Sipontum, the port of Arpi, which became a Roman colony in the year 194 before Christ and was left only in the thirteenth century.
britannica-1911-marsupialia:
Marsupialia is the group of mammals whose young ride in a pouch. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica takes the name from the Latin for a bag. The female carries her young in that pouch after birth. Some ranks set the group as a subclass beside the monotremes. Others group it with the placental mammals instead. The entry weighs both views at length.

It warns that the gap between monotremes and marsupials is vast. That gap far outruns the gap between marsupials and placentals. Marsupials bear live young in a raw, unformed state. The young fasten at once to the teats, usually inside the pouch. Two small bones at the pelvis mark the whole group. No true placenta links parent and young in most kinds. Where one forms, it stays incomplete. Teeth come in a full set of four kinds.
britannica-1911-maximilian-i-king-of-bav:
Maximilian the First, king of Bavaria, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. His full name was Maximilian Joseph. He lived from 1756 to 1825. He was the son of the count palatine Frederick of Zweibrücken-Birkenfeld. He was born in May 1756.

He was carefully educated under the watch of his uncle, Duke Christian. In 1777 he took service as a colonel in the French army. He rose quickly to the rank of major-general. From 1782 to 1789 he was stationed at Strassburg. At the outbreak of the revolution, he changed to the Austrian service. He took part in the opening campaigns of the revolutionary wars. In April 1795 he succeeded his brother as duke of Zweibrücken. In February 1799 he became elector of Bavaria. That came on the extinction of the Sulzbach line. The article opens a reign that would turn an elector into a king.
britannica-1911-maximilian-ii-king-of-ba:
Maximilian the Second, king of Bavaria, is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a studious king who came to the throne in the year of revolutions. Born on the twenty-eighth of November 1811, a son of King Louis the First, he studied at Gottingen and Berlin and travelled in Germany, Italy, and Greece. He said that had he not been born in a royal cradle he would have chosen to be a professor. As crown prince he gathered artists and scholars about him at Hohenschwangau.

His father's abdication in March 1848 raised him to the throne with hopes of a liberal rule. Yet he would not serve the clerical reaction, and he called famed scholars such as Liebig and Sybel to Munich whatever their faith. In 1859 he dropped the reaction ministry and granted a moderate constitution. He died at Munich in 1864.
britannica-1911-meloria:
Meloria is a rock isle ringed by a shoal, set past the port of Leghorn. It was the scene of two sea fights of the mid age. The first, in twelve forty-one, set a chiefs fleet and Pisa past a fleet of Genoa. That fleet bore church lords to a meet at Rome.

Three ships sank and more than twenty were took, and lords died or were seized. The next fight, in twelve eighty-four, holds more weight in the tale of those days. It broke Pisa as a sea power for good. Old foes had clashed for two years past twin claims to two isles.
britannica-1911-mercia:
Mercia is a history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It tells of one of the kingdoms of Saxon England in old times. The first realm lay in the high basin of the Trent river. Its name seems to mean the men of the border march.

The entry traces how the realm grew to swallow land after land. In time it took all the ground between two great rivers, and more past them. The roots of the realm stay dark, and its first kings are half myth. One early king wed his child to a northern king of fame. For a time the realm bowed to that northern king sway.
britannica-1911-mesopotamia:
Mesopotamia is a Greek name for the land between rivers. It renders older Semitic names for the river country that stretches east from north Syria. The first known Semitic name of this kind stands in the life of Ahmose of el-Kab, an old officer of the pharaoh Tethmosis I. As early as the late sixteenth century BC, the name Naharin was in use for that land.

The Egyptian scribes plainly tied that name to their word for a river. They wrote it with the water sign as well as the land sign. Yet they show no hint that they took the name as a plural form. The article asks if that sense of the word as a single name lived on to early Christian times. It notes that the Targum of Onkelos renders Naharaim by a phrase tied to the Euphrates river.
britannica-1911-messallina-valeria:
Valeria Messallina is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the third wife of Claudius, emperor of Rome. The text brands her with greed, ambition, and a wild life. With the help of the emperor's freedmen she held full sway over her weak willed husband.

The article tells how her rule ended in blood. While Claudius was away from the city, she forced a young man to wed her in full form. A freedman who feared her wrath told the emperor what had been done. He won consent for her removal from life. She was put to death in gardens she had seized from a slain foe. She was twenty six years old at her death, the text says.
britannica-1911-micronesia:
Micronesia, from Greek words for small and for isle, is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as one of three great parts of the isles of the Pacific. It lies north of the part called Melanesia. Five isle groups are named in its bounds. Notes send the reader to the tales of those groups.

The folk of these isles form in the main a branch of the great stock of the Pacific isles. Yet they stand apart from that stock in marks of face, of tongue, and of rule of life. More than one tract shows marks of mixed blood as well. The nearness of Japan is one cause. The Papuan isles to the south are a cause too. In some spots the slant eye of the north is seen.
britannica-1911-middletown-pennsylvania:
Middletown is a borough of Dauphin county, Pennsylvania, on the east bank of the Susquehanna river. It lies nine miles below Harrisburg. Its people numbered 5,608 in 1900 and 5,374 in 1910. The Pennsylvania and the Philadelphia and Reading railways serve the borough. A tram line also links it with Harrisburg. The borough does a fair trade with the farm country round it.

The nearness of the Yorkhaven power plant, across the river, helps make Middletown a centre of making. Good rail service helps it in that role as well. The town owns its own plant for electric light. Friends from Philadelphia and other parts of the state set up the town in 1755, with Scotch-Irish settlers beside them. Its name comes from its place midway between Lancaster and Carlisle. It was first made a borough in 1828.
britannica-1911-morata-olympia-fulvia:
Olympia Fulvia Morata, born at Ferrara in fifteen twenty six, was an Italian scholar of the classics. Her father had tutored the young princes of the house of Este. He moved among the most learned men of Italy, and his daughter grew up amid classical learning. At twelve she could converse with ease in Greek and Latin. She was then called to the palace at Ferrara.

At court she served as companion and teacher to Anne, daughter of the duchess Renee. Her father died a convert to Protestant faith, and her welcome at court cooled. She withdrew to her mother's house and took up the doctrines of Luther and Calvin. About fifteen fifty she wed a young student of medicine from Bavaria. War and siege later drove the pair from his home town to Heidelberg.
britannica-1911-moravia:
Moravia is the subject of a land entry in the 1911 Britannica. Moravia was a crown land of Austria at that time. Hungary, Lower Austria, Bohemia, and Silesia bound it round. Its area is given as over eight thousand square miles. In form it is a high plateau tilting south. Ranges of hills bound it on three of its sides. The Sudetes rise along its northern edge in height.

A river called the March gives the land its name. That river rises in the hills inside its bounds. It runs the full length of the land southward. It then joins the Danube near Pressburg town. Side streams from the hills feed it on the way. The Oder also rises in the north east hills. No stream in the land bears boats, save one short reach. Notes on springs and on the weather close the part shown.
britannica-1911-morelia:
Morelia, once called Valladolid, is a city in Mexico and capital of Michoacán. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it high on the Mexican plateau, west of Mexico City. Its people passed thirty seven thousand in 1900. A rail branch and a small tram line link its station to the center.

Streets form a neat grid with squares across a rocky hill site. Its cathedral shows fine old Spanish church craft in Mexico. An onyx font and silver shrine doors mark its rich interior. Water reaches the city by a long arched aqueduct built in 1785. The college of San Nicolas there is the oldest such school in Mexico.
britannica-1911-mott-lucretia:
Lucretia Mott is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was an American reformer born on Nantucket in seventeen ninety three. Her kin were among the first to settle that isle in old times. At a Friends school she met the man she would wed in time.

The entry tells how she taught school, then was known as a Friends preacher. Her husband left a rich trade so as not to gain from slave work. Both threw their strength into the fight to end slavery in their land. When her church split on points of faith, she took the more free side. Her voice in church and hall swayed crowds for just laws.
britannica-1911-mysia:
Mysia was a district of northwest Asia Minor in ancient times. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica fixes its borders and chief towns. Lydia and Phrygia bounded it to the south. Seas washed its north and west shores. Its exact edge toward Phrygia shifted and stayed vague.

Two mountain chains cross the land, Olympus and Temnus. Lakes and three rivers drain its north and south parts. Pergamum in the Caicus valley was its most famed city. Cyzicus on the Propontis ranked near it in weight. Greek towns studded the whole coast from end to end. The Mysi were a people apart, kin to Lydians and Carians. Shared rites at a great temple of Zeus prove that kinship. They never stood as a free nation in history, though.
britannica-1911-nara-india: Nara, an important water channel in Sind, India, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It probably represents a former bed of the Indus river, though it now crosses the desert far east of that river. Its total length is 250 miles. By means of cross cuts, weirs, and embankments, it has been made to irrigate no less than 429 square miles of land. Its navigable length is given as 425 miles, a striking figure for a desert channel.
britannica-1911-neuralgia:
Neuralgia is pain along a nerve or its branches with no clear change in the nerve itself. A 1911 Britannica medical entry gives the Greek roots as nerve and pain joined. Strict use needs no seen source of harm in nerve or centre at all. In real cases a source of pressure or rub is often found on search.

So the word in practice covers nerve pain from any cause that doctors meet. Few ills cause greater suffering to the sick, the entry states plainly at length. It most often strikes folk whose health is low or worn down. Poor food, strain, and gouty or rheumatic stock raise the risk of attacks.
britannica-1911-neurasthenia:
Neurasthenia was the general medical term for weakness of the nervous system, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists its signs in detail. The word joins the Greek words for nerve and for weakness. The entry warns that its signs vary widely from case to case.

Among the signs are a general ill feeling mixed with excitement and low spirits, headache, giddiness, and broken, unrefreshing sleep. Memory weakens, sight blurs, and ringing sounds trouble the ears. Coldness in the hands and feet, flushes, weak muscles, poor digestion, and racing of the heart all appear. The entry notes that the clear signs of organic disease are absent, while the knee-jerks are usually too lively.
britannica-1911-nomentana-via:
Via Nomentana is an old road of Italy in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It leads north east from Rome to Nomentum, a run of fourteen miles. At first it bore the name Via Ficulensis, from the old Latin village of Ficulea. That village lay about eight miles from Rome on the route.

The road was later pushed on to Nomentum as its end. It never rose to be a great highroad of the land. A few miles past Nomentum it merged into the Via Salaria. The modern highroad still follows it as far as Nomentum. Traces of its old stone paving still exist along the way.
britannica-1911-norcia:
Norcia is a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town in the province of Perugia in Italy. Its old name was Nursia. The town stands high, at 1,980 feet, at the foot of the Sibillini hills, and old walls still ring it.

The article counts 4,261 people in the town in 1901. It names a cathedral, a church of Saint Benedict, and a town hall with old arcades. Quakes hurt the town badly in 1730 and in 1859. The old town was a Sabine city that fought Rome's Octavian and paid for it. Norcia was the birth place of Saint Benedict, who founded a great order of monks. Pork goods and cloth are its famed trades.
britannica-1911-northumbria:
Northumbria, one of the chief Anglo Saxon kingdoms, stretched from the Humber to the Forth, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its early history as a king list with notes. It began as two free kingdoms, Bernicia and Deira, each with a royal house of its own. The first known king of Bernicia was Ida, who took the throne in 547 by tradition.

Ida is said to have founded Bamburgh, and four of his sons held his throne in turn. Of the first three nothing is known, but Theodoric was beset by the Welsh under Urien on Lindisfarne. Then came Aethelfrith, who spread his lands at Welsh cost and beat Aidan, king of the Scots, at Daegsastan in 603. For Deira, the first known king was Ella, still on the throne, by Bede's account, when Augustine reached England in 597. The entry weighs the Chronicle against Bede with care.
britannica-1911-nova-scotia:
Nova Scotia, a province of Canada, is the subject of a long entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is made of a mainland peninsula and the island of Cape Breton. A strait splits the island from the main land. A narrow neck joins the province to New Brunswick.

Chains of hills cross the land from east to west. The Cobequid range forms the chief ridge. Some heights reach eleven hundred feet and can be farmed near their tops. Rich farm tracts lie on each side of that range. A ridge of cliffs runs along the Bay of Fundy for a long stretch. Past those cliffs lies the Annapolis valley, called the garden of Nova Scotia. The Atlantic coast is high, with many good harbours.
britannica-1911-offa-king-of-mercia:
Offa (died 796) was king of Mercia, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows his grasping reign. He won the kingdom in the year 757 after driving out Beornred, who had followed the murdered Æthelbald. Offa traced his line back through Eowa, brother of Penda, and his own father was named Thingferth. In 779 he fought Cynewulf of Wessex and took Bensington from him.

About that time the Thames likely became the border between the two kingdoms. In 787 Offa showed his power at a church council. He stripped the archbishop of Canterbury of several sees and gave them to Lichfield, raised with the pope's leave into an archbishopric of its own. At the same meeting he had his son Ecgferth consecrated as his partner in rule. In 789 he won Berhtric of Wessex as an ally by giving him his daughter in marriage.
britannica-1911-olbia-sardinia:
Olbia was an old seaport city of Sardinia, on the east coast of the island, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sketches its past. The name is Greek and means happy, and the town was later called Terranova Pausania. Custom credits its founding to Boeotians and Thespians led by Iolaus. One scholar held instead that Phocaeans from Massilia founded it before the fourth century before Christ.

The city stood on low ground at the head of a deep bay. Cornelius Scipio besieged it without success in 259 before Christ. A Carthaginian fleet ravaged its lands in 210 before Christ. In Roman times Olbia was the usual landing place for travellers from Italy. Cicero mentions getting a letter from his brother there, which shows its place on the route.
britannica-1911-oswald-king-of-northumbr:
Oswald was king of Northumbria in the early age of the English kingdoms, one of the sons of a great king of the north. Driven from his land when a rival took the throne, though that rival was his uncle, he spent part of his exile on a holy isle of the Scots. There he was taught the faith of Christ.

In time he beat and slew a British king in battle at a stream named by a great church writer. By that win he paid back the death of his brother, who had held one half of the north realm. Oswald then took the crown and joined the two halves of his land as one. He raised his realm to the height it had held in his uncles day. His reign is marked by a close pact with the Celtic church.
britannica-1911-paeonia:
Paeonia, in ancient geography the land of the Paeonians, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The borders of the land, like the early history of its people, are very obscure. The Paeonians are regarded as descendants of the Phrygians of Asia Minor. Large numbers of Phrygians crossed into Europe in early times, the entry explains.

National legend, told by Herodotus, made them Teucrian colonists from Troy. Homer speaks of Paeonians from the Axius river fighting beside their Trojan kin. Before the reign of Darius they had pushed as far east as Perinthus in Thrace. At one time all Mygdonia and Crestonice were subject to them, the entry says. They held the whole valley of the Axius as far inland as Stobi. Emathia was once called Paeonia, and Paeonians lived in Pieria and Pelagonia as well. Macedonian growth and Thracian pressure later shrank their land.
britannica-1911-pamphylia:
Pamphylia, a region of the ancient world, is mapped in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lay in the south of Asia Minor, between Lycia and Cilicia. It ran from the sea coast up to Mount Taurus. Pisidia bounded it on the north.

The land was small in size. Its coast ran for about seventy five miles, with a breadth of about thirty miles. The entry holds that the folk of Pamphylia and Pisidia were the same people at root. Greek and other settlers joined the coast folk in time. With richer soil, they grew more settled and skilled than their kin in the hills. Herodotus names the coast folk but not the hill folk. The piece gives a clear frame for the old map of the south coast.
britannica-1911-pannonia:
Pannonia, a land of the ancient world, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Danube bounded it on the north and east, with Noricum and upper Italy to the west and Dalmatia and upper Moesia to the south. It thus matches the south-west part of Hungary, with bits of lower Austria, Styria, Carniola, Croatia, and Slavonia. Its first known people were most likely of Illyrian stock.

The article traces waves of change. From the fourth century before Christ, Celtic tribes moved in. Rome first struck in the year 35 of that era, when Augustus took Siscia. Full control came only later, and in the year 10 after Christ Pannonia was set up as its own district, after a hard two year revolt had been put down. The entry gives a clear map in words of a border land of the empire.
britannica-1911-paphlagonia:
Paphlagonia is a history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes an old district in Asia Minor on the Black Sea coast. Two rivers mark its west and east bounds in the old books. Its folk count among the most ancient peoples of that land.

The entry notes how small a part they play in the great tales of war. Great kings still swept them up in conquest more than once. Their own prince ruled them with no nod to nearby satraps for a time. Wild hills and hard passes may have kept that freedom safe. In the end the kings of Pontus took the land bit by bit.
britannica-1911-pappus-of-alexandria:
Pappus of Alexandria was a Greek worker in geometry of late old times. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says he thrived near the end of the third century. Maths then lay in a long slump. Pappus stands out as a rare bright name in that flat age. Other Greek writers barely cite him. His work did nothing to halt the decay of the science. In that sad fate he matches Diophantus.

His book, the Collection, names no dates for its sources. From it alone we would know only that he wrote after Ptolemy. A later writer put him in the age of Theon, near the year 380. The entry finds that hard to credit. Notes in a tenth century copy tie him to the reign of Diocletian instead. On thin proof, that date is held the best.
britannica-1911-pardo-bazan-emilia:
Pardo Bazán, Emilia is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Spanish author. Born at Corunna on the sixteenth of September 1851, she married at eighteen a Galician country gentleman. She took an interest in politics and is believed to have worked quietly against King Amadeo and later against the republic. In 1876 she won a literary prize at Oviedo.

The article follows her rise as a novelist. Her first novel showed little promise, but a story of 1881 brought French realism into Spain. Her best work is the novel of 1886 tracing a decaying Galician family. A sequel carried her naturalism further, and by 1889 her standing as a chief of the new movement in Spain was secure.
britannica-1911-pardoe-julia:
Julia Pardoe (1806-1862) was an English writer, and this short 1911 Britannica entry lists her life and her main books. She was born at Beverley in Yorkshire and brought out a volume of poems at the age of fourteen. In 1835 she travelled to Constantinople, and what she saw there fed her pictures of Eastern life. Those books include City of the Sultan, Romance of the Harem, and Beauties of the Bosphorus.

Her later works turned to French history and courts, among them lives and studies of Louis the Fourteenth, Francis the First, and Marie de Medici. The entry warns that these works are not always sound on the facts. She also wrote several sprightly novels. In 1860 she was granted a civil list pension, and she died in November 1862.
britannica-1911-passacaglia:
Passacaglia is the name of an old Spanish dance, as a brief note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. The word is thought to come from Spanish words for walking and for street. The tune was played by players who walked the streets.

It was a slow and grave dance for one or two dancers. Its tune was like that of the chaconne, and like it the music was built on a ground bass that runs through the piece. The note ends with a modern case: the fourth symphony of Brahms closes with a passacaglia of great craft.
britannica-1911-patti-adelina-juana-mari:
Adelina Juana Maria Patti, the famed singer, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was born at Madrid in 1843, the daughter of two singers. Her parents took her to America, where she was taught to sing. At the age of seven she sang in the concert halls of New York.

In 1859 she first sang in opera, as Lucia, in that same city. Two years later her Amina at Covent Garden made her the top prima donna of her day. Triumphs in London, Paris, and other great towns ran on for years. She left the opera stage in the eighties but still sang at concerts. Her fresh voice held late, which the entry credits to fine training. Singing Home, Sweet Home became her mark at those shows.
britannica-1911-perugia:
Perugia, a city of Italy and capital of Umbria, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands on a group of hills above the Tiber valley. The town lies about 1,444 feet above sea level. Its people numbered 22,321 in the town in 1906. The wider commune held 65,527 people. The town plan is irregular, spread along several ridge tops.

Deep valleys split the town into separate parts. Great terrace walls of the Etruscan age still stand. The Arco di Augusto is a town gate of that era. It bears the name Augusta Perusia in stone. A second gate, the Porta Marzia, was moved in 1540. Its upper part was rebuilt into the citadel walls. Four more Etruscan gates can still be traced. A fine mosaic of Orpheus among the beasts was found in 1876. Pope Paul the Third built the citadel in the 1540s.
britannica-1911-petunia:
Petunia is a genus of plants with about sixteen species, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on botany. Most species come from South America, in south Brazil and Argentina. The garden forms come from two species, one white flowered and one violet or purple flowered. Fine double forms make good pot plants, the entry adds.

Named sorts are raised from cuttings, not from seed. Stock plants are kept through winter on a dry warm shelf. In early spring they are moved to brisk moist heat. Young shoots are set in pans of sandy soil, where they root in a few days. They are then potted singly and hardened off step by step. Single sorts are raised from seed sown in light sandy soil in heat. Good seed strains give plants fit for bedding.
britannica-1911-phigalia:
Phigalia, an ancient Greek city in Arcadia, is described in a history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stood on a high rocky site among tall hills. Sparta took the city in 659 before Christ, but it soon won its freedom back. In later wars it changed hands more than once.

Odd cults were kept up near Phigalia, such as a fish tailed goddess. Notes on the city in Greek history are rare and scant. A great part of its city wall still stands, built in fine Greek masonry. Its chief glory stands five miles away at Bassae. That is the temple of Apollo the Preserver, raised to thank the god for halting a plague.
britannica-1911-philadelphia-pennsylvani:
Philadelphia, a great city of the United States, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It was the third city of the nation in population. It is the chief city of Pennsylvania and a port of entry. It is co-extensive with Philadelphia county. It stretches west from the Delaware river, beyond the Schuylkill river.

The city runs along the Delaware for about twenty-three miles. Its area is given in the text at over a hundred and thirty square miles. The port lies about a hundred miles from the Atlantic Ocean. The city hall stands ninety miles by rail from New York. It stands a hundred and thirty-five miles from Washington. At the southern end are lowlands guarded by dikes from the tide. The business centre lies between the two rivers. Independence Hall stands a few squares from the city hall.
britannica-1911-philip-i-king-of-macedon: Philip the First, king of Macedonia, is a half tale prince in this brief 1911 Britannica note. He was the son of Argaeus by old accounts. Herodotus and Thucydides count him as the third king of his land. Two late lists count him as the sixth king instead. Reign lengths of thirty eight and thirty five years are given by those lists. The note ends flat on proof. There is no real proof that he lived at all, it says.
britannica-1911-philip-ii-king-of-macedo:
Philip the Second ruled Macedonia from 359 to 336 before Christ, and the 1911 Britannica entry gives his reign at length. He was a son of Amyntas and spent three years as a hostage at Thebes as a boy. There he saw Greek war craft at close hand. When his brother fell in battle, the realm was in deep disorder with many rival claims.

Philip seized the throne, drove off his rivals, and built a strong national army. His new force beat the hill tribes in one battle in 358. He then took Amphipolis, a port that held the road to gold mines. The entry shows how one reign turned a weak fringe realm into a great power.
britannica-1911-phrygia:
Phrygia is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a large country of Asia Minor. Its people were called Phryges, or freemen, by the Greeks. In rough terms it covered the western central plateau of Anatolia. It reached east as far as the river Halys. Its boundaries were vague and shifted over time. For that reason a sketch of its history comes first. 

Greek tradition held the Phrygians akin to tribes of Macedonia. They were also held akin to tribes of Thrace. Their language and art prove a near link to the Hellenic stock. Almost every modern authority accepts that link today. The land of the known period lies inland from the sea. Paphlagonia, Bithynia, Mysia, and Lydia split it from the coast. Yet a Phrygian sea power is heard of early. That power dates to the start of the ninth century before Christ.
britannica-1911-pio-di-savoia:
Pio di Savoia is an old noble Italian family, first named in the thirteen hundreds, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a short entry. From the house of Este the family received the lordship of Carpi, and later gained the fiefs of Meldola, Sassuolo and more. Many of its members won note as soldiers for hire, envoys and churchmen.

Alberto Pio won from the house of Savoy in 1450 the right to add di Savoia to his name, as a reward for his service in war. A later Alberto Pio, who lived from 1475 to 1551, was French ambassador in Rome and won fame as a man of learning. Cardinal Rodolfo Pio was a trusted adviser to the pope and helped set up the Inquisition at Milan. Ascanio Pio was a verse dramatist. Spain gave the family the title of prince.
britannica-1911-pisidia:
Pisidia was a country in the south of Asia Minor in ancient geography, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It lay just north of Pamphylia, which split it from the Mediterranean Sea. It was bounded by Phrygia, Lycaonia, Isauria, Cilicia, and Lycia on its sides. It was a rugged and mountainous district in its whole extent.

Pisidia comprised some of the loftiest portions of the great Taurus range in its land. Offshoots of that chain ran toward the central table land of Phrygia from it. Such a region was naturally occupied from a very early period by wild and lawless races of mountaineers. Those races were very imperfectly reduced to subjection by the powers that ruled Asia Minor in turn. The Pisidians are not mentioned by Herodotus among the nations subdued by Croesus.
britannica-1911-pneumonia:
Pneumonia is inflammation of the lung substance, and a medical entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out how the disease was then classed. Older practice split it into three kinds: acute lobar pneumonia, broncho-pneumonia, and chronic pneumonia. The entry takes the acute lobar form first.

Lobar pneumonia is presented as an acute infective disease, marked by fever and poisoning of the system, running a set course. The germ most often found is the pneumococcus, present in the spit, the lung, and the blood of many cases. The entry notes the disease favors winter and spring, and cites Osler for the view that it spreads as an infection.
britannica-1911-pomerania:
Pomerania, in German Pommern, is a land of Germany and a sea province of Prussia. The Baltic bounds it on the north and Mecklenburg on the west. Brandenburg lies to the south and West Prussia to the east. The province covers 11,630 square miles, and its people numbered 1,684,125 in 1905. That gives 145 souls to the square mile. In rule it is split into the three districts of Stralsund, Stettin, and Köslin.

Older names hold more weight in its past: Vorpommern and Hinterpommern, Hither and Farther Pomerania. The first names the land west of the Oder, and the second the land east of it. Pomerania is one of the flattest parts of Germany. East of the Oder, though, a range of low hills crosses it, and a few lone rises stand in the west. Off the west coast lie the islands of Rügen, Usedom, and Wollin.
britannica-1911-popilia-via:
The Via Popilia was the name of two old Roman high roads. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica treats them in turn. The first ran from Capua down the length of Italy to Regium. That road of 321 miles was the main route through the interior. It did not hug the coast. A censor or consul named Popilius is credited with its building. Dates given run from 159 to 132 before Christ.

The second road ran from Ariminum to Aquileia along the Adriatic shore. It came into use when Aquileia was planted as a frontier fort in 181. Polybius gives its length as 178 miles. The consul Popilius rebuilt it in 132, and one of his milestones survives. Travellers often split the trip at Ravenna, taking ship and canal to Altinum, then road again.
britannica-1911-praenestina-via: Via Praenestina, an ancient road of Italy, is the subject of a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The road led from Rome east by south to Praeneste, twenty-three miles in all. Gabii sat almost exactly halfway along it. At the ninth mile the road crosses a ravine on a tall bridge of seven arches, well kept and called the finest ancient bridge near Rome. Beyond Gabii the line runs very straight for such hard country, though it serves only as a track.
britannica-1911-pretoria:
Pretoria, administrative capital of the Union of South Africa and of the Transvaal, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies forty six miles by rail north by east of Johannesburg. The entry gives it 36,839 people in 1904, of whom 21,114 were whites. It stands on both banks of the Aapies river, 4,470 feet above the sea.

The town is built in a hollow ringed by hills, with broad streets lined with willows, and is scenic in aspect. In summer the heat and moisture are excessive, and the Aapies is liable to floods. Pretoria is laid out in rectangular blocks of uniform width. The older part lies west of the river, with Church Square at its centre. Government buildings of 1892, in Renaissance style, face the south side of the square.
britannica-1911-ratafia: Ratafia is a sweet drink or cordial flavoured with fruit kernels or other fruits. Peach and cherry kernels are used, as are bitter almonds. Many forms of the drink are made. The same name is given to a flavouring essence like bitter almonds, and to a light biscuit. The word was taken from French in the seventeenth century. One guess at its roots joins Malay words for a spirit and for rum.
britannica-1911-reading-pennsylvania:
Reading is a city in Pennsylvania and the county seat of Berks county. A 1911 Britannica entry charts its fast growth across four census counts. It rose from about forty three thousand people in 1880 to over ninety six thousand in 1910. The city sits on the east bank of the Schuylkill river north west of Philadelphia.

Two railways, a canal, and electric lines serve the busy river city. Land slopes from the base of Mount Penn down to the river bank. That slope gives the city good natural drainage into the stream. The river forms its west edge for more than four miles and is crossed by bridges.
britannica-1911-reggio-calabria:
Reggio Calabria, a town in Calabria, Italy, on the Strait of Messina, is the subject of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It served as the end point of rail lines down both coasts of Calabria, and ferries crossed to Sicily from a point just north of the town. The entry gives near forty thousand people in the town in 1906.

Most of the space goes to quakes. Reggio was hurt by a shock in 1894, and far worse in 1783, but the great quake of December 1908 wrecked the town in full. The entry says some thirty five thousand of its forty thousand folk were lost. Its old church and castle were ruined, a wave from the sea swept the shore, and the land along the front sank. The piece is brief, and it points the reader to the Messina entry for more.
britannica-1911-reggio-nell-emilia:
Reggio nell Emilia, a city of Emilia in Italy, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the chief town of the province of the same name and the seat of a bishop. It lies north west of Bologna by rail. Its town count in nineteen hundred and six was near twenty thousand, with the commune past sixty four thousand.

The great church was first built in the twelve hundreds. It was reworked in the two ages that came next. Its front shows the marks of both builds, with the new work whole in the low part alone. A church close by has a front of fifteen hundred and four. Six stone lions of the first church are set in that front.
britannica-1911-reichenbach-silesia:
Reichenbach is a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town in the Prussian province of Silesia, in Germany. It stands on the Peile river, at the foot of a range of hills, thirty miles south west of Breslau by rail. Its count in 1905 was 15,984.

The article lists weaving, spinning, dyeing, brewing, and machine building as its trades. A brisk trade in grain and cattle adds to its work. Most of the piece deals with three past events. In August 1762 the Prussians beat the Austrians in a battle there. In July 1790 a congress there sealed a pact that kept Turkey whole. In June 1813 a pact of alliance against France was signed in the town. The piece ends with a note on a short history of the town.
britannica-1911-rhodesia:
Rhodesia is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a British land in south central Africa. It takes its name from Cecil Rhodes, the entry notes at the start. Its bounds touch the Transvaal, the Congo, and lands held by Germany and Portugal. The whole tract covers about 450,000 square miles of ground.

That is more land than France, Germany, and the Low Countries put together. The Zambezi river cuts the land into two parts by its mid course. The south part joins Matabeleland and Mashonaland as one block. North of the river lie two more tracts with their own names. Most streams drain to the Zambezi, though some flow to the Limpopo. The high tableland of inland Africa forms its base.
britannica-1911-richardia: Richardia is a small group of plants from South Africa, described in a brief plant entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The famed arum lily belongs to this group. All are greenhouse herbs with thick roots and large arrow shaped leaves. Their flower spathes are white or yellow. They want rich, moist soil and much water. They flower all year round but cannot stand frost.
britannica-1911-rudolph-duke-of-swabia:
Rudolph, duke of Swabia, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a German king. He was a son of Kuno, count of Rheinfelden, who held lands in Burgundy and Swabia. In 1057 he got the duchy of Swabia from Agnes, the young king's mother. Two years later he wed the king's sister Matilda.

Doubt about his faith grew in the Saxon War of 1073. When Henry the Fourth was cast out by Pope Gregory the Seventh, the princes chose Rudolph as king. He was crowned at Mainz on the 27th of March 1077. He won two fights against Henry's troops with Saxon help. Wounded at Hohenmolsen in 1080, he died the next day.
britannica-1911-sarnia:
Sarnia is the subject of a town entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a town and port in Ontario, Canada, on the left bank of the Saint Clair river. The entry gives its population in nineteen hundred one. It sat north east of Detroit and served as the capital of Lambton county.

Inside, readers learn that steamers on the Great Lakes called at its port. Rail lines served the town from two firms. A large oil refinery handled most of the yield from the Ontario oil fields. The Saint Clair tunnel linked Sarnia by rail to Port Huron in Michigan, across the river in the United States.
britannica-1911-sedalia:
Sedalia, a city in Missouri, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the county seat of Pettis county, a bit west of the centre of the state. Its count rose from fifteen thousand in nineteen hundred to near eighteen thousand in nineteen ten. Two rail systems serve it, and it is a hub for transport.

The city has a high and fair site on rolling grass land. It is laid out as an exact square. Fine public halls include a court house built of blue stone and a free book house given by Andrew Carnegie. A college for Black students, founded in eighteen ninety four, has its seat here. A town park of sixty acres lies in the west part. Broadway, the main street for homes, is wide and parked on both sides. The portrait suits a rail town in full growth.
britannica-1911-senigallia:
Senigallia is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a city of Italy. It is also an episcopal see of the Marches. It lies in the province of Ancona on the Adriatic coast. Ancona stands fifteen miles to the south by rail. Counts from 1901 give the town 5556 people. The wider commune held 23,195 in that count. The city sits just fourteen feet above the sea. Despite its ancient origin, it looks modern in aspect.

Its streets are wide, and its town hall dates from the 1600s. The cathedral was erected after the year 1787. The castle is of Gothic origin in its first build. Baccio Pontelli, a famous military architect, restored it in 1492. A church outside the town is one of his known works. The small port is formed by the lower Misa stream.
britannica-1911-sepia:
Sepia is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a deep brown pigment taken from cuttlefish. The Greek word in its heading means cuttlefish, and the pigment comes from the ink sacs of several kinds. To make it, the sac is taken out at once when the animal is caught and dried fast to stop decay. The contents are then powdered and treated for use.

The entry gives the steps in plain order. The powder is dissolved in caustic alkali, then brought back out of the liquid by adding acid. After washing with water, the solid is ready to be made into any form a user needs. A second part covers sepia bone, the inner shell of the cuttlefish. That light, porous bone serves for polishing, for tooth powder, and for moulds for fine casting in precious metals.
britannica-1911-setia:
Setia, now Sezze, is an old town of Latium in Italy in this 1911 Britannica place entry. It stands on the edge of the Volscian hills above the Pomptine Marshes. Its height tops a thousand feet above the sea at that post. Rome lies to its north west by rail at a fair run. It was a Volscian town and a link in the Latin league of old.

Rome made it a Latin colony in three eighty two before Christ. Its strong fort post gave it weight in the wars of Rome for years. Sulla took the town by force in eighty two before Christ. Wine from its slopes was the pick of Augustus past the best of Italy. Great blocks of stone in its old walls still stand in part.
britannica-1911-severiana-via: Via Severiana was an ancient high road of Italy, treated in a brief 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It ran south east from Ostia to Terracina, a distance of seventy three miles along the coast. Its name most likely comes from work done on an older road by Septimius Severus. He was a great benefactor of Ostia. The road ran at first along the shore, behind a line of villas. Remains of it are scanty, since building stuff is rare in that sandy district.
britannica-1911-sophia:
Sophia (1630-1714), electress of Hanover, is the subject of an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, which traces her link to the English throne. Born at the Hague, she was the twelfth child of Frederick V of the Rhine and of Elizabeth, daughter of James I of England. In 1658 she married Ernest Augustus, later elector of Hanover.

The entry calls her married life unhappy, with an unfaithful husband and three of her six sons lost in battle. Widowed in 1698, she stood as the nearest Protestant heir to the English crown once Anne's only surviving child had died. The Act of Settlement of 1701 therefore placed the crown, failing Anne's issue, with Sophia and her heirs.
britannica-1911-south-australia:
South Australia is a British colonial state in the Commonwealth of Australia, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens its survey with bounds and coast. The state lies between fixed lines of longitude in the south of the continent. Queensland, New South Wales, and Victoria stand to its east. Western Australia lies to the west, and the Southern Ocean to the south.

The north line of the state first stood at a set latitude. The adding of the Northern Territory then stretched its area from 380,070 to 903,690 square miles. That change carried its border to the Indian Ocean. By acts of 1910, the territory was made over to the federal government. The southern coast shows two large gulfs, the entry notes. Spencer Gulf runs 180 miles long, and St Vincent Gulf runs 100 miles.
britannica-1911-south-georgia:
South Georgia is an uninhabited British island in the South Atlantic Ocean, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It lies about 900 miles south east of the Falkland Islands, with an area of 1,600 square miles. The island is mountainous throughout its length and breadth. Snowy peaks rise from 6,000 to 8,000 feet, and deep gorges cut with glaciers score their slopes.

Its rocks are gneiss and clay schists, with no trace of fossils in them. That fact marks it as a surviving fragment of a greater land mass now vanished. The text links that lost mass to a former reach of the Andean system far to the north. At Royal Bay a German party was stationed in 1882 to watch the transit of Venus. The damp, foggy climate rules out the sheep and cattle farming the land would otherwise suit, but the plant life is surprisingly rich.
britannica-1911-sulpicia:
Sulpicia is the name of two Roman poets, both women. The elder lived in the reign of Augustus and was a niece of Messalla, a patron of letters. Her verses were kept with those of Tibullus and were long given to him as their author. They are poems of love in elegiac form, addressed to a lover called Cerinthus.

The younger Sulpicia lived in the reign of Domitian. Martial praises her and sets her beside Sappho as a model of a devoted wife. She wrote a book of poems on how she kept the love of her husband Calenus. A poem of seventy hexameters also bears her name. It takes the form of a talk between Sulpicia and the muse Calliope. Its chief theme is a protest against Domitian's banishment of the philosophers in the year 89.
britannica-1911-susa-tunisia:
Susa, called Sousse in French, is a city of Tunisia described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Gulf of Hammamet and serves as the port of Kairawan. It holds part of the site of the old city of Hadrumetum. A wall with towers wraps round the town, which climbs a hill that slopes to the sea.

The entry points out the citadel, the grand mosque, and two odd old buildings. One is a square fort with a high tower, the other a domed house once perhaps a church. A museum holds fine mosaics and carved stones. The new port, finished in 1901, lets large steamers lie at the quays. Trade out is chiefly in oil, grain, and minerals.
britannica-1911-svanetia: Svanetia is a mountain district in the Caucasus described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies on the south slopes of the range, just under the tallest ice-clad peaks of the middle part. It covers the upper valleys of three rivers, the Rion, the Ingur and the Tskhenis-tskhali. In the terms of the day it fell in the government of Kutais. The Svanetians who live there belong to the Georgian race. The note points readers to the entries on Caucasia and the Caucasus.
britannica-1911-swabia:
Swabia was one of the stem duchies of the Germany of the middle ages. It takes its name from a tribe who held the district in the first age of the Christian era. They dwelt in the angle made by two great rivers. Other tribes joined them there, and the whole took a new name.

The district bore that tribe name till a late age, when the form Swabia came to rule. The tribe was beat by a king of the Franks in a famed fight, the entry says. It was brought under Frankish rule, and dukes who owed their posts to those kings held sway. In time the folk took the Christian faith. Great church seats and abbeys rose in the land. The tribe threw off the Frankish yoke by bits, till a strong mayor cut them down once more.
britannica-1911-symphonia:
Symphonia is a much-debated old word for musical instruments, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tracks its shifting sense. At varied times it named the bagpipe, the drum, the hurdy-gurdy, and last a kind of clavichord. The entry argues the instrument listed in the Book of Daniel, wrongly rendered dulcimer, was most likely the bagpipe.

The entry cites Isidore of Seville for the drum sense, with a Latin passage likening the drum to half a pearl, drawn from Pliny. In the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries the word meant the hurdy-gurdy, chiefly in Latin lands. Praetorius later used it for a keyboard instrument classed with the clavichord and spinet.
britannica-1911-telesia:
Telesia, the modern Telese, is covered in a short entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The text calls it a town of the Samnites, north west from Beneventum. Only brief lines follow, but they pack in the main marks of the old site.

What remains gives the entry its weight. Walls in a net like stone pattern run for more than a mile in all. Two texts from the time of the Republic record the building of towers. Ruins of baths and of a ring for shows still stand. A raised water line fed the town, and sulphur springs nearby may have fed the baths. The note is a neat guide to what a visitor or student can still trace on the ground.
britannica-1911-tempio-pausania: Tempio Pausania is a town of Sardinia, in the province of Sassari, described in a brief 1911 Britannica article. It lies in a mountainous district 1,856 feet above sea level, north-north-west of Monte Limbara. It had 6,511 people in the town and 14,573 in the commune in 1901. It is the chief town of the Gallura and has been the seat of a bishop since the 900s. The cathedral is a modern building, the district is given to farming and herding, and the local costumes are picturesque.
britannica-1911-terranova-pausania:
Terranova Pausania is a seaport of Sardinia in the province of Sassari, on the east coast of the island. The 1911 Britannica article gives its count as 4,348 in 1901. The town sits in the deep, sheltered gulf of Terranova. It stands on the site of the ancient Olbia. Till its traffic moved to Golfo Aranci, it was the port of embarkation for Italy, as in old times. Some trade in cork and charcoal remains.

The place lies low and suffers from malaria. Its one building of note is the Romanesque church of Saint Simplicio, once the cathedral. The church as it stands dates most likely from the eleventh century. The town was the seat of judges sent by Pisa in that age. Its second name, Pausania, rests on an error. It is a bent form of Fausiana, a town whose true site is not known.
britannica-1911-thargelia:
Thargelia, one of the chief feasts of ancient Athens, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The feast honoured the Delian Apollo and Artemis on their birthdays. It fell on the sixth and seventh days of the month Thargelion, near the end of May. At its heart it was a farm feast, tied to the first fruits of the earth.

The rite joined thanks with a grim act of cleansing. Folk gave the first yield to the god, yet also sought to ward off heat that could spoil the crop. On the first day a sheep was offered to Demeter Chloe on the Acropolis. Two men, picked as the most ugly to be found, were led out, beaten with rods, and put to death. Their ashes were cast into the sea or spread on the land.
britannica-1911-thaxter-celia:
Celia Thaxter, American poet born at Portsmouth in New Hampshire on 29 June 1836, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Her father, Thomas Laighton, broke with his fellows in state politics. At about 1841 he withdrew to the bare and lonely Isles of Shoals, ten miles off Portsmouth. For about ten years he kept the White Island lighthouse there.

Her girlhood thus passed amid marine scenes and sounds. That world coloured the best of the verse she wrote in later years. Her poems, mostly in lyric form, treat the beacon light, the sea storm, and the glint of sails. The sandpiper and the flower among the rocks find their place too. She also wrote prose sketches of life on the isles, tales and poems for children, and a book on island gardening.
britannica-1911-thelbald-king-of-mercia:
Æthelbald was king of Mercia from 716, and a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry sums up his reign. Before his accession he lived in exile, driven out by King Ceolred. Felix, in his life of St Guthlac, tells how Æthelbald visited the saint at Crowland. The saint cheered the exile with forecasts of his future greatness.

Bede records that all Britain as far north as the Humber lay within Æthelbald’s sphere of power. The Chronicle shows his drive to hold that sway. In 733 he marched against Wessex and took the royal vill of Somerton. In 740 he struck into Northumbria while its king campaigned against the Picts. Three years later he joined Cuthred of Wessex in war against the Welsh.
britannica-1911-tibia: Tibia was a pipe played by means of a reed mouthpiece, used widely in classic Rome, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. It is often wrongly translated as flute in English versions of Latin texts. As it was made with a straight bore or with a cone bore, it may be seen as the forerunner of our clarinet or of our oboe. The tibia was used at musical contests, in the theatre, in the arena, and at banquets.
britannica-1911-transbaikalia:
Transbaikalia, also known as Dauria, is a province of east Siberia that lies east of Lake Baikal. The 1911 Britannica entry sets its bounds by Russian districts, the Amur lands, and Mongolia. Its area is near as large as a great empire of Europe, yet its folk count is a mere half million or so.

The entry calls the province a link between Siberia, Mongolia, and the north Pacific shore. A range of hills runs north east across it and splits it in two. West of the range lies a high shelf of the great east Asian table land. East of it the same table land steps down to a lower shelf, a spur of a vast desert. A deep broad vale cuts in from the lake at its west edge.
britannica-1911-transcaucasia: Transcaucasia is a broad name for the governments and provinces of Russian Caucasia, with some lands left out. The steppe lands of Kuban, Terek, and Stavropol do not count as part of it. It takes in the governments of Baku, Elisavetpol, Erivan, Kutais, and Tiflis. It also takes in the provinces of Batum, Daghestan, and Kars, and two military districts. Its area is 95,402 square miles. Its people were put at 6,114,600 in 1906.
britannica-1911-tunisia:
Tunisia, a country of North Africa under French protection, is described at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Mediterranean bounds it to the north, Algeria to the west, and the Sahara to the south. It reaches farther north than any other part of Africa. Its area is put at about fifty thousand square miles.

In land and in life the country belongs more to Europe than to the desert south. Four regions make up its map. The north is a mountain land tied to the Aures range of Algeria. Its chief river, the Majerda, waters a rich and well peopled vale. Peaks near Ain Draham rise past four thousand feet. The land round Bizerta is rugged and well watered, with streams that flow all year. The French took the Kroumir hills as a pretext to invade in 1881.
britannica-1911-urmia:
Urmia is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a town in Persia. It sits 4,400 feet up in a rich, well farmed plain. The town lies near the west shore of the lake of the same name. A wall and a deep ditch that can be flooded ring it.

Orchards and gardens spread round it for miles on all sides. They push in even to the heart of the town itself. Its streets are broader than is usual in Persian towns. A stream of water runs down the mid of most streets. The folk count is about thirty-five thousand in the town. A busy bazaar and old mosques are among its sights. Church missions of four lands have their base there.
britannica-1911-veleia:
Veleia, an ancient town of Aemilia in Italy, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lay about twenty miles south of Placentia. Pliny named it among the towns of the eighth region, though its people were Ligurians by race. In the census of Vespasian they were noted for their long lives.

Little more was known of Veleia until 1747, when ploughmen found a vast bronze tablet there. That tablet, now at Parma, lists estates where Trajan had lent funds on mortgage. The interest fed and kept more than two hundred poor boys and girls each month. Digs begun in 1760 laid bare the forum, basilica, baths, and theatre of the town. Statues, inscriptions, and early cremation tombs also came to light.
britannica-1911-venetia:
Venetia is a region of northern Italy that lies between the Alps and the Adriatic Sea. The 1911 Britannica article gives its size as 9,476 square miles. Its count in 1901 was 3,192,897 people. Eight provinces make it up, among them Venice, Padua, Verona, and Vicenza. The land runs from the Austrian frontier in the north-east to the lower Po and Lombardy in the south-west.

Farms there grow maize, wheat, rice, grapes, and hemp, and raise silkworms. Shops and mills make wool, cotton, silk, glass, lace, and paper. Copper and lignite are mined in the hills. The Po and other rivers end in a wide delta that keeps growing seaward. Shore lagoons stay fresh through the tides. The entry lists the chief towns of each province with their counts.
britannica-1911-victoria-australia:
Victoria is a state in the south east tip of Australia, of a rough three side form. A great stream marks most of its north line. Its south line is the shore of two seas. Its most far south point is a cape of note. Its span east to west runs past four hundred miles, and its land mass past eighty thousand square miles.

Its shore runs past eight hundred miles of bold stone cliffs and cave worn capes. A port bay at its heart holds the chief city of the state. Past that bay lie sand banks, then bold cliffs once more. A round mass of stone hills with grand wild views forms its far south point.
britannica-1911-vindelicia:
Vindelicia is a short geography article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a land of the ancient world north of the Alps. Raetia bounded it on the south, the Danube on the north, the river Inn on the east, and the lands of the Helvetii on the west. In modern terms it matched the north east of Switzerland, the south east of Baden, and the south of Wurttemberg and Bavaria.

With its neighbours the land was subdued by Tiberius in 15 before Christ, and toward the end of the first century it was folded into Raetia. Its chief town was Augusta Vindelicorum, the modern Augsburg. The people were most likely of Celtic stock, since the prefix Vind recurs in Celtic names such as Vindobona, though some writers hold them to be German. Dio Cassius calls them a farming people, and later writers praise the rich soil.
britannica-1911-volhynia:
Volhynia is a province of south western Russia, on the Polish border. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its area as near twenty eight thousand square miles. A flat Carpathian spur fills its south, with marshy lowland to the north. Its people were put at over three and a half million in 1906.

Most people there are Little Russians, with Poles, Jews, and Germans as well. Peasants hold about half the land, a pattern unlike most of Russia. Forests cover near half the north and far less in the south. Grain farming thrives in the south, while timber work rules the north. Sugar works and mills form the chief factory base there.
britannica-1911-warwick-australia:
Warwick, a town in Queensland in Australia, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the bank of the river Condamine, far inland from Brisbane. In 1901 it held just under four thousand people. The entry calls it perhaps the most pleasing inland town in the colony.

Good farm land wraps round the town on all sides. Its fields are famed for vines, and much good wine is made there. Wheat and maize are the chief crops, with oats and lucerne also grown. Coal lies near the town, as do marble and good stone for building. Two large parks and smaller grounds give the town open green space.
britannica-1911-washington-district-of-c:
Washington is the capital city of the United States of America. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica treats it as one with the District of Columbia. It stands on the north east bank of the Potomac river. The 1910 count put its people at 331,069. The city proper spans about ten square miles. It lies between the Anacostia river and Rock Creek. Hills ring the low ground near the river.

The street plan fills much of the entry. It came from Major L'Enfant, under the eye of President Washington and Thomas Jefferson. Streets run east and west by letter names. Streets running north and south carry numbers. Broad avenues named for states cut across the grid. They fan out from the Capitol and the White House. The avenues run from 120 to 160 feet wide. Quarters of the city are marked by points of the compass after each street name.
britannica-1911-westphalia:
Westphalia is the subject of a province article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Westphalia is a province of the kingdom of Prussia. Its area is over seven thousand eight hundred square miles. It runs about a hundred thirty miles each way. Hanover bounds it on the north, and the Netherlands on the northwest. The old duchy and the Napoleonic kingdom of the same name had different bounds.

The article says nearly half the province is a stretch of the great north German plain. Low ranges bound that plain, among them the Teutoburger Wald. The plain is not very fertile, save in one rich zone. Wide fens lie in the north and west. The south is a rugged region of slate hills and wooded valleys. Its highest summit rises over twenty seven hundred feet. Rivers drain the land toward the Rhine, the Ems, and the Weser systems.
britannica-1911-winchester-virginia:
Winchester is a city of Virginia described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the county seat of Frederick county and lies by rail west-north-west of Washington. Its people numbered about five thousand two hundred in 1890 and five thousand eight hundred and sixty-four in 1910. Two rail lines serve it, and it sits in the rich Shenandoah Valley.

Schools in the city include a seminary for girls on the site of old Fort Loudoun and a military academy for boys. The town owns a library raised in memory of John Handley in 1910 and an auditorium. Near it lies a national graveyard with the graves of more than four thousand Union soldiers. The chief trade is the making of gloves, with woollen goods, flour, leather, and paper as well. A settlement stood here as early as 1732, and George Washington had his headquarters here in the Seven Years' War.
britannica-1911-wingfield-edward-maria: Edward Maria Wingfield (c. 1560–c. 1614) was an English colonist in America, born at Stoneley in Huntingdonshire. He served as a soldier in Ireland and in the Low Countries. He was one of the patentees of Virginia in 1606 and sailed with the first colonists to Jamestown in 1607. The Council chose him as its president in May of that year, but he lost the post in September.
britannica-1911-york-pennsylvania:
York, a city in Pennsylvania, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the county seat of York County, west of Philadelphia. The census of 1910 counted 44,750 people there. Three railways serve the city and its trade.

Its public buildings include a court house and a federal building. The York Collegiate Institute and the older York County Academy teach its youth. York is the market centre for a rich farming region around it. Its factories turn out foundry goods, machine-shop products, and silk wares. The factory product of 1905 passed fourteen million dollars in value. York was the first lasting settlement west of the Susquehanna river. It was laid out in 1741 and named for York in England. Its first settlers were chiefly Germans of Lutheran and Reformed faiths.
britannica-1911-zenobia:
Zenobia, queen of Palmyra, is profiled at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as a heroine of the ancient world. Her native name was Septimia Bathzabbai. She was famed for beauty, bold energy, and a strong mind. In life she backed the policy of her husband Odaenathus, chief of the Roman east.

After his death in about 267 she took his place and aimed higher still. Her young son held the royal title while she ruled in fact. Her armies took Egypt in the year 270 and set garrisons far into Asia Minor. At first she claimed to act for Rome. Coins then dropped the emperors head and took imperial titles. That open break forced Aurelian to act. Egypt was won back at once, and the emperor marched east in force.
buried-cities-volume-2-olympia:
Jennie Hall wrote the Olympia part of her buried cities tales for the young, as part two of the set. Hall taught history and English at the Francis W. Parker School in Chicago. The same foreword on dug wealth opens this book as the first. Drawings and photos from first sources fill its pages.

Temple ground rules this part. A boy named Charmides walks the old temple of Hera in the tale's heart. Rows of statues in marble, gold, and ivory line its side rooms. Zeus and Hera stand at the front, with priests at prayer. One small room stops the boy cold: his Hermes, with the baby Dionysus in its arms. Gold sandal and soft joy mark the meet. Games ground, gods, and the long dig that freed the site form the rest. Part one holds Pompeii and part three Mycenae.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abecedaria:
Abecedaria are alphabet lists, whole or partial, cut into ancient monuments in Greek and Latin, on pagan and Christian stones alike. The Latin alphabet settled into a fixed system near the start of the Christian era, while Greek shapes drew closer to Latin forms. Three extra letters added by Emperor Claudius never appear in Christian inscriptions. Formal monumental lettering differed widely from everyday cursive, and uncial script stayed in books until the fourth century.

Christian examples are rare, apart from two Carthage vases, while pagan ones include stonecutters' practice tablets and puzzling catacomb letter strings. One stone from the cemetery of St. Alexander looks like a schoolboy exercise in paired letters, a memory drill St. Jerome describes. A Rome stone found in 1877, of sixth- or seventh-century date, apparently served a school as a model alphabet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abyssinia:
Abyssinia, stretching between the sixth and fifteenth degrees of north latitude, south of Nubia, is likened to a vast fortress towering above eastern Africa's plains. It is a huge granitic and basaltic mass, a great mountainous oval, ridged mainly eastward. A chain over 650 miles long runs north to south. From the Red Sea it resembles a vast wall, about 8,000 feet high near Kasen and over 10,000 feet at Angolala.

On the west the mass breaks into plateaux of varying height, split by volcanic mountains, with Tigre summits over 6,500 feet and Simien summits from 13,000 to 16,000. Lake Tana hollows the highlands to the southwest, Gojam rises above 13,000 feet, and Kaffa's peaks reach some 12,000. That remarkable elevation gives Abyssinia a peculiar climate, which scholars divide into three chief zones, beginning with the low valleys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acacia:
Acacia in the Bible is the Hebrew shittah, plural shittim, linked to Egyptian shent, Coptic shonte, and Arabic sunt, all pointing to thorn. Hence the Greek akantha and Latin acanthus for the Egyptian acacia. The Septuagint calls its wood incorruptible wood, and the Vulgate calls it setim-wood. The biblical acacia, genus Mimosa, is no doubt the Acacia seyal or Acacia tortilis, called torrent trees, from sayl, torrent.

They grow in Sinai's desert wadis, or torrent valleys. Their wood is light, hard, and durable, blackening almost to ebony over time. The ark of the covenant and the table of the loaves were made of setim-wood. So were the holocaust altar, the incense altar, and the wooden parts of the tabernacle, as Exodus 25:5 records.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acadia:
Acadia's precise location and extent were disputed, with consequent warfare, between French and English colonists in America for over one hundred and fifty years. Henry IV of France granted the Sieur de Monts the territory called La Cadie. The grant was to cultivate it, people it, and hunt for gold and silver mines between the 46th and 40th degrees of north latitude. The Marquise de Guercheville, who bought the claim, imagined she owned Florida to the St. Lawrence.

Later Acadia was taken as the present peninsula of Nova Scotia. Now it usually means the small district on the Bay of Fundy's south shore, from Annapolis to the Basin of Minas. His concession came on 8 November 1603, and with Champlain and Pontgrave he reached Port Royal, now Annapolis. The entry closes with the Acadian dispersion and its descendants, put at 270,000 by Richard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achaia:
Achaia, also called Aegialeia, was, before Rome's conquest in 146 BC, a coastal strip between the Gulf of Corinth and Elis and Arcadia, holding twelve cities leagued together. The Achaean League stood prominent in the Greek struggle against Roman domination. Probably for that reason the name later spread across the country south of Macedonia and Illyricum, roughly modern Greece.

Under Rome, Achaia was usually a senatorial province, governed by an ex-praetor titled proconsul, with Corinth as capital. When St. Paul came into Achaia, Gallio, Seneca's brother, held the proconsulship. His refusal to meddle in Jewish religious affairs, and the tolerance of his rule, favoured the spread of Christianity, and Paul founded a flourishing church at Corinth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acmonia: Acmonia, a Phrygian Pacatiana titular see in Asia Minor, is now Ahat-Keui. Cicero mentions it in his speech Pro Flacco, and it stood on the road from Dorylaeum to Philadelphia. The entry gives this brief identification of site, classical mention, and road position, and cites Smith's geography and Mas Latrie's chronology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acolouthia:
Acolouthia, from Greek akoloutheo, to follow, means in church language the Divine Office's order or arrangement, and, broadly, the office itself. The parts follow closely in order, which explains the name. The office joins musical and rhetorical elements, with music given in one of eight modes, four primary and four secondary.

Greeks seldom used notated texts, so they learned a standard hymn or canticle by heart as a model for others of the same rhythm. A model stanza is called a hirmos, and a final one a catabasia by some writers.
