Feria, Latin for free day, began as a Roman public and legal holiday. On feriae the people, especially slaves, were not obliged to work. No courts sat, and the days marked public rest. Christian feasts and fasts later took the name for days of religious rest and worship.

Great feast crowds drew markets, giving rise to the English word fair. Today feria names the weekdays except Sunday and Saturday. Major feriae of Advent, Lent, and Ember days must at least be commemorated. Ash Wednesday and Holy Week days keep their own office always.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-florilegia:
Florilegia are systematic collections of excerpts from the Fathers and early church writers. They served dogmatic or ethical ends, gathering approved teaching for ready reference. The need arose in fifth-century Christological disputes, when councils wanted handy summaries. Cyril laid such a summary before Ephesus in 431; others served Chalcedon in 451.

Dogmatic florilegia reached full form in the seventh century, notably at the Sixth Council in 680. The oldest great example, the Doctrina Patrum, holds 977 citations from 93 writers. Ascetical florilegia gather moral sentences on virtues, vices, and duties of religious life. The Sacred Parallels, long ascribed to John Damascene, contrasted virtues with vices side by side.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-foggia:
Foggia is a diocese in Apulia, in a rich farming plain between the Cervaro and Celone. It grew around the church of the Madonna of the Seven Veils, built in 1072 by Robert Guiscard. Its name comes from fogia, or marsh, for the swampy ground it stands on. Frederick II built an imperial fortress there; Charles of Anjou destroyed the city in 1268.

Made a diocese by Pius IX in 1855, it was united with Troia in 1907. Its cathedral, often restored, holds the tombs of the Princes of Durazzo. The city counts 81,000 people in nine parishes, with schools and religious houses. A severe earthquake greatly damaged Foggia in 1781.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fortunato-of-:
Fortunato of Brescia, born in 1701 and dead at Madrid in 1754, was a Franciscan Minorite, philosopher, theologian, and pioneer of modern morphology. Morphology is the study of the forms and structures of living things. He took the religious habit in 1718, became secretary general of his order, favoured at the Bourbon court of Spain. His philosophical writing tried to bring scholastic thought together with the new discoveries of physical science.

His fame rests on the microscope. Following Malpighi, he studied the fine structure of organs. He argued that microscopic anatomy holds the key to nature. He was the first to draw a clear line between tissues, parts with a definite structure seen under the microscope, and organs built from them. He described connective and bony tissue and classified tissues and organs years before Bichat, who later got the credit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-ant:
Francesco Antonio Zaccaria, born at Venice on 27 March 1714 and dead at Rome on 10 October 1795. He was a Jesuit theologian, historian, and astonishingly prolific writer, with 161 printed works to his name. He joined the Austrian province of the Society of Jesus in 1731, was ordained at Rome in 1740, preached and lectured in Ancona, Fermo, and Pistoia. In 1751 he succeeded the great Muratori as ducal archivist and librarian of Modena.

Removed in 1768 for his Antifebronio, a vigorous defence of the rights of the Holy See, he became librarian at the Jesuit professed house in Rome. He drew a papal pension, and was made professor of church history at the Sapienza and director of the Academy of Noble Ecclesiastics. He belonged to at least nineteen Italian academies. His works include histories of bishoprics, defences of the Bollandist saints' lives, and editions of canonists and historians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-lor:
Francesco Lorenzo Brancati di Lauria, born at Lauria in the Kingdom of Naples on 10 April 1612 and dead at Rome on 30 November 1693. He was a Conventual Franciscan cardinal and theologian. Stricken with a dangerous illness at seventeen, he vowed to enter the Minor Conventuals if he recovered and took the habit at Lecce in July 1630. He taught philosophy and theology with notable success in the noted convents of his order.

In 1653 he took the chair of dogmatic theology at the Roman University and became consultor of the Holy Office, whom Alexander VII called a mainstay of the Apostolic See. He was chief librarian of the Vatican under Clement X. Innocent XI made him cardinal in 1681. He served on at least ten Roman congregations, coming within fifteen votes of the papacy itself after Innocent's death, blocked only by Spain's veto. His ascetical writings show a master of the spiritual life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francia:
Francia, born Francesco Raibolini at Bologna about 1450 and dead in 1517, was a goldsmith, engraver, and painter who shows what Italian art owed to the minor arts. His father carved wood. Francesco joined the goldsmiths' guild in 1482 and led it the next year, taking the name Francia from his master Duc, either in gratitude or as a valuable trade mark. In his age painting had not yet been ranked above crafts, and the goldsmith's care for detail, ornament, and beauty lifted painting above routine pious imagery.

His medals, nielli, enamels, jewellery, armour, and type founding display the industrial side of his art. His paintings, pure and original, kept him apart from the pagan and rationalist movement of his century. The entry calls him the leading personality in northern Italian art before Titian and Correggio, a solitary man of great and noble gifts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-borgi:
Francis Borgia, born 28 October 1510 and dead 30 September 1572, was a Spanish saint whose life ran from the highest court in Europe to the leadership of the Jesuits. Great-grandson of Pope Alexander VI on his father's side and of King Ferdinand of Aragon on his mother's, he grew up at the court of Charles V. He married Eleanor de Castro in 1529 and became Marquess of Lombay, equerry to the empress, and a model courtier gifted in sacred music.

The empress's death in 1539 turned him toward a stricter Christian life. As viceroy of Catalonia from that year he reformed justice, finance, and monasteries, and in 1543 he became Duke of Gandia. After his wife's death in 1546 he joined the Jesuits in 1548 and became commissary-general in Spain in 1554. He took charge of all Jesuit missions and was canonized by Clement X in 1670.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-of-vi:
Francis of Vittoria, born about 1480 at Vittoria in Old Castile and dead on 12 August 1546. He was a Spanish Dominican theologian called the father of the Salamanca school and of the new scholasticism. Moving young with his parents to Burgos, he entered the Dominicans and studied at the order's chief house in Paris. He taught there from 1516 with Dominic de Soto among his pupils, and returned to Spain in 1522, teaching at Valladolid until 1524. He then took the principal theology chair at Salamanca, holding it until 1544.

 He left many valuable manuscripts, but his sole published work is the twelve theological relections, printed at Antwerp in 1604. His commentary on the whole Summa of St. Thomas remains among his unpublished writings, a monument to his teaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-de-:
Francisco de Vargas y Mexia, born at Madrid at an unknown date and dead at the Hieronymite monastery of La Sisla in 1566. He was a Spanish diplomat and ecclesiastical writer of the Council of Trent. Of an old family of the lower nobility, he studied law at Alcala, became licentiate in law, and rose to fiscal, or attorney-general, of the Council of Castile. In 1545 Charles V sent him to Trent. In 1548 he protested the council's transfer to Bologna, and in 1551 he welcomed its return to Trent.

From 1552 to 1559 he served as Spanish ambassador at Venice and negotiated at Rome in 1558 over recognising Ferdinand I as emperor and founding new dioceses in the Netherlands. From 1559 he succeeded Figueroa as ambassador to the Curia, taking an important part in electing Pius IV.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fray-nicolas-:
Nicolás Armentia, a Spanish Minorite who became bishop of La Paz in 1901, spent his best years as a missionary in Bolivia's Beni region. Born in 1845, he had studied physics, astronomy, and natural science in France. He then sailed to South America under Father Rafael Sans. The entry traces a scholar-priest who cut his own paths between remote hamlets.

Among small, often hostile tribes thinned by smallpox, Armentia preached and rebuilt missions. He also gathered notes on the land, its creatures, and its peoples. His books include a diary of exploring the Madre de Dios in 1884 and 1885. He also wrote a description of the Mojos province and a Shipibo vocabulary of more than 3,800 words, still the fullest word list of its language family.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaudentius-of:
Gaudentius of Brescia, a Capuchin theologian born in 1612, ranks among the foremost voices of the Franciscan school. Sprung from the noble Bontempi house, he entered the Capuchins and served as lector of theology, visiting convents across his Brescia province and other Italian houses of study. He fell ill at Oriano while preaching a Lenten course and died there in March 1672.

His fame rests on the Palladium Theologicum, a scholastic theology built on Saint Bonaventure, praised for style, depth, and sound doctrine. His pupil Durantio published it after his death, and Louis XIV had it vetted by Sorbonne doctors before its Lyons issue in seven folio volumes in 1676. His remains now rest at the Capuchin church of Verola.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-georgia:
Georgia, the largest of the original thirteen states, is surveyed here in its geography, growth, and Catholic life. Bounded by Tennessee and North Carolina north, the Savannah River and Atlantic east, and Florida and Alabama south and west, it spans 59,475 square miles. Population rose from 82,548 in 1790 to 2,216,331 in 1900, with Savannah the largest city at 54,244.

Cotton leads an unmatched variety of farm products, with 1,920,000 bales in 1907, while manufactures reached over 151 million dollars in 1905 and railroads ran 6,786 miles in 1907. Schools run from the state university at Athens, founded in 1785, to Atlanta, Clark, Emory, and Morris Brown colleges. The Diocese of Savannah, comprising the whole state and established in 1850, counted 23,000 Catholics in the 1908 census, with eighteen secular and forty-one religious priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-germanicia:
Germanicia, a titular see in Euphratensis under Antioch, is often misplaced and misnamed. An 1884 Propaganda catalogue expressly fixes it in Euphratensis, not Germaniciana in Byzacene, Africa. Le Quien names five Greek bishops, among them the Arian Eudoxius, later Bishop of Antioch and Constantinople. He adds four Jacobite bishops and at least eighteen more from the eighth to the thirteenth centuries, if Germanicia equals Marash, which remains unproven.

Müller's Ptolemy texts contradict each other so sharply that no conclusion stands, and he prefers the nearby ruins of Altun-Tash-Kale. If Germanicia is Marash, that industrial city in Aleppo's province counts 52,000 people. About 15,000 are Catholics of Melchite, Armenian, Chaldean, and Latin rites, with 22,000 Muslims and the rest schismatic Christians or Jews. Its climate is described as very healthy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-germia:
Germia, a titular see of Galatia Secunda suffragan of Pessinus, rose and vanished across seven centuries of lists. Hierocles names it in the sixth century, and about 650 it already stood as an autocephalous archdiocese directly under Constantinople. The same rank held in the ninth century, under Leo the Wise from 901 to 907, under Constantine Porphyrogenitus, and under Alexius I Comnenus after 1084.

About 1260, under Michael Palaeologus, Germia must have become an autocephalous metropolitan see, a rank it kept under Andronicus II about 1300 and Andronicus III about 1330, before soon disappearing. Lequien knows four titular bishops. From Justinian's reign it bore the name Myriangeloi for its church of Saint Michael and the Holy Angels, and Justinian took its baths in 556. Today it is Germa village, twenty-one miles southeast of Sivri-Hissar, its ancient baths and Justinian's inn still visible. It must not be confused with Germa of Cyzicus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ghardaia:
In 1901 the French Sahara gained a Prefecture Apostolic at Ghardaia, carved from the Vicariate Apostolic covering Sahara and the Soudan. Its region stretched from Morocco's prefecture and the Algerian and Tunisian dioceses to Tripoli's mission and the twentieth parallel north. About three hundred thousand people lived there, all Muslims of Arab and Berber stock. Nomadic tribes crossed the wastes, while settled folk kept the oases, including the Mozabites of the Mzab district.

Three stations carried the mission: Ghardaia, Wargla, and Elgolea. The White Fathers staffed them with twelve missionaries and three lay brothers, in a land where open preaching could not begin at once. Their task was preparation through charity, teaching, and steady friendly contact. Only slowly, the article argues, would old prejudice toward Christians soften, and a younger generation arise among whom lasting conversions could take hold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gift-of-tongu:
The gift of tongues, or glossolalia, is a supernatural grace meant to help the early Church grow outward. A Catholic Encyclopedia article treats its scriptural and historical side, leaving its theology to the article on charismata. At Pentecost, Luke relates, one hundred and twenty Galilean disciples were heard speaking in many tongues as the Holy Spirit gave them speech.

Devout Jews and proselytes from fifteen lands, gathered at Jerusalem, each heard the wonderful things of God in his own tongue. Peter explained the marvel by prophecy as a sign of the last times. The article stresses that the speech was real, clear, and intelligible, with the variety belonging to the group rather than to single speakers. Later outpourings followed at Caesarea, Ephesus, and Corinth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-anim:
Giovanni Animuccia was an Italian composer born at Florence about 1500, who died in 1571. A pupil of Claude Goudimel, he became choir-master at the Vatican and kept the post until his death. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls him the real predecessor of Palestrina, in office and in his search for harmonic clearness amid the counterpoint of the day.

He sought to perfect the old Flemish style with fuller harmony, more natural voice leading, and a closer fit between melody and text. His friendship with St. Philip Neri made him music-master of the saint's new society. For it he wrote the first laudi, songs of praise sung after the sermon. Those laudi, in volumes of 1566 and 1570, became the germs of the later oratorio.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista Beccaria was a physicist born at Mondovì in 1716, who died at Turin in 1781. At sixteen he entered the Order of Clerks Regular of St. Joseph Calasanz, and taught at Palermo and Rome. In 1748 royal authority made him professor of physics at the University of Turin. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his eager study of atmospheric electricity.

With kites, rockets, and iron wire he probed the electrical state of the air, finding both charges in stormy weather and positive charge alone in calm, fair skies. He blamed the forked shape of lightning on air resistance, and held that charge on a conductor sits only on its surface. He adopted Franklin's two-fluid theory and his views on lightning rods. His treatise on artificial and natural electricity appeared in 1753.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregory-of-va:
Gregory of Valencia was professor of theology at the University of Ingolstadt, born at Medina, Spain, in March 1550, who died at Naples on 25 April 1603. Sent by his superiors to Rome in 1598, he took part in the discussions on grace held before the pope. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a man Clement VIII titled Doctor doctorum.

During twenty-four years at Ingolstadt, sixteen as professor of theology, he gave general satisfaction and advanced science. He combated error with success in polemical writings. Paris was eager to secure him, as was Stephen, King of Poland, and Duke Maximilian supplied horses, servants, and money for his journey to Italy. His four-volume work covered the whole field of scholastic theology, and broken in health by incessant work, he served as prefect of studies at the Roman College.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guglielmo-mas:
Guglielmo Massaia, a Piedmont Capuchin born Lorenzo in 1809, became a cardinal after thirty-five years as a missionary in Abyssinia. Refusing bishoprics at home so he could join his order's foreign missions, he was made first vicar-apostolic of the Galla in 1846 and consecrated in Rome that May.

Banished and exiled seven times, he kept returning, ordained native priests, founded missions, opened a Marseilles school for Galla boys freed from slavery, and wrote a Galla grammar published in 1867. Ill health forced his resignation in 1880, Leo XIII made him cardinal in 1884. His memoir of thirty-five years in high Ethiopia, published from 1883, covers mission work with Abyssinia's politics and economy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hesychius-of-:
Hesychius of Alexandria was a grammarian and lexicographer of uncertain date, placed by most authorities in the late fourth or early fifth century. Nothing is known of his parentage or life beyond what his own preface to his Lexicon reveals. That letter, addressed to his friend Eulogius, says he built his work on Diogenianus, who had gathered Homeric, comic, tragic, lyric, and oratorical Greek dictionaries into one lexicon.

Hesychius added vocabularies of medicine and history to that stock, and his classical material remains of the greatest value to Greek scholars. The work has not come down in its original form: biblical and church glosses, which the preface never hints at, are generally agreed to be later additions. The entry also warns against confusing him with a third-century bishop, and a Scripture translator, who share his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-himeria: Himeria, a titular see of Osrhoene under Edessa, still appears in Anastasius's sixth-century Notitia, within that province and Antioch's patriarchate. Procopius credits Justinian with rebuilding its walls. Seven or more bishops are known between the fourth and sixth centuries, starting with Eustathius, who wrote to Basil. The ruined town remains undiscovered, though it likely lay near the Euphrates.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-honoratus-a-s:
Honoratus a Sancta Maria was a Discalced Carmelite, born Blaise Vauxelles at Limoges in 1651 and dead at Lille in 1729. He took his vows at Toulouse in 1671 and set out for missionary life, but superiors detained him at Malta as sub-prior. Returning to France, he served in turn as professor of philosophy and theology, prior, provincial, and visitor general.

His life's interest lies in polemical writings on the burning questions of his age: Quietism, Jansenism, Gallicanism, Cartesian philosophy, and Rationalism in Scripture and history. Uncommon acumen and painstaking research marked his work, while modest diction and moderate attack won even adversaries' esteem. His range, however, was too wide for one man, and critics already in his lifetime charged him with occasional slips.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-illyria:
Illyria, a Balkan district whose size shifted over time, meant for Greek geographers the Adriatic's eastern shore plus the mountains just inland, home of Illyrian tribes. Some Illyrians moved to Italy. Early traces of them sit in central Italy, in Picenum and Umbria. The eighth century B.C. saw the Japyges cross into Apulia and Calabria, and the early seventh century B.C. saw the Veneti reach northern Italy and modern Carinthia.

Those who stayed never formed one nation. Bardylis and his son Kleitos built a kingdom of some weight in the fourth century B.C. Philip crushed it in 357 B.C., and Alexander the Great did so again in 335 B.C. About 250 B.C. the Ardriaii and Antariates, under Pleuratos and Agron, terrorized the sea with fleets and raided Greek colonies on the Adriatic's eastern coast and nearby islands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-improperia:
On Good Friday, during the Adoration of the Cross, the choir sings the Improperia: reproaches the liturgy puts in the Saviour's mouth against the Jews. They answer divine kindness with cruelty: God freed them from Egypt and led them safely to the Promised Land, yet they gave him the Passion's shame and a cruel death.

Three parts make up the whole. The third part, strictly speaking, is not Improperia at all. It holds the antiphon Crucem tuam adoramus, Psalm 66's first verse, the hymn Pange lingua gloriosi lauream, and the versicle Crux fidelis. Part one has three reproaches, Popule meus, Ego eduxi, and Quid ultra, each followed by the Trisagion in Latin and Greek. Part two holds nine more reproaches in the same vein of protest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-india:
A vast survey of India as the British Empire knew it opens with geography on a grand scale. In its widest popular sense the name took in British India, the native states, Portuguese and French India, Burma, and Ceylon. In strict use it meant the Indian Empire alone. The entry gives its size at over 1,800,000 square miles, its length and breadth, and its long land frontier and coastline.

From that map the entry moves through peoples, faiths, rule, and church life. Separate sections cover British, Portuguese, and French India. Schooling in British India and the native states gets its own section. Its scale makes it a starting point for readers who want the shape of the whole subcontinent. It also shows the state of Catholic work there, in one early twentieth-century reference survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-isaac-of-arme:
Isaac the Great was catholicos or patriarch of Armenia from 338 to 439. He was also called Sahak and Parthev for his Parthian blood. He was son of St Narses and heir of St Gregory the Illuminator's house. Orphaned very young, he won a fine literary schooling at Constantinople, above all in Eastern tongues. Once elected patriarch, he gave himself to the religious and scholarly training of his people.

Armenia was in crisis: in 387 it lost independence and was split between Byzantium and Persia under feudatory Armenian kings. In Byzantine lands Syriac, till then the sole tongue of worship, was banned for Greek, while in Persian lands Greek was banned outright. Isaac's work of teaching and translation answered a nation being pulled between two empires and two liturgical tongues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-isaac-of-sele:
Patriarch of the Persian Church until his death in 410, Isaac is honored for rebuilding his church after the savage persecution under Shapur II. Little is known for certain about his early years. The likeliest account says his standing with King Yazdegerd I let him restore the Catholicate of Seleucia, empty for twenty-two years. Another story has him replacing a deposed predecessor named Qayom.

His great work was the Council of Seleucia, the Eastern Syrian Church's counterpart to Nicaea. Persian bishops met at the Sassanid capital by the king's express order, with Isaac presiding alongside Maruthas of Martyropolis, sent by the Western fathers of Antioch to help rebuild. The entry presents a churchman who turned royal favor and conciliar order into a second life for Persian Christianity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ischia:
Ischia, a diocese under Naples, takes the whole volcanic island of the same name in the Mediterranean, a seaward spur of Naples' volcanic country. Monte Epomeo, about 2,570 feet high, has been a dead crater since 1302, yet earthquakes still strike the island, worst at Casamicciola in 1883. Fertile soil and mineral springs, helped by a mild climate and pleasant setting, draw many visitors, above all to the hot springs of Fontana d'Ischia and Formello.

The island capital, also called Ischia, sits on a basalt rock crowned by a castle now used as a prison. Greeks called the island Pithecusae and Romans Aenaria. Euboeans colonized it, Hiero I of Syracuse took it in 474 before Christ, Rome followed in 326, and Augustus later gave it to Naples. The entry pairs a holiday island's geology with its diocese and ancient past.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-itineraria:
Medieval Christian guidebooks, called itineraria from the Latin for journey, fall into two kinds in this entry's sorting. Some are travelers' own accounts of places and lands visited, with voyage incidents worth noting. Others are compilations gathering such accounts to guide future travelers — the ancestors of modern travel books and guidebooks. Nearly all medieval examples concern the road to the Holy Land and its neighbors.

Long travel in those days was beset with danger and difficulty. Few set out except for religious motives. Pilgrims were drawn above all to places hallowed by the Saviour's presence or famed in sacred story. Many pilgrims wrote their journeys, and others harvested those writings into usable guides. Readers get the birth of travel writing as an act of devotion, not of leisure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacopo-della-:
Sculptor Jacopo della Quercia was born, it is said, at Quercia Grossa near Siena in 1374. He died on 20 October 1438. His father, a goldsmith, taught him design. At about sixteen he made a wooden equestrian statue for Azzo Ubaldini's funeral. Soon after, party strife likely drove him from Siena. In 1401 he reappeared at Florence as a rival for St John's gates, a contest Ghiberti won.

In 1408 he worked at Ferrara, notably on the Madonna of the Pomegranate. About 1413 he carved the tomb of Ilaria del Carretto at Lucca cathedral. About 1416 came the Gothic altarpiece at St Frediano, Lucca. He spent ten years on Siena's Fonte Gaia in the Campo. It shows Our Lady with theological and cardinal virtues. It also shows reliefs of man's creation and expulsion from paradise. The entry follows a sculptor bridging Gothic and Renaissance art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-of-bres:
Theologian James of Brescia lived in the fifteenth century and entered the Dominican order in his native city. In 1450 he was appointed inquisitor. He helped papal auditor Bernardo da Bosco end impious teaching at Bergamo. He also played a prominent part in the Dominican-Minorite dispute over the Precious Blood. During Easter Week 1462, St James of the Marches preached at Brescia. He was a famed Minorite preacher. He taught that Christ's Blood, separated from His Body in the Passion, was thereby separated from His Divinity.

Hence, James of the Marches argued, that Blood deserved no adoration while Christ lay in the sepulchre. Since Clement VI had proscribed that doctrine in 1351, James of Brescia cited James of the Marches before his tribunal unless he retracted. A dispute at once arose between Dominicans and Friars Minor. The entry presents an inquisitor policing a subtle theological boundary about Christ's Blood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jesu-dulcis-m:
Jesu Dulcis Memoria is a long Latin poem, running forty-two to fifty-three stanzas across manuscripts. Three hymns for the Office of the Holy Name come from it: Jesu Dulcis Memoria for Vespers, Jesu Rex Admirabilis for Matins, and Jesu Decus Angelicum for Lauds. Each stanza follows a single rhyme scheme, praising Jesus's sweet memory and presence.

Authorship is disputed, and the entry weighs the claims. Ascription to Saint Bernard is general and, in Mearns's view, probable. Yet Guéranger argued manuscripts prove a fourteenth-century Benedictine abbess wrote it. Pothier found it in an eleventh-century manuscript tied to an abbess, before Bernard's birth. The poem's tender devotion kept it in prayer books regardless.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jesu-logia:
Jesu Logia, the Sayings of Jesus, covers words found both in inspired New Testament books and in uninspired writings, the latter called Agrapha, not written under inspiration. This entry limits itself to canonical sayings, yet even that title spans more than the technical term.

Strictly, every word of Christ in inspired books counts as a Logion, while the technical use covers only the Sayings Papias mentions in a passage kept by Eusebius. That narrower question matters for the Synoptic Problem, how Matthew, Mark, and Luke relate. Lessing, Eichhorn, Bleek, and De Wette each proposed an early source gospel behind the three, in Aramaic or Galilean form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-segov:
John of Segovia was a Spanish theologian and historian of the Council of Basle who helped elect an antipope. Born at Segovia late in the fourteenth century, he was archdeacon of Villaviciosa, canon of Toledo, and professor at Salamanca. Salamanca and King John II sent him to Basle in 1432 as an able defender of council over pope.

At first he tried to soften the clash with Eugene IV, spending time with him at Florence in 1435. He became a chief supporter of the council's revolutionary party, voting Eugene contumacious in 1437 and a heretic in 1439. After the council deposed Eugene, he sat on the committee that chose electors. He joined the thirty-three who elected Felix V in November 1439, and was made cardinal by the antipope in 1440. At the schism's end in 1449 he resigned, became titular Bishop of Caesarea, and retired to a Spanish monastery, leaving an eighteen-book history of Basle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-talaia:
John Talaia was the Orthodox Patriarch of Alexandria whose brief reign in 481 to 482 foundered on court intrigue. A monk of Canopus and administrator of the diocese under Patriarch Timothy Salofaciolus, he served as legate to Emperor Zeno, who favored him warmly and foresaw his succession. Enemies called him vain and ambitious, accusing him of bribing courtiers, and he quarreled with Acacius of Constantinople, who became his implacable foe.

When Timothy died in 481, Alexandria's Catholics chose Talaia, but he offended Zeno by announcing his succession to Rome and Antioch without notifying Constantinople, leaving it to a courtier who was away. Acacius persuaded Zeno that Talaia had broken an oath not to accept the patriarchate and had restored the Monophysite Dioscorus to the diptychs, a sheer calumny against an unimpeachably orthodox man. Zeno refused to recognize him and backed his Monophysite rival Peter Mongus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-torrubia:
José Torrubia was a Spanish Franciscan missionary, linguist, and early naturalist who died in 1768. Born at Granada toward the close of the seventeenth century, he first joined the order of St. Peter of Alcántara, worked in the Philippines, and later became a Franciscan in Rome. He traveled widely in America and Asia, spending time at Canton in China.

Torrubia collected fossils and books and wrote on history, politics, and religion, winning esteem in Spain and Rome, above all from Pope Benedict XIV. His works include a history and geography of the Philippines, a poem against Freemasonry, and an introduction to the natural history of Spain. The entry sketches a restless scholar-priest of many trades.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karinthia:
Karinthia was a crownland of the Austrian Empire bounded by Styria, Salzburg, the Tyrol, Italy, Görz, and Krain. Its 370,000 people were about sixty-five percent Germans or germanized Slovenes and thirty-five percent true Slovenes, with ninety-five percent Catholic. Upper Karinthia held the mountain and lake country west of Villach; Lower Karinthia held the valley of Celovec among the Noric and Carnic Alps. The Drave ran its length west to east, and the Gross Glockner rose 12,444 feet.

Celovec, with 24,000 people, was the prince-bishop's see and home of the St. Mohor literary society, circulating 500,000 books a year. Grain, cattle, and flax filled the valleys, while lead, zinc, iron, and coal mines worked busily. The name comes from the Celtic Karni, and the Gospel reached the land from Aquileia and Salzburg.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-la-plata-boli:
La Plata, or Charcas, now Sucre, is the metropolitan see of Bolivia and one of its three chief cities, with La Paz and Cochabamba. Silver mine owners from chilly Potosi founded it, said as early as 1536, as a milder home sixty miles north-east, and General Sucre's 1824 victory gave it his name.

The city stands on a plateau 8,837 feet high with 20,907 people in 1900, chiefly Indians and mestizos. Its cathedral of Our Lady of Guadalupe, three-naved with an imposing tower, guards a seven-foot jewelled image valued near two million dollars, though President Melgarejo melted part of its silver treasure. A medical institute, a Franciscan missionary college of 1837, and a Salesian arts college round out its institutions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lacedonia:
Lacedonia, in Avellino province in southern Italy, is famous for the barons' conspiracy against King Ferdinand I of Naples, hatched in its cathedral in 1484. Its episcopal see dates from the eleventh century, with Desiderius, named in 1082, as first known bishop.

Later bishops include the mathematician Marco Pedacca, the learned Giacomo Candido, and Giacomo Giordano, who raised the episcopal palace and drew up plans for a new cathedral. Benedetto Bartolo was seized by brigands and ransomed by the Marquess of Carpi. Earthquakes battered the town, above all in 1694 and 1702. The diocese, suffragan of Conza and Campagna, holds 11 parishes with 28,000 souls, a Capuchin house, and a house of the Daughters of St. Anne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lagania:
Lagania was a titular see in Galatia Prima, named by Ptolemy and in ancient geographies, often under altered names and with no history attached. Renamed Anastasiopolis under Emperor Anastasius I, it is very likely today's Bey-Bazar, chief town of a caza in the Angora vilayet, with 2,500 Muslim inhabitants.

Its bishopric, suffragan of Ancyra, appears in the Notitiae Episcopatuum into the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Lequien wrongly split Lagania and Anastasiopolis into two sees, and his bishop list needs correction. The revised roll runs from Euphrasius at Nicaea in 325 through Theodosius, Timothy, St. Theodore the Syceote, who died in 613, Genesius, Theophilus, and Marianus at Constantinople in 879.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-latria:
Latria, from Greek latreia, first meant the state of a hired servant, then service in general, and especially divine service. Plato uses it for service to God, and Aeschylus for a servant's lot.

In Christian writing it hardened into a technical term for the supreme honour due to God alone, set against dulia, the honour given to angels and saints as his servants. Etymology alone gives no reason to prefer latria for supreme honour, and the two words were often used interchangeably. The sharp distinction belongs to St. Augustine, who defines latria as the service that pertains to worshipping God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liberia:
Liberia is a republic on Africa's west coast, between 4 degrees 20 minutes and 7 degrees 20 minutes north latitude. It runs from the Sherbro River in the northwest to the Pedro River in the southeast, nearly 600 miles along the coast. It has held sovereign status since 1874, when England, France, and Germany recognized its independence.

Liberia sprang from the American Colonization Society's plan to found in Africa a home to which free blacks might return from the United States. The society sent its first colony to Africa on 6 February 1820. There the colony took permanent root and stayed under the society until 26 July 1847, when Liberia declared independence. Monrovia, a Cape Mesurado seaport named for James Monroe, is the capital and largest town. Temperatures run from 56 to 105 degrees Fahrenheit, averaging 80, with about 100 inches of rain a year. Some 12,000 quasi-American negroes form the ruling class, with about 30,000 civilized native-born people affiliated to them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lismore-austr:
Lismore is a Catholic diocese in north-east New South Wales, Australia. It stretches some 21,000 square miles along the coast from Point Danger toward Port Macquarie. Rivers like the Clarence, the Richmond, and the Macleay water rich farm and dairy land, where sugar and maize were chief crops.

Catholic life came slowly to this rugged coast. The first Catholic family reached Grafton in 1841, and no priest lived in the region until 1862. The first coastal church opened at South Grafton in 1857. Grafton became a bishop's seat in 1887. The entry follows the diocese as priests, Sisters of Mercy, schools, and parishes spread across a thinly settled frontier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lithuania:
Lithuania was an ancient grand duchy in north-east Europe, joined to Poland in the fourteenth century. Its people, kin to the Letts and the vanished Old Prussians, lived in clans through the twelfth century, warring with neighbours and with the crusading Sword Brothers along the Baltic coast.

Prince Mindowe pulled the scattered princes under one rule in the mid-thirteenth century. He and his wife sought baptism around 1250, and Innocent IV sent him a royal crown in 1252. Yet faith took shallow root at first, and the entry follows the land through pagan revival, Polish union, and the slow growth of Catholic life under later rulers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lucia-di-simo:
Luca della Robbia was a Florentine sculptor, born in 1400 and dead in 1481. Trained, it is thought, with a goldsmith, then in marble and bronze under Ghiberti, he was called early to work for Florence cathedral and its bell tower.

His Cantoria panels of singing boys, made 1431 to 1438 for the organ gallery, remain his most loved work, with tower reliefs of Philosophy, Arithmetic, and Grammar beside them. His lasting fame, though, lies in glazed earthenware: a tin glaze of his own secret, fired hard and bright, in blues no rival matched. Madonnas, medallions, and chapel ceilings in that fresh, simple style spread across Florence and beyond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luis-martin-y:
Luis Martin y Garcia was the twenty-fourth general of the Society of Jesus, born at Melgar de Fernamental in 1846 and dead at Fiesole in 1906. Of humble parents, he studied six years at Burgos seminary, joined the Society at Loyola in 1864, and learned philosophy and theology in Spain and France.

Ordained in 1876, he led Salamanca seminary, edited El Mensajero, headed Deusto-Bilbao college, and served as Castile provincial before becoming general in 1892. Sarcoma took an arm and forced painful operations, borne with fortitude. He rebuilt Salamanca's great seminary, founded the Comillas seminary, and planned a history of the Society, writing prose with nervous grace and verse with robust music.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-magnesia:
Magnesia covers two ancient bishoprics in Asia Minor that shared one name. The Lydian one stood under Ephesus, about forty miles north-east of Smyrna. Settlers from Thessaly were said to have founded it in the fifth century B.C. That is the first of the pair.

There, Lucius Scipio beat Antiochus of Syria in 190 B.C. An earthquake under Tiberius laid the town low. It rose again as Manisa, a thriving town of 35,000 people with twenty mosques and Greek and Armenian churches. Its bishops run from Eusebius in 431 to Luke in 879. The second Magnesia stood on the Meander in Ionia. It held a famed temple of Diana, built by Hermogenes, with asylum rights and eight bishops of its own.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manchuria:
Manchuria was the north-eastern division of the Chinese Empire and cradle of its then-ruling dynasty. It lay north-east of the Eighteen Provinces, from about 38 to 49 degrees north and 120 to 133 degrees east. The Amur and Russian land bounded it north, the Usuri east, Korea and the Yellow Sea south, and the Nonni and a palisade line west.

Its southern part was called the three Manchu provinces beyond Shanhaikwan, or the country east of the pass. An imperial decree of 1907 replaced its military governors with a governor general. The Liao and Kin Tatars, rulers of northern China from the tenth to the thirteenth century, came out of Manchuria. Railways follow, above all the Chinese Eastern line of 1896. Trade at Newchwang, Dalny, and Harbin follows too, with the Vicariate Apostolic of Manchuria, created in 1838 from Peking, under Paris Foreign Mission bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manfredonia:
Manfredonia was a city in Foggia province, Apulia, on the edge of Mount Gargano, built by King Manfred in 1256 near ruined Sipontum. Sipontum had been a flourishing Greek colony, retaken about 335 B.C. by Alexander of Epirus, made a Roman colony in 189 B.C., and wrecked by Slavs in A.D. 663. 

Legend credits St Peter and St Mark with preaching there, but firmer tradition tells of St Justin's martyrdom about 255. Felix, at Rome in 465, is the first bishop with a fixed date. Under Bishop Lawrence, in the reign of Gelasius I, St Michael appeared on Mount Gargano, and his famed monastery followed. The see, entrusted to Benevento about 688, was restored in 1034 and became an archdiocese under St Gerard in 1066. Later bishops include Giovanni del Monte, later Julius III, and Vincenzo Orsini, later Benedict XIII. By 1818 it held 16 parishes and 101,800 faithful.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maronia:
Maronia was a titular see in Rhodopis, under Trajanopolis. Its town was ancient, said to have been founded by Maron, reputed son of Dionysus or companion of Osiris. The legend likely grew from Maronia's famed Dionysiac worship, fed by its celebrated wine, praised even in Homer's day.

Its commanding spot on the Thracian Sea and a Chian colony of about 560 B.C. gave it weight. Philip V of Macedon took it in 200 B.C., but Rome ordered it freed at once. Rome then gave it to Attalus of Pergamos, revoked the gift, and left it free. About 640 it became an autocephalous archdiocese, rising to metropolitan rank in the thirteenth century under Andronicus II. Today it remains a Greek metropolitan see, its titular living at Gumuldjina, while the old coastal town lies abandoned and its name belongs to an inland village of two thousand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-of-val:
Martin of Valencia, born Juan Martin de Boil, was a Franciscan missionary born at Villa de Valencia about the mid-fifteenth century and dead at Tlalmanalco, Mexico, in 1534. He joined the Franciscans at Mayorga in Santiago province, built Santa Maria del Berrogal monastery, and founded the Custody of San Gabriel, visiting Rome for it.

In 1523 he was chosen to lead twelve Franciscans to convert Mexican natives. They landed in May 1524 and won profound veneration from Hernando Cortes. As apostolic delegate Martin presided over the New World's first ecclesiastical synod on 2 July 1524 and set up the Custody of the Holy Gospel, becoming its first custos. After a three-year interval he was re-elected to that office. He lived with great austerity, and he and his eleven companions, the Twelve Apostles of Mexico, reportedly baptised several million natives. He died in the odour of sanctity in 1534.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-menevia:
Menevia, said to come from Menapia, a Roman settlement thought to have stood in Pembrokeshire, or from Hen Meneu, old bush, where St. David was born, is a Welsh diocese. From the four vicars apostolic set up in England in 1688, Wales belonged to the Western District vicariate. In 1840 Gregory XVI made it a separate vicariate, and in 1850, when the hierarchy returned, Wales split between Shrewsbury and Newport.

In 1895 the principality, save Glamorganshire, became a vicariate apostolic again. Francis Joseph Mostyn, son of Sir Pyers Mostyn of Talacre, became first vicar apostolic with Ascalon as titular see. In 1898 he moved to Menevia when Leo XIII raised the vicariate to a diocese. Its bishop alone holds an ancient pre-Reformation title. The diocese, under Our Lady Help of Christians, St. David, and St. Winefride, covers 6,500 rugged square miles with some 8,500 scattered Catholics and forty-three churches, chapels, and stations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mesopotamia-k:
Mesopotamia, Kurdistan, and Armenia form an apostolic delegation created by Gregory XVI on 17 December 1832. Mgr Trioche, Archbishop of Babylon or Bagdad, became its first titular and lived habitually in Bagdad. Resigning in 1850, he returned to France, keeping his Bagdad title but losing the delegate's charge, which passed to other bishops. Those bishops, while administering the Bagdad archdiocese, lived at Mosul, where they could better serve Chaldeans, Syrians, and Armenians.

Four of six delegates from 1850 to 1887 were Dominicans. When Trioche died in France on 27 November 1887, the delegate apostolic, Mgr Altmayer, took the title of Archbishop of Babylon or Bagdad but stayed at Mosul. In 1902 he resigned, and a Carmelite, Mgr Drure, replaced him in the Bagdad see, receiving the delegate's title for Mesopotamia on 5 March 1904, which he still bears. He usually lives at Mosul. The delegation nearly matches the Bagdad archdiocese, but also takes in part of Greater Armenia's mission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mission-india:
Mission Indians of California is a name of no real ethnic significance. It is a handy popular and official term for the modern heirs of California's tribes, of many stocks and tongues. The Franciscans won them to the faith in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, starting in 1769. The historic California missions numbered twenty-one, excluding branch foundations.

They stretched along the coast or a short distance inland, from San Diego in the south to Sonoma, beyond San Francisco Bay, in the north. San Diego de Alcala, founded by Father Junipero Serra in 1769, was the first. In 1909 the southern mission Indians, in San Diego and Riverside counties, numbered 2,775 souls in five tribes and languages. They were practically all Catholics, served by twelve government day schools and seventeen Catholic schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mongolia:
Mongolia, as this entry uses the name, is the vast uneven plateau within the Chinese Empire. It stretches from the Tarbagatai ranges to the Great Khingan chain. Siberia bounds it in the north, Manchuria in the east, and the Great Wall country in the south. Its area is put near 1,358,000 square miles. Population guesses range from about 2.6 million to 5 million.

Three regions divide it. The central Mongolian desert, the northwestern plateau around Kobdo and Urga toward the Altai, and the southwestern Khingan mountains form the three. The entry then covers climate, rivers, peoples and their nomadic life. It describes the Buddhist lamas and monasteries that dominate religion, trade routes, and Catholic missions among Mongols. The political tug between China and Russia shapes its modern story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mopsuestia:
Mopsuestia, a titular see of Cilicia Secunda in Asia Minor and suffragan of Anazarbus, traces its founding legend to the seer Mopsus. He lived before the Trojan War, though history barely mentions the city before the Christian era. Pliny calls it the free city of Mopsos. It later bore the names Seleucia, Hadriana under Hadrian and Decia under Decius.

Constantius built a splendid bridge over the Pyramus there, restored by Justinian and still standing in poor repair. Christianity reached it early. Bishop Theodorus opposed Paul of Samosata in the third century, Saint Auxentius lived there in the fourth, and Theodore, teacher of Nestorius, counted among its bishops. Its Greek diocese under Antioch lasted into the fourteenth century, and by 879 it stood as an autocephalous archbishopric.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moravia:
Moravia, the Austrian crown land east of Bohemia, was held before the Christian era by the Germanic Quadi. They were kin to the Marcomanni who had driven the Celtic Boii from Bohemia. Both tribes are known mainly through their wars with Rome under Marcus Aurelius and Valentinian I. The Huns under Attila drove most of both tribes out, and Slavs settled the empty land in the fifth century.

Conquered by Avars in the sixth century, the Slavs won temporary freedom under Samo between 622 and 658. Final release came when Charlemagne crushed the Avars in 796. A principality grew into the kingdom of the Moimirids, dependent on the Frankish Empire yet asserting itself. The entry follows Moravia through Great Moravia, the missions of Cyril and Methodius, Bohemian and Habsburg rule, and its church, schools and peoples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nacolia:
Phrygia Salutaris once counted Nacolia among its titular metropolitan sees, a town named for the nymph Nacola with no ancient history to speak of. Imperial politics reached it when Valens stood against the pretender Procopius there. Later, while Arcadius ruled, Gothic troops quartered in the town turned on their emperor. Synnada first held authority over the see; it then gained independence sometime from 787 to 862, and rose to metropolitan rank sometime from 1035 to 1066.

Seven bishops of Nacolia are recorded. Constantine stands out among them. A backer of image-breaking under Leo the Isaurian, he pretended to renounce his error before Patriarch Saint Germanus. He then faced condemnation as a heresiarch at Nicaea's second council in 787. Today the place is Seyyid el-Ghazi, a village roughly twenty-two miles southeast of Eski Sheir. Its name recalls an Arab sheikh killed in 739, whose grave lies in a lodge of Bektashi dervishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-caledonia:
New Caledonia, a vicariate apostolic and one of Oceania's largest islands, lies about 900 miles east of Queensland, Australia, between 20 and 22 degrees south and 164 to 167 degrees east. It measures about 250 miles long by 30 broad, covering 7,650 square miles. A French colony, its dependencies include the Isle of Pines and Loyalty Islands, and its population with them is estimated at 53,000.

The coasts are deeply indented, and an immense coral reef almost surrounds the island, leaving a broad calm channel that eases coastal travel. The island is very mountainous, about half uncultivatable, with a central chain over 5,500 feet and coastal hills mostly under 600 feet. Fertile plains stretch between the ranges. The entry covers the island's peoples, resources, penal history, and the Catholic mission's stations, schools and converts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-norcia:
New Norcia is a Benedictine abbey in Western Australia, founded on 1 March 1846 by the Spanish Benedictine Rudesindus Salvado for christianising the Australian aborigines. It stands eighty-two miles from Perth, bounded south and east by the Diocese of Perth and north by Geraldton. At first the mission held no territory.

Its holy founder, like the Baptist of old, dwelt in the wilds, sharing the wandering life of the people he had come to rescue from darkness. His food varied wildly: wild roots dug by his neophytes' spears, lizards, iguanas, even worms in distress, or kangaroo when fortunate in the chase. After three years of unparalleled hardship among this cannibal race, Salvado judged them capable of Christianity. He sailed for Rome in 1849 seeking helpers and money, was made Bishop of Port Victoria, then begged to return to his Australian flock.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-pomerania:
New Pomerania, the largest island of the Bismarck Archipelago, lies separated from New Guinea by Dampier Strait, extending from 148 to 152 degrees east and 4 to 7 degrees south. It runs about 348 miles long and 12 to 92 miles broad, covering 9,650 square miles. Two regions stand out.

The northeastern Gazelle Peninsula is largely wooded mountains, though soil near Blanche Bay is very fertile and well watered by rivers like the Toriu and Kerawat, yielding abundant fish. Whites cluster in the north, where the capital Herbertshohe stands. The larger western section also holds extensive mountain chains with numerous active volcanoes. Natives' warlike nature, fiercely resisting landings, leaves the interior almost unknown. The entry covers their build, weapons, shell money, feuds, and the Catholic mission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolo-tartag:
Italian mathematician Nicolo Tartaglia, born at Brescia around 1500, solved the cubic equation after teaching himself mathematics. A French soldier's blow across the mouth at the sack of Brescia in 1512 left him stammering, and the nickname Tartaglia, meaning stammerer, stuck for life.

By 1541 he had cracked the cubic, beating Antonio del Fiore in a 1535 contest, yet Cardano published the method in 1545 after learning it under pledge of secrecy. A bitter quarrel followed, and Tartaglia died at Venice in 1557. In 1548 he took the Euclid chair at Brescia, but returned to Venice after eighteen months. His will asked for burial in San Silvestro at Venice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicomedia:
Nicomedia, a great city of Bithynia on the Sea of Marmara, served kings, emperors, and bishops across a thousand years. Founded by King Zipoetes and refounded by his son Nicomedes I around 264 BC, it sheltered Hannibal, stayed capital under Rome, and became Diocletian's favored home.

Pliny the Younger describes its senate house, aqueduct, and forum, and Diocletian raised a palace, hippodrome, mint, and arsenal there. In 303 its bishop Anthimus and many Christians died in the last great persecution, and later emperors and councils kept the city in the story of the church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-norcia:
Norcia, a diocese and city in Perugia, stands in the Apennines as the birthplace of Saint Benedict. A republic in the ninth century and a prize fought over by Spoleto's dukes and popes, it was defended in 1453 by the pope's general Cesarini against Spoleto and Cascia.

Besides Benedict, Norcia gave the church abbots Spes and Eutychius, the monk Florentius, and the physician Benedict Pegardati, while meat-preserving remains its chief trade. Re-established as a see in 1820, it counts 100 parishes and 28,000 people. Its first known bishop was Stephen, dated to about 495.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nova-scotia:
Nova Scotia, a maritime province of Canada formed from old Acadia, joins a mainland peninsula to Cape Breton Island across the Strait of Canso. Bounded by the Bay of Fundy, New Brunswick, and the Atlantic, it holds Sable Island, the graveyard of the Atlantic, where a French settler failed in 1518.

The entry surveys its coasts, fisheries, forests, and farms, then its peoples and church. Acadian Catholics, Irish and Scottish settlers, dioceses at Halifax and Antigonish, and schools and parishes carried the faith through deportation and return. Sable Island, twenty-five miles long, earned the name graveyard of the Atlantic from its wrecks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nubia:
Nubia, a vast region of northeast Africa stretching from Sennar beyond Khartoum through the Egyptian Sudan, mixes Ethiopian, Berber, Arab, and southern peoples. Its divisions run from Meroe and Sennar in the south through Dongola and Kordofan to Darfur in the west, with Taka in the east.

Khartoum, founded in 1823 at the White and Blue Nile junction, destroyed by the Mahdi in 1885 and rebuilt in 1898, anchors the account, beside Omdurman, Berber, and Suakin's successor Port Sudan. The entry gives areas, populations, and the missions that worked among its peoples. Dongola, Berber, Khartoum, Fashoda, and Sennar anchor its central and southern sections.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nueva-segovia:
Nueva Segovia, a Philippine diocese named for a Spanish town, began when Clement VIII split Manila's vast see in 1595. Founded as a town in Cagayan in 1581, it gave its name to a see that moved to Vigan in the mid-eighteenth century, while the town itself merged with Lalloc.

Leo XIII later carved Tuguegarao from its territory, leaving Ilocos Norte and Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Abra, and the Mountain Province. About a million people, chiefly Ilocanos and Pangasinans with Igorot mountaineers, fill a diocese the entry maps parish by parish.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-o-salutaris-h:
O Salutaris Hostia, meaning O Saving Host, opens the second-last stanza of Aquinas's hymn for Lauds on Corpus Christi. Joined to its closing doxology, the stanza became a separate hymn for Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament, sung as the tabernacle opens or the monstrance is enthroned.

English custom enjoins it in the Ritus Servandus, though rubrics do not bind it everywhere, and other fitting texts remain allowed. As a liturgical text it may not be sung in the vernacular, and it also serves as a motet at solemn Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-offa-king-of-:
Offa, king of Mercia from 757 to his death in 796, made his kingdom supreme south of the Humber. After fourteen years ordering his realm, he beat Kent at Otford in 775, Wessex at Bensington in 779, and the Welsh, seizing much of Powys including Pengwern.

To curb Welsh raids he raised Offa's Dyke, roughly fixing the England-Wales border ever since. Seeking freedom from Canterbury, he persuaded Hadrian I to erect a Mercian archbishopric at Lichfield, and his coinage and laws show a king dealing as an equal with Charlemagne. He took the throne in 757 when his cousin King Aethelbald was murdered by Beornraed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oria:
Oria, an Apulian diocese suffragan to Taranto, passed from Borromei princes to bishops fleeing Saracen Brindisi. In the Middle Ages a principality sold by Saint Charles for 40,000 crowns for the poor, it endured Manfred's siege in 1266 and Muslim sacks in 924 and 977.

When Saracens ruined Brindisi in the ninth century, its bishops settled at Oria and styled themselves bishops of Brindisi and Oria after their return. Erected as its own see in 1591 under Vincent Tufo, Oria counts 15 parishes, 120,000 people, and twenty religious houses. Bishop Andrew was slain by Porphyrius in 979, after Muslim sacks in 924 and 977.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palencia:
Palencia is a Spanish diocese covering the provinces of Palencia, Santander, Valladolid, Burgos, and Leon. Its capital city counts 15,050 people. Florez dates the see from the first centuries, and its bishop may have sat among those who deposed Basilides of Astorga in the third century. Suevi and Visigoths nearly wrecked the city in 457.

Priscillianism spread over the Tierra de Campos from Galicia, and Saint Toribius of Astorga fought it hard. Maurila, an Arian bishop set in Palencia by Leovigild, gave up his heresy when King Reccared converted in 587. Conantius, who ruled over thirty years, wrote church melodies and a prayer book from the Psalms. Later pages follow the see through Moorish years, restoration, and its bishops into modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patagonia:
Patagonia is South America's southernmost tip, bounded north near latitude 44 south, south by the Straits of Magellan, west by the Andes and Chile, and east by the South Atlantic. It spans about 300,000 square miles. Magellan found it in 1520, though a 1428 world map described by Galvao already showed the straits as the Dragon's Tail. Magellan supposedly named the people Patagoas for their big feet, and they still wear colt-skin shoes jutting past their toes.

Trackless pampas climb in terraces to Andean ranges webbed with lakes and lagoons, rolling south in tussock grass, thorn bush, guanacos, and mirages. Primeval forests cloak the western flanks, barely explored at their edges, while eastern rivers like the Chubut and Deseado run to the Atlantic. Later pages cover missions, sheep farming, Welsh settlers, and the Salesian work among native peoples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pavia:
Pavia, or Papia, is a city in Lombardy, Italy, set in a fertile plain, linked to Milan by canal. Once famed for organ making, it kept few of the towers behind its name city of a hundred towers, with a fourteenth-century covered bridge surviving. Its cathedral, built by Rocchi and Omodeo from 1488, holds paintings by Crespi and Gatti, a silver reliquary of the Holy Thorns, and a carved pulpit by Zanella.

Saint Peter in the Golden Sky, the former cathedral restored in the twelfth century, takes its name from its golden-ground mosaics. Saint Augustine's body rests there, brought by King Luitprand from Sardinia, hidden, and rediscovered in 1695 in a lead and silver casket within marble. Its fourteenth-century tomb, ordered by Prior Bonifacio Bottigello, bears fifty bas-reliefs and ninety-five statuettes. Boethius is also buried there, near Gothic Saint Mary of Carmel of 1376 and Saint Francis of 1260.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pelagia:
Pelagia is the name shared by several saints, and this Catholic Encyclopedia entry sorts the historical figure from the legends around her. The oldest record concerns a fifteen-year-old Christian virgin of Antioch. Soldiers sought her during the Diocletian persecution and ordered her to sacrifice to pagan gods. Alone in her house, she asked to change her clothes, climbed to the roof, and leapt to her death rather than face dishonour.

Later storytellers reshaped her into a converted Antioch courtesan. Won over by Bishop Nonnus, she supposedly lived disguised as a man named Pelagius in a grotto on the Mount of Olives. The entry argues this penitent is a legendary reworking of the martyr, drawn from a homily of Chrysostom. It adds a third Pelagia of Tarsus, and gives the feast days each figure holds in East and West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pennsylvania:
Pennsylvania was one of the thirteen original American states, and this long Catholic Encyclopedia survey treats its land, history, and church together. It opens with geography. The landlocked state covers 45,215 square miles, ridged by parallel mountains and cut by the Susquehanna. The Delaware bounds it east, and the Allegheny and Monongahela join into the Ohio west. Its shore on Lake Erie ran only 45 miles.

History follows, from John Smith's and Henry Hudson's brushes with its edges to Etienne Brulé's Susquehanna journey and William Penn's charter of 1681, which paid a crown debt of £16,000 with land. Penn's toleration, which barred only atheists and polytheists, set the colony apart. Later sections cover government, education, and the dioceses of Pittsburgh, Erie, Harrisburg, Scranton, and Altoona.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pentacomia: Pentacomia was a titular see of Palestine that, this brief Catholic Encyclopedia entry argues, never truly existed as a bishopric. Crusader writers mistook a civil geography by George of Cyprus for a list of bishoprics, and Le Quien repeated the error without naming a single bishop. Places of the name also stood in Arabia and near Samaria, but the site of Pentacomia itself remains unknown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peoria:
Peoria was a diocese of central Illinois, cut from Chicago in 1875 and enlarged six years later. Its Catholic roots reach Marquette's rest at the Indian village in 1673 and the Masses said at La Salle's Fort Crèvecoeur by Recollect fathers. A broken line of missionaries runs down to modern Peoria, where Father Drew raised St. Mary's, the city's first Catholic church, in 1846.

Irish labourers on the Illinois and Michigan Canal, paid in land scrip when their company failed, settled as farmers and became the pioneer Catholics, joined later by Germans. Poles, Slavs, Croatians, Lithuanians, and Italians followed to work the coal mines, forming parishes served by priests of their own peoples. The poet-priest Abram Ryan numbered among the diocese's early clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-persia:
Persia was the great Iranian empire whose history, religion, and civilisation grew from Median roots. Medes and Persians were both Aryan peoples, with the Medes leading first. In the sixth century BC Persian kings took the lead and built an empire reaching from Egypt to Bactria. This vast Catholic Encyclopedia survey follows that empire to the Arab conquest and beyond, into modern Persia.

Geography opens the account: a high plateau of some 642,000 square miles, over a fifth the size of the United States, between the Caspian, the Indian Ocean, and the Persian Gulf. Later sections cover the ancient Persians' hardy pastoral life and the faith of Zoroaster. They follow the long line of kings and conquerors, and the Christian missions that carried the Gospel into a land shaped by Islam.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-perugia:
Perugia was an Umbrian hill city on the Tiber, and this Catholic Encyclopedia entry tours its churches, university, and ancient stones. Its fourteenth-century Gothic cathedral is still unfinished in front. Inside are paintings by Barocci, Manni, and Signorelli, the tombs of Urban IV and Martin IV, and an onyx ring honoured as Our Lady's wedding ring. The university, founded in 1320, keeps a museum of Etruscan, Roman, and Christian antiquities.

History runs deep here. An Etruscan power, Perugia fought Rome in 310 and 295 BC, and the Perugian War of 41 BC trapped Antony's troops inside its walls until surrender. Gothic War sieges followed, and the city later held its place among the papal states. Etruscan walls, the Porta Augusta, and the Volumni tomb, found in 1840, still mark its oldest layers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pescia:
Pescia was a Tuscan diocese on the Pescia Maggiore and Minore, set in a fertile plain with a strong textile trade. Its ancient cathedral, restored by Ferri in 1663, holds paintings by Gabbiani and the tomb of Baldassare Turini. Older churches include S. Michele and S. Stefano, predating the twelfth century, and S. Francesco from 1211. The town is first mentioned in the eighth century.

Lucca ruled it until Florence conquered it in the fourteenth century and held it against Sforza in 1430. The exile Pietro Strozzi seized it in 1554 but yielded to Duke Cosimo de' Medici. Leo X freed it from Lucca in 1519 as a prelacy, and it became a diocese suffragan to Pisa in 1726. Its first bishop was Bartolommeo Pucci, and Francesco Vicenti founded its seminary in 1784.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-of-alex:
Peter of Alexandria was bishop of his city from 300 and a martyr of November 311. Once head of Alexandria's famous catechetical school, he likely began the reaction there against extreme Origenism. When the Diocletian persecution drove him into hiding, the Meletian schism broke out, and this Catholic Encyclopedia entry weighs three conflicting accounts of its origin.

Latin documents say Meletius of Lycopolis seized Peter's functions and consecrated bishops to occupied sees. Athanasius adds charges of sacrifice and denunciation, though the entry warns the sacrifice charge rests on rumour. Epiphanius traces the quarrel to the treatment of the lapsed, with Meletius taking the sterner line. Peter excommunicated Meletius, and the schism outlived them both.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philadelphia:
Philadelphia was an American archdiocese erected in 1808 and raised in 1875, covering the city and county plus nine surrounding counties across 5,043 square miles. In 1910 its territory held 2,712,708 people, with 1,549,008 in the city itself, then America's third city and its leader in shipbuilding, locomotives, streetcars, carpets, and leather. Until 1800 the city had been the nation's capital.

Penn's holy experiment of 1682 drew persecuted Catholics from neighbouring colonies, and Jesuit missionaries riding between New York and Maryland gathered them in private houses for Mass. Parishes multiplied through the nineteenth century, from St. John's cathedral under Bishop Kenrick to German, Irish, and suburban churches. The entry follows that growth parish by parish to a mature archdiocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philo-of-alex:
Philo of Alexandria was a Jewish philosopher who wedded Moses to Greek thought, born about 25 BC. His priestly family ranked among Alexandria's most powerful Jews: his brother Alexander served Antony's daughter and married into Herod Agrippa's house, while his nephew Tiberius Alexander apostatized to become procurator of Judea. Philo took a Jewish education and the Greek course of grammar, geometry, rhetoric, and dialectics as philosophy's preparation.

His writings show first-hand Stoicism, Plato, neo-Pythagorean works, and Cynic moral tales, yet he stayed loyal to Jewish practice and Jerusalem's Temple. Two convictions drive his work: Jewish law matches natural law, giving the faith a universality beyond narrow national messianism, and Scripture yields its meaning through allegory. His embassy to Caligula and his treatise on Flaccus's persecution anchor him in his city's troubled life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-phoenecia:
Phoenicia was a narrow coastal strip, some 150 miles long and 30 wide, between the Mediterranean and Lebanon's heights. Fertile, well-watered, and wooded with cedars, cypresses, and palms, it held twenty-five cities, chief among them Tyre, Sidon, Aradus, Byblus, Marathus, and Tripolis. Its name likely comes from Greek phoinix, blood-red, and its earliest inscription dates from the ninth century BC.

Trade was its genius. The only ancient eastern people with a navy, Phoenicians pushed caravans to Arabia, India, and Mesopotamia and sailed the whole Mediterranean to Spain, France, and England, planting colonies from Cyprus to Africa. They simplified writing into a twenty-two-letter alphabet, ancestor of Semitic and European scripts, and advanced glass, weights, measures, and navigation. Their polytheism, known from the Old Testament and votive stones, centred on nature gods.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pisidia:
Pisidia lay in southwest Asia Minor, with the high Phrygian plateau on one side and Pamphylia's coastal plain on the other. Towering ridges of the western Taurus shaped its country. Before Christ its people were tough, half-wild highlanders, never fully brought under control, and old authors call them restless raiders.

Paul crossed the region two or perhaps three times, and may have meant it when he spoke of dangers from rivers and from robbers. Free until 36 BC, the Pisidians fell to Amyntas, king of Galatia, and with him came under Rome. Passed between provinces, Pisidia gained its own governor in 297 AD. Cremna, Adada, Serge, Termessos, Pednalissos, and Sagalassos were its leading towns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pius-melia:
Pius Melia was an Italian Jesuit theologian who left his order and became embroiled in a bitter quarrel over the philosopher Rosmini. He was born at Rome in 1800 and joined the Jesuits in 1815. He taught literature at Reggio and preached before leaving the Society in 1853.

He wrote a defence of the Jesuits in 1847 and an attack on Rosmini, above all on Rosmini's teaching about original sin, the inherited fault of humankind. Rosmini answered in 1841 and Pagani in 1842, and the dispute grew so sharp that Pius IX himself had to order it stopped. Melia died in London in 1883.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plasencia:
Plasencia is a Spanish diocese spanning the provinces of Cáceres, Salamanca, and Badajoz, with its capital city of 8,044 people. It was founded by Alfonso VIII on the Moorish site of Ambroz and named Placentia, that it might please God and man. It was made a see by Clement III in 1189.

Its early bishops were warriors as much as shepherds: Domingo fought at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 and against Jaén, while Adán joined Saint Ferdinand's conquest of Córdoba. The entry follows the diocese's later bishops and its cathedrals. An early Gothic church is now Santa María parish. A late Gothic and Renaissance cathedral begun in 1498 has a high altar by Gregorio Hernández.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pomaria:
Pomaria, a titular see of Mauretania Caesarea, lay north of Tlemcen in Algeria, facing the ruins of Agadir, a town raised over Pomaria itself. Orchards gave it its name, and it thrived in the shade of a Roman camp. Latin inscriptions abound at Agadir and nearby, mostly Christian, the latest from the seventh century.

One bishop only is recorded: Longinus, called up by King Huneric, who came back to Carthage in 484 and faced banishment. Victor of Vita praised him, as did Gregory of Tours and Fredegarius, and Usuard's martyrology enters his name under 1 February. Late in the eighth century Idris I built Agadir over Pomaria's site, and Tlemcen, founded late in the eleventh century, at last replaced it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pomerania:
Pomerania, a Prussian province on the Baltic, straddles both banks of the Oder, with Hither Pomerania west and Farther Pomerania east. It spans 11,628 square miles and holds 1,684,345 people. Over half its soil, 55.2 per cent, goes to farming and market gardening, with grassland at 10.2 per cent, pasturage at 6.5 per cent, and woodland at 20.2 per cent. Farming, cattle raising, shipping, and fishing employ most people.

German tribes, Goths, Rugians, and Burgundians among them, lived there first. Near the middle of the second century they drifted southeast, and Slavs, or Wends, slowly filled the province. Pommern, the name, is Slavonic for along the sea. Charlemagne forced recognition of his overlordship as far as the Oder, and the Wends paid tribute again under Henry I and Otto the Great.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontificalia:
Pontificalia is the collective name for the insignia of the episcopal order worn by bishops alone. In a broad sense it covers all attire proper to bishops, even choir dress such as the cappa magna or the hat with green cord. More strictly, rubricians limit it to the ornaments a prelate wears when celebrating pontifically.

The eight pontificals common to all, listed by Pius VII in 1823, are buskins, sandals, gloves, dalmatic, tunicle, ring, pectoral cross, and mitre. Abbots, prothonotaries, and some canons may use them by papal indult, but only at Mass and under restrictions. They may not bless the people in procession. They have no seventh candle, they vest in the sacristy, and they wash hands only once, at the offertory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-port-victoria:
Port Victoria covers the Seychelles in the Indian Ocean: eighty-nine islands with dependencies, spanning 148 and a half square miles. Mahé, Praslin, Silhouette, Curieuse, and La Digue lead the group. France held the islands from about 1742, Britain captured them in 1794 and received them formally in 1848. Port Victoria, Mahé's capital on the northeast coast, holds the colonial government.

In December 1909 the population stood at 22,409. State-aided Catholic and Anglican primary schools serve the children. Mahé and Praslin grow the double coconut, Coco de Mer, while distant Aldabra is famed for giant land tortoises. A papal decree of November 1852 split the Seychelles from Port Louis as a prefecture apostolic, joined in 1854 by the Amirantes and Agalega. Jeremias Paglietti was the first prefect. Capuchins took the mission in 1863, it became a vicariate in 1880, and the Diocese of Port Victoria, erected in July 1892, answered directly to Rome from June 1899.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-praxedes-and-:
Praxedes and Pudentia are martyrs of unknown date. Seventh century guides name two women martyrs in the catacomb of Priscilla, Potentiana and Praxedis, in graves side by side. Among Martyrologium Hieronymianum manuscripts, only Echternach's Codex names St Praxedes, on 21 July. It reads like a later add on, not a piece of the fourth century Roman Martyrology. Both were honoured as martyrs at Rome.

Later lore ties them to Rome's old title church, the titulus Pudentis. Lore counts Pudens as St Peter's pupil, with Praxedes and Potentiana as his daughters. In time Potentiana came to be called Pudentiana, likely because the church was styled ecclesia sanctae Pudentianae and Pudentiana was taken to be Potentiana. About then a new church, the titulus Praxedis, rose near Santa Maria Maggiore, and St Praxedes' cult clung to it instead.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-precaria:
A precaria, from preces, prayers, is a deal giving a petitioner the use and fruits of a church property that bears revenue. The grant runs for a set time or for his life, chiefly for services done to the Church. The deal rests on the Roman law precarium, but differs from it: the Roman precarium could cover goods that move or stand, and could be called back at the owner's whim. Both deals left ownership with the owner.

The deal hurt the Church twice over: it stripped her of revenues and put her ownership at risk, above all when kings forced the grant, the precaria verbo regis. For that cause the Council of Meaux in 825 bade such grants be renewed each five years. The grant ended at the grantee's death or at the term's end, and then the giver could call it back at will.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prussia:
Prussia, the Kingdom of Prussia, dominates this very long encyclopedia entry. At the time of writing it covered 134,616 square miles, about 64.8 per cent of the German Empire. It held most of the north German plain and the central mountain chain. It also held most of Germany's mineral wealth: coal, iron, salt and potash. Great rivers crossed it, and its farms grew rye, oats and wheat. In 1905 its population stood at 37,282,935.

History fills the bulk of the piece, from the kingdom's origins through its humiliation under Napoleon. Russia's intercession saved a remnant of Hohenzollern territory after defeat. The Peace of Tilsit in July 1807 stripped Prussia of its Franconian lands, its lands west of the Elbe, and its Polish gains. French troops garrisoned what remained, and a huge war indemnity followed. Yet the entry argues that this low point opened the way to reform, and a long bibliography closes the survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-regalia:
Regalia almost always means the insignia of royalty, the crown jewels. This encyclopedia entry lists the objects the term covers: the crown, the ring, the orb, the spurs, the swords, the sceptre with the cross, and the sceptre with the dove. It adds the vestments worn after the anointing: the colobium sindonis, the dalmatic, the armill and the royal robe or pall. The ampulla for the oil with its spoon, and Saint Edward's staff, join them.

All descend from pre-Reformation days, and many spring from religion. England, Germany and France alike tended to link these insignia with sacred meanings. A Byzantine thread follows: the lorum, an embroidered scarf hanging in front, passing round the body and falling over the left arm, formed the chief part of imperial state dress. It likely stands behind the armill, now a sort of stole, and almost certainly fathered the archiepiscopal pallium.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reggio-dell-e:
The Diocese of Reggio dell'Emilia, under Modena in central Italy, centres on a city where the ancient Via Aemilia meets the small River Crostolo, flowing to the Po through very fertile land. This encyclopedia entry names silk, straw and osier work as the chief industries. Its cathedral is Romanesque, from the twelfth century, restored in the fifteenth and sixteenth, with remains of thirteenth-century frescoes. The museum holds Abbate Spallanzani's scientific collection, prehistoric antiquities and an art collection.

The library holds about 1,000 manuscripts, and the state archives stand nearby. The famous Castle of Canossa lies close to Reggio. Regium once belonged to the Boii, and the consul Aemilius Lepidus reduced it to a colony, naming it Regium Lepidi, in 187 or 178 BC. The Treaty of Quiercy later included Reggio, the entry notes, and Cappelletti's churches of Italy with Saccani's bishops of Reggio supply its sources on a fertile Emilian see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reggio-di-cal:
